title: Measuring the Quantum Phase of Multiphoton Systems
abstract: The quantum phase of a multiparticle system has remained a long-standing mystery in quantum physics. The absence of a phase operator that faithfully represents this physical quantity has prevented the formulation of a meaningful uncertainty relation with particle number. Here, we resolve this problem by measuring, for the first time, the quantum phase of multiparticle systems containing up to fifteen particles. We achieve this through a new quantum state tomography scheme that combines homodyne interferometry with photon-number-resolving detection. This approach enables us to reconstruct complementary photon-number and phase representations and establish the corresponding number-phase uncertainty relation. Our measurements further provide access to the mutually unbiased basis of a multiparticle system, a fundamental resource for multiparticle quantum information processing. Furthermore, we report the spatially resolved characterization of the quantum phase. These results provide an operational framework for measuring quantum phase in multiparticle systems, with implications for fundamental quantum physics and scalable multiparticle quantum technologies.
one_liner: Homodyne interferometry and photon-number-resolving detection directly reconstruct quantum phase for systems of up to 15 photons.
why_it_matters: The method makes multiphoton phase operationally measurable and exposes a mutually unbiased basis useful for quantum-information protocols.
detailed_summary: The authors combine homodyne interferometry with photon-number-resolving detection to reconstruct complementary number and phase representations of multiphoton states. Measurements on systems containing up to 15 photons establish an operational number-phase uncertainty relation. The experiment also resolves spatial phase structure and accesses the mutually unbiased phase basis.
main_result: Quantum phase was measured and spatially characterized for multiphoton systems containing up to 15 photons.
application_angle: The tomography scheme could support phase-sensitive characterization and mutually unbiased measurements in multiphoton quantum processors and sensors.

title: Perturbation theory for quantum information quantities of Gaussian states
abstract: Many quantum-information tasks can benefit from Gaussian quantum resources, while their fundamental performance limits are characterized by quantum information quantities. However, a unified perturbation theory for these quantities directly within the Gaussian-state formalism has been lacking. We develop such a theory for the von Neumann entropy, quantum relative entropy, quantum Chernoff quantity, and quantum fidelity, using perturbations of the moments of a reference Gaussian state. Using general Fréchet-derivative identities, we derive compact second-order expressions for reference-state covariance matrices whose symplectic eigenvalues are all greater than $1/2$. We also show that the perturbative quantum Chernoff quantity is maximized at its symmetric point, yielding the quantum Chernoff exponent (QCE). We further show that symplectic eigenvalues equal to 1/2 can lead to slower asymptotic vanishing, potentially improving the corresponding fundamental performance limits. For reference-state covariance matrices containing symplectic eigenvalues both equal to and greater than 1/2, we identify sufficient conditions under which the former determine the leading covariance-matrix contributions, allowing the remaining modes to be traced out without changing the leading-order asymptotic scaling or the coefficient. Applying the framework to quantum illumination and incoherent-light sub-Rayleigh object discrimination, we recover known asymptotic QCEs directly within the Gaussian-state formalism. In the latter problem, the slower asymptotic vanishing explains the known quadratic scaling of the QCE with the source separation.
one_liner: A Gaussian-state perturbation framework yields second-order entropy, fidelity, relative-entropy, and Chernoff expressions.
why_it_matters: It provides tractable performance bounds for Gaussian sensing and discrimination, including quantum illumination and sub-Rayleigh imaging.
detailed_summary: The work develops perturbative expansions of several quantum-information quantities directly from Gaussian-state moments. Compact second-order formulas are obtained when all symplectic eigenvalues exceed one half, while modes at one half can produce slower leading-order decay. Applications recover known quantum Chernoff exponents for quantum illumination and incoherent-light sub-Rayleigh object discrimination.
main_result: The framework recovers established asymptotic discrimination limits and explains the quadratic Chernoff scaling with source separation in sub-Rayleigh imaging.
application_angle: The formulas enable efficient sensitivity and error-exponent analysis for Gaussian quantum sensors, receivers, and imaging systems.

title: Online Scheduling and Distribution of Quantum Circuits over Quantum Networks
abstract: Emerging quantum networks enable distributed quantum computing (DQC) by interconnecting modest, noisy quantum processors. However, practical deployments face tight memory budgets, probabilistic entanglement generation, and decoherence, all while serving multiple users. In realistic settings -- cloud execution, iterative/interactive workloads and concurrent jobs -- circuits do not arrive in a single batch but as a stream. This creates a fundamentally online problem: the system must react to stochastic arrivals, balance latency and throughput, and remain stable under varying loads without foresight of future jobs. We study Online Scheduling and Distribution of Quantum Circuits (OS-DQC) and formalize the online scheduling problem for quantum networks: circuits arrive over time and must be executed without knowledge of future arrivals. At each event time (arrival or completion), the system decides which waiting circuits to launch and how to place their qubits, while accounting for congestion from in-flight circuits and constraints due to finite memories and decoherence. The objective is to minimize the mean completion time and makespan under these physical and resource constraints.
one_liner: OS-DQC formalizes online placement and scheduling of streaming quantum circuits across resource-constrained quantum networks.
why_it_matters: The framework targets realistic distributed quantum clouds where stochastic arrivals, finite memories, entanglement delays, and decoherence interact.
detailed_summary: The paper formulates circuit distribution as an online scheduling problem in which jobs arrive without advance knowledge. At each arrival or completion event, the scheduler selects circuits and maps their qubits while accounting for occupied resources, finite quantum memories, probabilistic entanglement generation, and decoherence. The objectives are reduced mean completion time and makespan under changing load.
main_result: A physically constrained online formulation is introduced for jointly scheduling and placing streaming distributed quantum circuits.
application_angle: The model provides a foundation for runtime schedulers serving concurrent users on future distributed quantum-computing clouds.

title: How Quantum Is Light? Concepts, Measures, and Applications of Optical Quantumness
abstract: Quantum states are ultimately responsible for numerous counterintuitive phenomena that defy classical intuition. As the development of quantum technologies accelerates, our ability to harness these quantum resources becomes essential. This review addresses a fundamental question. How do we quantify the quantumness of a state, and which specific traits distinguish it from its classical counterparts? We examine quantumness through both theoretical and operational lenses, providing a clear framework for state characterization. Ultimately, we demonstrate that certifying quantumness is not just a theoretical exercise. It is a practical necessity for identifying, and realizing quantum advantage in real-world applications.
one_liner: This review organizes theoretical and operational measures for distinguishing genuinely quantum optical states from classical light.
why_it_matters: Reliable quantumness certification is essential for validating the optical resources behind claimed sensing or information-processing advantages.
detailed_summary: The review examines how optical quantumness can be defined, quantified, and experimentally certified. It connects formal state properties with operational tests and applications. The central emphasis is that resource certification is necessary to substantiate practical quantum advantage.
main_result: The article presents a unified conceptual and operational framework for assessing the quantumness of light.
application_angle: Its framework can guide experimental validation of optical resources used in quantum sensing, communication, and photonic processing.

title: Entanglement-enhanced Ramsey spectroscopy of broadband signals
abstract: The use of entanglement in sensing is often motivated by improved sensitivity arising from non-classical correlations among probes. For static signals, however, this quantum advantage in Ramsey spectroscopy with $N$ probes is known to be highly susceptible to dephasing, which severely limits the possible gain from entanglement. In contrast, we consider sensing of signals that vary in time. Considering the simplest example of dephasing by classical white noise, we show that entanglement allows a large increase in bandwidth when estimating the frequency components of a time-dependent signal. Without sacrificing any sensitivity, entanglement allows for an increase in bandwidth by a factor of $N$. Alternatively, when interrogation times are limited by the signal bandwidth rather than by dephasing, the average estimation uncertainty over a fixed bandwidth is reduced by a factor of $\sqrt{N}$ compared with separable states.
one_liner: Entangled probes expand Ramsey-spectroscopy bandwidth by N or reduce broadband estimation uncertainty by √N without losing sensitivity.
why_it_matters: The result identifies a robust quantum advantage for time-varying signals even when dephasing limits gains for static-field sensing.
detailed_summary: The study analyzes Ramsey estimation of time-dependent signals using N entangled probes under classical white-noise dephasing. At fixed sensitivity, entanglement increases the accessible bandwidth by a factor of N. When bandwidth rather than dephasing limits interrogation time, it lowers average uncertainty across a fixed band by a factor of √N relative to separable probes.
main_result: Entanglement yields an N-fold bandwidth increase or a √N reduction in broadband estimation uncertainty, depending on the operating constraint.
application_angle: The approach could improve wideband quantum spectroscopy and detection of rapidly varying electromagnetic or frequency signals.

title: A Dual-Uplink Dual-Satellite Architecture for Entanglement Distribution
abstract: Satellite-based quantum links are a promising enabler of long-distance entanglement distribution, overcoming the exponential losses of optical fibers. In uplink architectures, entangled photons are generated at ground stations and transmitted to orbiting satellites, reducing space-segment complexity but introducing significant atmospheric and geometric losses. Single-satellite dual-uplink configurations are additionally limited by the requirement of simultaneous visibility between both ground stations and the satellite. In this work, we investigate a dual-uplink dual-satellite network architecture and compare its performance with the single-satellite scheme under identical physical assumptions. The proposed topology introduces an inter-satellite link (ISL) that decouples the ground-station separation from the atmospheric uplink geometry. A realistic channel model is employed, incorporating geometric attenuation, atmospheric turbulence, background noise, and Bell-state measurement efficiency. The overall success probability and practical fidelity are evaluated as functions of satellite altitude and ground-station separation. Our results show that while the single-satellite configuration is suitable for regional-scale networks, it becomes infeasible for large separations due to geometric constraints. The proposed dual-satellite architecture mitigates this limitation and significantly extends the achievable communication distance, representing a key step toward scalable quantum internet infrastructures.
one_liner: A dual-uplink, dual-satellite topology uses an inter-satellite link to extend entanglement distribution beyond regional scales.
why_it_matters: Decoupling ground separation from a single satellite's visibility geometry addresses a central obstacle to global quantum-network coverage.
detailed_summary: The proposed architecture sends photons from two ground stations to separate satellites and connects the space nodes through an inter-satellite link. Its channel model includes geometric loss, atmospheric turbulence, background noise, and Bell-state-measurement efficiency. Calculated success probability and practical fidelity show that the dual-satellite topology remains viable at separations where single-satellite dual uplinks become geometrically infeasible.
main_result: Modeling shows that the dual-satellite architecture significantly extends entanglement-distribution distance relative to a single-satellite uplink scheme.
application_angle: The topology offers a scalable route toward long-distance and eventually global satellite-enabled quantum internet infrastructure.

title: Distributing Quantum Circuits Using Pre-Distributed Entanglement Pairs over Quantum Networks
abstract: Distributing quantum circuits across a network of quantum devices is a recent approach to improve the scalability of quantum computation. Entangled pairs of qubits distributed across network nodes are used as a communication resource for executing inter-node (remote) gates. However, establishing these entanglement pairs incurs significant latency, and doing so during the circuit's execution may lead to the decoherence of logical qubits. Instead, it may be beneficial to distribute certain entanglement pairs before the circuit is executed. Thus, we consider the problem of distributing a quantum circuit across a quantum network containing some pre-distributed entanglement pairs and seek to minimize the execution time of the circuit. We address this problem in three steps. First, given the quantum network and (optionally) a probability distribution over training circuits, we determine a set of pre-distributed entanglement pairs under a specified budget. Second, we compute a qubit-to-memory allocation that minimizes the expected execution time given these pre-distributed resources. Finally, we identify any additional entanglement pairs required during execution, generate them concurrently, and execute the circuit gates. We evaluate our methods on a broad range of benchmark circuits.
one_liner: Pre-distributed entanglement is optimized to reduce the execution time of quantum circuits partitioned across networked processors.
why_it_matters: The method targets a major distributed-computing bottleneck: generating remote-gate entanglement without leaving logical qubits waiting and decohering.
detailed_summary: The work formulates distributed circuit execution when a quantum network already contains a budgeted set of entangled qubit pairs. Its workflow selects which pairs to pre-distribute, maps circuit qubits to node memories to minimize expected runtime, and schedules additional pair generation concurrently during execution. The approach is evaluated across a broad set of benchmark circuits.
platform_or_system: Networked quantum processors with entangled links
main_result: A three-stage optimization framework uses pre-distributed and dynamically generated entanglement to shorten distributed quantum-circuit execution.
application_angle: The framework could improve throughput and reduce decoherence exposure in modular quantum computers and networked quantum data centers.

title: Multi-path Security in Quantum Networks with Trusted Nodes
abstract: Quantum communication networks promise information-theoretic security but this security collapses if intermediate relay nodes are compromised, a risk that grows sharply when compromised nodes cannot be identified. We address this twofold: first, we show that multi-path routing provides quantifiable protection against unidentified compromised nodes. Second, we provide a comprehensive statistical and graph-theoretic analysis of network and node security under compromise, covering full and partial node compromise, optimal placement of additional edges via an iterative method, and comparative hacking-probability analysis across network topologies. Together, these results identify the topology and multi-path routing strategy that most improves security for a given network. We apply this framework to quantum key distribution across multiple network topologies, demonstrating a scalable route to secure, reliable quantum communication under realistic, unidentified adversarial threats, without relying on quantum memory.
one_liner: Multi-path routing is quantified as a defense for trusted-node quantum networks containing unidentified compromised relays.
why_it_matters: It offers a memory-free way to retain measurable QKD security when operators cannot determine which trusted relay nodes have been breached.
detailed_summary: The authors combine statistical compromise models with graph-theoretic analysis to quantify network and node security under full or partial trusted-node compromise. They compare topologies, analyze hacking probabilities, and introduce an iterative procedure for placing additional edges. Applied to QKD networks, the framework identifies routing and topology choices that improve resilience without quantum memories.
main_result: The study establishes quantifiable multi-path protection and a topology-optimization framework against unidentified compromised relay nodes.
application_angle: Network operators can use the analysis to prioritize new links and routing policies for more resilient metropolitan or wide-area QKD deployments.

title: Demonstration of continuous non-invasive monitoring of plant metabolism using mid-infrared photoacoustic spectroscopy
abstract: Life is a rhythmic process driven by cellular and physiological mechanisms that allow plants to respond and adapt to their environment. In addition to natural fluctuations, plants are increasingly exposed to environmental stresses, mainly caused by climate change and anthropogenic pollution. Multiple approaches across different biological scales (gene, cell, metabolite, and physiology) have shed light on acclimation mechanisms but generally lack sufficient temporal resolution. Establishing a non-invasive and high-temporal-resolution monitoring method to measure plant activity across different conditions is therefore needed to fully assess how plant metabolism changes under stress. Here, we established a novel approach to perform continuous and non-invasive mid-infrared photoacoustic spectroscopy on vascular plants, with the aim of identifying and monitoring the chemical composition of peripheral tissues, including sap, over periods ranging from a few minutes to several months. We describe an experimental setup, the physics underlying its operation, and present a multi-day acquisition. Compared with controls, data enabled to identify a diurnal pattern, with peaks of approximately equal duration, that recurred consistently over the experiment. Estimations of the impact of instrumental and environmental fluctuations indicate that the signal amplitude and trends cannot be explained by instrumental drifts. The experiment thus demonstrated the detection of a signal associated with plant physiological activity. While its origins remain to be clarified, this preliminary experiment demonstrates the feasibility of the measurements and provides a basis for future developments.
one_liner: Mid-infrared photoacoustic spectroscopy continuously tracks plant tissue chemistry and reveals repeatable multi-day physiological rhythms.
why_it_matters: The non-invasive method provides temporal coverage from minutes to months, potentially exposing metabolic responses that destructive sampling misses.
detailed_summary: The study builds a mid-infrared photoacoustic setup for continuously probing the chemical composition of peripheral vascular-plant tissues, including sap-associated signals. A multi-day acquisition reveals recurring diurnal peaks of approximately equal duration relative to controls. Estimates of instrumental and environmental fluctuations indicate that drift alone cannot explain the observed amplitude and trends, although the signal's precise physiological origin remains unresolved.
main_result: The experiment demonstrates continuous, non-invasive detection of a reproducible signal associated with plant physiological activity over multiple days.
application_angle: The technique could support long-duration monitoring of crop metabolism and stress responses under climate, pollution, or controlled-growth conditions.

title: A Readout-Aware Theory of Approximate Heisenberg Propagation
abstract: Classical methods for computing quantum expectation values often propagate observables in the Heisenberg picture. To remain tractable, these methods rely on approximations that discard operator components during evolution. Yet the magnitude of these components alone does not determine the resulting expectation-value error, which also depends on their subsequent evolution and the input state. We develop \emph{generalized Pauli propagation}, a common algebraic framework encompassing Pauli propagation, Lie-algebraic simulation, and Krylov subspace methods. Using weighted commutator graphs, we derive exact identities that relate approximation errors to the signed contributions of omitted and discarded operator components. Our central result establishes \emph{delayed observability}, identifying conditions under which these contributions vanish at low orders in propagation time. We use this structure to develop finite-order error estimates and state-dependent selection rules. We further prove that retaining the symmetry-preserving part of a weak perturbation eliminates first-order expectation-value errors under suitable symmetry conditions. By revealing how approximation errors affect the desired expectation value, our framework provides a basis for more informative error analysis and the development of readout-aware simulation strategies.
one_liner: A unified, readout-aware theory explains when discarded operators do—or do not—produce errors in simulated quantum expectation values.
why_it_matters: Sharper state- and observable-dependent error estimates could reduce classical simulation cost while preserving the quantities relevant to experiments.
detailed_summary: Generalized Pauli propagation unifies Pauli, Lie-algebraic, and Krylov-subspace approaches to approximate Heisenberg evolution. Weighted commutator graphs yield exact identities connecting expectation-value error to signed contributions from omitted and later-discarded operator components. The authors derive delayed-observability conditions, finite-order estimates, state-dependent selection rules, and symmetry conditions that remove first-order errors from weak perturbations.
main_result: The theory shows that discarded operator components can remain unobservable at low orders and provides readout-specific rules for controlling their errors.
application_angle: Readout-aware truncation can make modeling quantum sensors and many-body experiments more efficient without demanding uniformly accurate operator evolution.

title: Sidewall Metrology Protocol for Superconducting Qubit Devices
abstract: Sidewall morphology is a potentially important factor influencing superconducting qubit performance, yet its quantitative characterization remains challenging due to the absence of standardized measurement protocols. In this work, we develop a scanning probe microscopy-based measurement framework for the quantitative characterization of superconducting qubit sidewalls. The framework introduces a refined root mean square lateral sidewall roughness descriptor and a new curvature-equivalent radius for quantifying vertical sidewall morphology. The descriptors and measurement procedures are applied to different components of qubit devices, forming the basis of a proposed sidewall characterization protocol. This provides a foundation for quantitative comparisons of fabrication processes across laboratories, enabling future investigations of correlations between sidewall geometry and qubit performance.
one_liner: Scanning-probe descriptors and procedures standardize quantitative sidewall metrology for superconducting-qubit device structures.
why_it_matters: Comparable sidewall metrics can help laboratories connect fabrication-induced geometry with qubit loss, variability, and process yield.
detailed_summary: The authors develop a scanning-probe-microscopy framework for characterizing sidewalls in superconducting-qubit device components. It introduces a refined RMS lateral-roughness descriptor and a curvature-equivalent radius for vertical morphology. Applying these measures to multiple device features provides the basis for a proposed cross-laboratory characterization protocol.
main_result: A quantitative protocol measures lateral sidewall roughness and vertical curvature using standardized scanning-probe descriptors.
application_angle: The protocol enables fabrication-process benchmarking and systematic studies of how etched geometry correlates with qubit coherence and performance.

title: The Fundamental Memory Ceiling of Noisy Quantum Reservoirs
abstract: Fresh qubits, not size, set how long a noisy quantum system can remember. With $k$ input qubits reinitialized per time step, the longest memory any reservoir can attain under depolarizing noise is $\exp[Θ(k)]$ time steps, whatever its size, dynamics, and input encoding. A universal upper bound and an explicit reservoir that attains the exponential scaling establish this optimal resource law. The bound depends on the dynamics only through the entropy that fresh qubits remove per time step, so it holds for any Markovian noisy dynamics without feedback, including measurement-free error correction.
one_liner: Under depolarizing noise, a quantum reservoir's maximum memory time scales exponentially with refreshed input qubits—not total system size.
why_it_matters: The result identifies qubit refresh and entropy removal as the fundamental resources governing memory in noisy quantum information processors.
detailed_summary: For reservoirs receiving k reinitialized input qubits per time step, the authors prove a universal memory upper bound of exp[Θ(k)], independent of reservoir size, dynamics, and encoding. They also construct an explicit reservoir attaining this exponential scaling, establishing optimality. The bound depends only on entropy removed by fresh qubits and extends to Markovian, feedback-free dynamics, including measurement-free error correction.
platform_or_system: Noisy quantum reservoirs with refreshed qubits
main_result: The work proves and saturates an exponential-in-k memory ceiling set by the number of qubits refreshed at each time step.
application_angle: The resource law guides hardware allocation for quantum reservoir computing, autonomous memories, and measurement-free error-correction architectures.

title: Strong-to-Weak Spontaneous Symmetry Breaking Transitions on a Quantum Processor
abstract: Mixed quantum states can exhibit unconventional forms of symmetry breaking without pure-state counterparts. A prominent example is strong-to-weak spontaneous symmetry breaking (SW-SSB), which cannot be diagnosed by observables linear in the density matrix. Here, we experimentally resolve finite-size critical signatures of SW-SSB transitions on a superconducting quantum processor. We develop a measurement protocol that combines quantum measurements with classical processing based on the known dephasing channel to reconstruct nonlinear mixed-state correlators. Using only two measurement settings, the protocol reconstructs fidelity, Rényi-2, and linear correlators, as well as string observables. Applying this approach to matrix-product states subjected to power-law-correlated dephasing, we observe finite-size crossings and scaling collapses in nonlinear correlators, accompanied by decaying linear correlations. We further map the estimated SW-SSB transition points across initial-state and channel parameters. Measurements of linear and Rényi-2 string observables further reveal signatures of mixed-state symmetry-protected topological (SPT) phases, with a nonlinear string-order crossover aligned with an independently estimated SW-SSB transition point. Our results establish a quantum-classical approach to probing SW-SSB critical behavior and mixed-state SPT order.
one_liner: A superconducting processor resolves finite-size signatures of strong-to-weak symmetry-breaking transitions in noisy mixed quantum states.
why_it_matters: The two-setting quantum-classical protocol makes nonlinear mixed-state criticality and topological order experimentally accessible on current processors.
detailed_summary: The experiment prepares matrix-product states on a superconducting quantum processor and subjects them to power-law-correlated dephasing. A two-setting measurement protocol, combined with classical knowledge of the channel, reconstructs fidelity, Rényi-2 and linear correlators, and string observables. Finite-size crossings and scaling collapses reveal SW-SSB critical behavior, while nonlinear string order provides evidence of mixed-state SPT structure.
main_result: The processor experimentally resolves finite-size SW-SSB transitions and associated mixed-state SPT signatures using only two measurement settings.
application_angle: The method enables efficient characterization of noise-driven phases and nonlinear order in near-term quantum processors.

title: Study of non-uniformity-induced structured spectrum in a tapered optical fiber through stimulated four-wave mixing
abstract: Tapered optical fibers offer tunable dispersion and a small mode area, yielding high nonlinearity, which makes them ideal for nonlinear and quantum optics. Because phase-matched four-wave mixing strongly depends on dispersion, the taper diameter becomes a key parameter. For sub-micrometer tapers, identifying the exact diameter is challenging. Here, we show that when seeding with a broad spectrum, stimulated four-wave mixing yields a comb-like spectrum that is directly linked to the overall taper profile opening possibility for non-destructive evaluation of sub-micron taper. Our model based on joint-spectral amplitude includes the phase accumulated over the fiber length.
one_liner: Broadband-seeded four-wave mixing converts submicron taper nonuniformity into a diagnostic comb-like optical spectrum.
why_it_matters: The approach could provide a nondestructive optical measurement of taper profiles that are difficult to determine by direct diameter metrology.
detailed_summary: The study analyzes stimulated four-wave mixing in a nonuniform tapered optical fiber driven by a broadband seed. Longitudinal diameter variations alter dispersion and accumulated phase, producing a structured, comb-like output spectrum tied to the full taper profile. A joint-spectral-amplitude model incorporates phase accumulation along the fiber to connect spectral features with geometry.
main_result: The work shows that stimulated four-wave-mixing spectra can encode the longitudinal profile of a nonuniform submicron fiber taper.
application_angle: This spectral technique offers a route to nondestructive quality control and geometric characterization of nanophotonic fiber devices.

title: Squeezing-type lower bounds on generalized metrological sensitivity
abstract: We introduce squeezing-type lower bounds for a hierarchy of variance bounds under specific unbiasedness constraints, which generalizes the quantum Cramér-Rao bound. Our construction directly extends standard squeezing coefficients to the corresponding generalized metrological sensitivities while retaining their experimentally accessible structure. We show how observables maximizing these bounds can be identified analytically within families of accessible observables. If arbitrary observables are accessible, the optimized squeezing-type bound recovers the exact generalized metrological sensitivity. These bounds provide efficient and experimentally viable characterizations of generalized metrological sensitivities that are especially relevant in finite-shot scenarios and in the transition from local to global parameter estimation.
one_liner: Experiment-friendly squeezing bounds estimate generalized metrological sensitivity under finite-shot and nonlocal estimation conditions.
why_it_matters: The framework extends accessible squeezing measurements beyond the standard quantum Cramér–Rao setting without requiring full state characterization.
detailed_summary: The authors derive squeezing-type lower bounds for a hierarchy of variance-based metrological sensitivities subject to specified unbiasedness constraints. Optimal witnesses can be found analytically within experimentally accessible observable families. When arbitrary observables are available, optimization recovers the exact generalized sensitivity, including regimes relevant to finite data and the transition from local to global estimation.
main_result: Optimized squeezing-type witnesses provide experimentally accessible lower bounds that become exact when unrestricted observables can be measured.
application_angle: The bounds can benchmark useful sensing resources with limited measurement settings and finite experimental shot budgets.

title: Self-Oscillating Photonic Frequency Comb for Sub-THz Local Oscillator Generation in Earth Observation Systems
abstract: Earth observation missions rely on microwave and sub-terahertz radiometry for retrieving atmospheric parameters such as temperature, humidity, and cloud properties, with the 183- and 229-GHz spectral regions being particularly relevant. Local-oscillator (LO) generation at these frequencies requires low phase noise and high frequency stability while meeting stringent size, weight, and power (SWaP) constraints. Conventional architectures employ dielectric resonator oscillators followed by cascaded frequency-multiplication stages, requiring dedicated generation chains for different frequency bands and increasing hardware complexity. Furthermore, frequency multiplication degrades the phase noise of the generated signal. This work proposes and numerically investigates a reconfigurable self-oscillating microwave photonic architecture for LO generation in Earth observation receivers. Cascaded Mach-Zehnder and phase modulation within an optoelectronic feedback loop generate an optical frequency comb with enhanced higher-order components. A combination of optical filters is used to select the required comb line. First, a conventional bandpass filter with a bandwidth of approximately 10 GHz isolates the spectral region containing the desired component, after which a narrowband dual cavity Bragg grating ring resonator (BGRR) with a bandwidth of approximately 3 MHz provides the final line selection. The selected comb line is then combined with an optical reference derived from the same laser and photodetected to generate the desired millimeter-wave or sub-terahertz signal through optical heterodyning. Numerical simulations are presented for 183- and 229-GHz generation, demonstrating the ability of the same underlying architecture to address multiple LO frequencies by tuning the OEO electrical filter to the appropriate oscillation frequency and selecting the corresponding comb order.
one_liner: A reconfigurable self-oscillating photonic comb architecture generates 183- and 229-GHz local-oscillator signals in simulation.
why_it_matters: One photonic source could replace multiple multiplied microwave chains while targeting lower complexity and better phase-noise performance.
detailed_summary: The proposed optoelectronic feedback loop uses cascaded Mach–Zehnder and phase modulation to enhance high-order optical-comb components. A roughly 10-GHz bandpass filter and a roughly 3-MHz dual-cavity Bragg-grating ring resonator isolate the desired line. Numerical simulations show reconfiguration between 183 and 229 GHz by tuning the electrical oscillation filter and selecting the appropriate comb order.
main_result: Simulations demonstrate a shared, tunable photonic architecture for generating 183- and 229-GHz local oscillators by optical heterodyning.
application_angle: The design targets compact, frequency-agile local oscillators for atmospheric radiometers under stringent spacecraft SWaP constraints.

title: Higher-order Parity Constraints for Quantum Approximate Optimization
abstract: The Parity Architecture was originally introduced in the context of quantum optimization algorithms to overcome hardware connectivity constraints. Here, we show that its benefits extend beyond this role by identifying specific parity transformations that enhance the success probability of the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) for optimization problems defined on hardware-native and sparse graphs. Numerical simulations suggest that this enhancement originates from the higher-order operators introduced by the Parity representation, which accelerate the propagation of correlations across the physical device. We investigate this mechanism for the Signed Max-Cut problem on 3-regular graph instances and demonstrate its practical relevance on IBM Heron quantum processors. QAOA parameters are first classically optimized on small training instances containing up to 14 vertices and subsequently transferred to larger instances executed on quantum hardware. We consider Signed Max-Cut instances of up to 40 vertices and find that, together with an error mitigation technique, the parity-based QAOA identifies the optimal solutions for all the considered 40-vertex instances, whereas the conventional QAOA fails under the same conditions.
one_liner: Higher-order parity constraints improve QAOA correlation spreading and solve tested 40-vertex Signed Max-Cut instances on IBM Heron hardware.
why_it_matters: The result suggests encoding choice can improve practical optimization performance beyond merely adapting problems to limited qubit connectivity.
detailed_summary: The parity representation introduces higher-order operators that simulations associate with faster correlation propagation across a device. Parameters optimized on training graphs of up to 14 vertices are transferred to larger Signed Max-Cut instances on IBM Heron processors. With error mitigation, parity-based QAOA finds optimal solutions for every tested 40-vertex instance, while conventional QAOA fails under the same conditions.
main_result: Parity-based QAOA with error mitigation identifies optimal solutions for all tested 40-vertex Signed Max-Cut instances.
application_angle: The method offers a hardware-relevant encoding strategy for improving variational optimization on sparse and native-connectivity graphs.

title: Two-qubit cryo-CMOS control of a spin register in diamond
abstract: Utility-scale quantum technologies will not only require a well-performing quantum platform, but also classical control hardware that is scalable, efficient, and meets the design requirements set by the quantum system of interest. One approach is the application of silicon CMOS technology, a highly scalable and mature technology, to design application-specific integrated circuits (ASIC) that are optimized for the quantum system. In this work, we present two-qubit control of electron and nuclear spins in NV centres in diamond, using a cryogenic CMOS qubit controller integrated with a diamond quantum device in a cryostat. Using Gate Set Tomography (GST) we characterize the performance of the single-qubit gates on both electron- and carbon nuclear spins, and analyze the limiting noise processes. We use dynamical decoupling to engineer a two-qubit gate, and estimate $F_\text{2q,avg} = 95(2)\%$ for the electron-nuclear two-qubit gate fidelity. Our demonstration of cryo-CMOS-driven two-qubit gates is a key step towards highly-integrated quantum devices based on colour centres.
one_liner: A cryogenic CMOS controller drives electron and carbon-nuclear spin qubits in diamond, including a 95(2)% electron–nuclear two-qubit gate.
why_it_matters: Integrating scalable CMOS control with color-center qubits addresses a major wiring, power, and packaging bottleneck for deployable quantum devices.
detailed_summary: A cryogenic CMOS ASIC integrated with a diamond device controls both the NV electron spin and a nearby carbon nuclear spin inside a cryostat. Gate Set Tomography characterizes single-qubit operations and identifies limiting noise processes. Dynamical decoupling engineers the coupled electron–nuclear gate, yielding an estimated average two-qubit fidelity of 95(2)%.
main_result: The integrated controller demonstrates single-qubit control and a 95(2)% average-fidelity electron–nuclear two-qubit gate in diamond.
application_angle: The architecture supports compact, highly integrated color-center processors and sensor nodes with scalable local control electronics.

title: Giant Rydberg Excitons Delineated as Relativistic Bound States
abstract: We examined the energy-momentum relationship of the valence band of Cu$_2$O, which has gained interest as an emerging solid host for giant Rydberg states. Our findings reveal a nonparabolic dispersion, described using the rest mass (0.570 times the free electron mass) and rescaled light speed ($1.6\times 10^5$ m/s), which draws parallels with relativistic theory for high-energy particles. We propose a straightforward expression for the bound-state energies of Rydberg excitons with finite quantum defects, whose energy scheme deviates from the hydrogenic series. This formulation identifies relativistic kinematics as the physical origin of quantum defects, offering a streamlined basis for future studies on complex many-body correlations.
one_liner: A relativistic-band model explains nonhydrogenic quantum defects in giant Rydberg excitons hosted by Cu2O.
why_it_matters: The compact model links semiconductor band dispersion to exciton spectra, improving the physical basis for designing and interpreting solid-state Rydberg platforms.
detailed_summary: The authors find that the Cu2O valence band follows a nonparabolic energy-momentum relation parameterized by an effective rest mass of 0.570 electron masses and a rescaled light speed of 1.6×10^5 m/s. They derive a bound-state expression for giant Rydberg excitons with finite quantum defects and attribute the departure from a hydrogenic spectrum to relativistic-like kinematics. The model offers a streamlined foundation for studying correlations among solid-state Rydberg excitations.
main_result: A relativistic effective-band description reproduces finite quantum defects and the resulting nonhydrogenic Rydberg-exciton energy series.
application_angle: A clearer spectral model can support the engineering of Cu2O Rydberg excitons for interacting quantum devices and many-body experiments.

title: End-to-End Optimization of Partial Fault Tolerance in Neutral-Atom Arrays
abstract: Fault-tolerant (FT) quantum computation offers a pathway to quantum advantage, but its realization is hindered by its significant overhead. The partially FT "STAR" architecture reduces the cost of universal computation at the price of relaxing FT requirements for non-Clifford operations, increasing exposure to hardware noise. Therefore, maximizing its performance and applicability demands careful co-design with the underlying hardware. In this work we investigate the co-design of the STAR architecture with neutral-atom platforms, connecting the underlying atomic physics to logical error modeling and application-level performance. At the physical level, we identify a favorable noise bias in $^{171}\mathrm{Yb}$ Rydberg gates, and show how it can be enhanced through error-selective pulse optimization. At the logical level, we identify an intrinsic error suppression mechanism, yielding vanishing logical coherent noise in leading order. Detailed circuit-level simulations of surface code implementations show more than an order of magnitude reduction in logical error relative to previous estimates. As a concrete target application, we focus on the Fermi-Hubbard model with periodic boundaries, for which we design a simulation circuit particularly suited to early implementations. We quantify the resource tradeoff of partially and fully FT approaches to gate synthesis, with the former showing approximately an order of magnitude reduction in state-injection depth, and an even larger reduction in Clifford resources. Comparing with classical and fully FT approaches, we identify regimes where partial fault tolerance provides both lower overheads and lower error rates. In our estimates, this is accessible with moderate error rates $p\sim 10^{-3}$ and a few thousand qubits, underlining that for these types of problems, partial FT approaches provide a compelling pathway to early quantum advantage.
one_liner: Hardware-aware optimization makes partial fault tolerance competitive for neutral-atom simulations using a few thousand qubits.
why_it_matters: It connects atomic gate physics, logical-error suppression, and application resources to identify experimentally plausible routes toward early quantum advantage.
detailed_summary: The study co-designs the partially fault-tolerant STAR architecture with 171Yb neutral-atom arrays, identifying a favorable Rydberg-gate noise bias that can be strengthened through error-selective pulse optimization. An intrinsic logical mechanism cancels leading-order coherent noise, while circuit-level surface-code simulations predict over an order-of-magnitude lower logical error than earlier estimates. For periodic Fermi-Hubbard simulation, partial fault tolerance reduces state-injection depth by roughly tenfold and cuts Clifford resources even further.
main_result: Partial fault tolerance is projected to outperform classical and fully fault-tolerant alternatives in accessible regimes near 10^-3 physical error and a few thousand qubits.
application_angle: The approach offers a lower-overhead path to useful Fermi-Hubbard simulations and potentially early quantum advantage on emerging neutral-atom processors.

title: KrMM Recurrences: HPC-Enhanced Estimators for Nonlinear Classical Shadows
abstract: While quantum technologies are rapidly evolving, near-term applications heavily rely on hybrid quantum-classical paradigms. Among these, the classical shadows framework has gained a lot of traction, not only for quantum information science, but also for the development and verification of quantum hardware. It allows to efficiently classically estimate many properties of quantum states from randomized measurements alone, a task that is otherwise intractable due to the destructive nature of measurements in quantum systems. There are, however, many properties of interest that are, due to their very problem formulation, not efficiently estimable. In this work, we identify a computational kernel occurring in estimators of polynomial functions, a class of problems that are in general computationally difficult to solve. We show that this structure allows a row-wise partition that, together with a custom SIMD vectorization, enables massive parallelization and can reduce the computational cost significantly. We show applicability and scalability of the approach on different tasks, and our results showcase that the approach allows high sequential throughput and close-to-ideal parallel scaling. The work thus provides a new way of identifying and exploiting structure in classical shadow estimators, resulting in practical advantages on inherently difficult problems.
one_liner: A partitioned, SIMD-vectorized kernel accelerates nonlinear classical-shadow estimators with near-ideal parallel scaling.
why_it_matters: Faster nonlinear estimators make randomized-measurement data more practical for quantum-state analysis and hardware verification at scale.
detailed_summary: The authors identify a recurring computational kernel in classical-shadow estimators for polynomial functions of quantum states. A row-wise data partition combined with custom SIMD vectorization exposes substantial fine- and coarse-grained parallelism. Benchmarks across several tasks show high sequential throughput and parallel scaling close to ideal for calculations that are otherwise computationally difficult.
platform_or_system: HPC processing of randomized quantum measurements
main_result: The KrMM recurrence formulation substantially reduces the classical cost of nonlinear shadow estimation while retaining strong multicore scalability.
application_angle: The method can accelerate state-property extraction, calibration, and verification workflows for increasingly large quantum experiments and processors.

title: Observation and control of polariton noise in a thermal Rydberg atom electrometer
abstract: The establishment of metrics and control of fundamental noise sources in quantum sensing is a long-standing goal in quantum science and technology. We report on the observation of polariton-mediated optical noise in a thermal Rydberg atom vapor and demonstrate its active control and suppression using a radio-frequency field in Rydberg electrometry. The noise exhibits structured amplification and reduction across the Rydberg electromagnetically induced transparency resonance. This reveals a nonlinear slow-light feedback mechanism in which the polariton medium stores and releases probe-field energy. We show that the reference radio-frequency field used in Rydberg heterodyne receivers can also tune the medium into an operating regime where high electromagnetic-field responsivity coincides with reduced optical noise. This operating-point control enables optimization of the electric-field sensitivity within the constraints imposed by Rydberg-polariton physics. These results establish polariton noise as a previously unrecognized intrinsic noise source in thermal Rydberg vapors and the corresponding control method as a crucial aspect of continued efforts to achieve fundamental sensitivity limits in Rydberg electrometry.
one_liner: A reference RF field actively suppresses intrinsic polariton optical noise while preserving high responsivity in a thermal Rydberg electrometer.
why_it_matters: Identifying and controlling this previously unrecognized noise source opens a direct route toward improved sensitivity in vapor-cell RF receivers.
detailed_summary: The experiment observes structured optical-noise amplification and suppression across a Rydberg electromagnetically induced transparency resonance in a thermal atomic vapor. The behavior is attributed to nonlinear slow-light feedback in which the polariton medium stores and releases probe energy. By tuning the heterodyne reference RF field, the authors reach operating points combining reduced optical noise with high electric-field responsivity.
main_result: Radio-frequency control suppresses polariton-mediated optical noise and optimizes electric-field sensitivity without sacrificing strong responsivity.
application_angle: The control strategy can improve practical atomic RF sensors, heterodyne receivers, and calibration protocols approaching fundamental sensitivity limits.

title: Exploring ground state phase diagrams of Rydberg atom arrays with finite projected entangled-pair states
abstract: Rydberg atom arrays (RAA) have been advocated as a promising avenue for the quantum simulation of different exotic quantum states. Numerical predictions for the ground state properties of this experimental platform can, however, be challenging in two-dimensional setups. In particular, faithfully treating long-range interactions is often crucial for distinguishing the fate of competing phases, but it usually comes at considerable cost. Projected entangled-pair states (PEPS), optimized via a sampling-based approach, have been shown to deal with such terms on the same ground as shorter-range ones. In this work, we employ these tools to investigate debated physical questions in different frustrated geometries of RAA, from the emergence of spin-glass physics on the Kagomé lattice to topological order beyond the PXP model on the Ruby lattice. By that, we contribute to establishing PEPS as well-suited tools for creating digital twins of RAA experiments.
one_liner: Finite PEPS simulations provide digital twins for frustrated 2D Rydberg arrays with faithfully retained long-range interactions.
why_it_matters: Reliable numerical twins can distinguish competing glassy and topological phases and guide measurements on programmable Rydberg simulators.
detailed_summary: The work applies sampling-optimized finite projected entangled-pair states to two-dimensional Rydberg-atom arrays, treating long-range interactions on the same footing as local terms. It examines disputed ground-state behavior, including possible spin-glass physics on the Kagome lattice and topological order beyond the PXP model on the Ruby lattice. The results position PEPS calculations as practical digital twins for frustrated Rydberg-array experiments.
main_result: Finite PEPS can resolve competing ground-state phases in realistic Rydberg geometries while explicitly retaining long-range interactions.
application_angle: The simulations can guide array geometry, parameter scans, and phase-detection protocols before costly experiments on programmable analog quantum hardware.

title: Single-Mode Laser Arrays with Size-Invariant Loss Discrimination
abstract: In conventional coupled oscillator lattices and laser arrays, expanding the active volume inevitably causes spectral crowding and degrades spatial uniformity, posing a long-standing barrier to high-power single-mode operation. We uncover a dissipative selection mechanism in sparse star networks that decouples modal selectivity from lattice size constraints. By engineering dissipative auxiliary couplings between a central hub and N peripheral resonators, the system establishes an exact star-Laplacian symmetry. This enforces a target eigenstate that is immune to all lossy channels while maintaining equal amplitude across all main nodes. All competing eigenstates break this symmetry, driving the auxiliary loss and opening a persistent, size-independent modal loss gap that prevents multi-mode competition. Realistic microring simulations validate the robustness of this dark-state isolation under electromagnetic dispersion and mechanism extension to arbitrary arrays is allowed when meets the system's exceptional point. By exploiting graph topology to bypass multi-mode competition, this work establishes a general route toward scalable high-power single-supermode laser arrays and robust state selection in coupled non-Hermitian systems.
one_liner: A sparse star-coupled laser network maintains an exact single supermode and a size-independent loss gap as the array grows.
why_it_matters: Size-invariant mode discrimination addresses spectral crowding and nonuniformity that limit scalable, high-power coherent laser arrays.
detailed_summary: The proposed architecture couples a central hub to peripheral resonators through dissipative auxiliary channels, producing an exact star-Laplacian symmetry. Its target dark eigenstate has equal amplitude across the main nodes and remains immune to auxiliary loss, whereas competing modes activate lossy channels. Microring simulations indicate that the resulting modal loss gap persists with array size and remains robust to electromagnetic dispersion.
main_result: The star-network design preserves uniform single-supermode operation with a modal loss gap that does not shrink as more lasers are added.
application_angle: The topology could enable scalable coherent high-power laser arrays and robust mode selection in integrated non-Hermitian photonic circuits.

title: Proximity Transient Absorption in van der Waals Heterostructures
abstract: Transient absorption spectroscopy is a widely used technique for investigating ultrafast electronic dynamics, where transient optical signals are generally interpreted as arising from excitations within the material hosting the probed optical transition. A distinct form of transient absorption spectroscopy, termed proximity transient absorption (PTA), is demonstrated, in which the probed optical transition and the monitored photoexcited carriers reside in different materials. Using graphene/hBN/WS$_2$ heterostructures, photoexcited carriers in graphene induce a strong transient optical response at the excitonic resonance of a WS$_2$ monolayer through Coulomb screening, even when the two layers remain electronically isolated by an atomically thin hBN spacer. The resulting signal follows the carrier dynamics of graphene rather than those of WS$_2$, demonstrating that the WS$_2$ exciton acts as an optical transducer of electronic processes in a neighboring material. The signal decreases systematically with increasing hBN thickness, confirming its proximity origin while remaining substantial for separations approaching 2 nm. PTA provides a noncontact approach for optically modulating one material using photoexcited carriers in another and enables probing of carrier dynamics in materials that are otherwise difficult to investigate directly. More broadly, PTA establishes a new modality of ultrafast spectroscopy and reveals that transient optical signals in van der Waals heterostructures can originate from excitations residing in spatially separated layers.
one_liner: A WS₂ exciton optically tracks ultrafast carrier dynamics in nearby, electronically isolated graphene through Coulomb screening.
why_it_matters: Proximity transient absorption enables noncontact ultrafast probing and modulation of materials whose carrier dynamics are difficult to access directly.
detailed_summary: In graphene/hBN/WS₂ heterostructures, photoexcited graphene carriers modify the WS₂ excitonic resonance through Coulomb screening despite electronic isolation by hBN. The transient response follows graphene carrier dynamics and remains substantial at layer separations approaching 2 nm. Its systematic reduction with spacer thickness supports a proximity-mediated origin.
main_result: The work demonstrates proximity transient absorption, using a WS₂ exciton as an optical transducer for carrier dynamics in adjacent graphene.
application_angle: The method could provide contact-free ultrafast diagnostics and optical control for buried or optically inaccessible two-dimensional materials.

title: PPT-assisted capacities of bosonic Gaussian channels
abstract: We determine the exact quantum communication and entanglement-distribution capacities of three fundamental bosonic channels, namely thermal loss, thermal amplification and additive Gaussian noise, assisted by operations that completely preserve positive partial transpose (PPT). These operations are more powerful than local operations and classical communication (LOCC), but cannot generate distillable entanglement on their own. For thermal loss, the unconstrained capacity coincides with the Pirandola-Laurenza-Ottaviani-Banchi (PLOB) bound throughout the non-entanglement-breaking regime. The corresponding upper bounds are also attained for thermal amplification and additive noise. We extend these results to energy-constrained communication, establishing exact capacities for all three channels at every prescribed mean input energy. Our results solve a class of bosonic capacity problems under PPT assistance and establish exact benchmarks for determining whether the same communication rates can be achieved via LOCC alone.
one_liner: Exact PPT-assisted quantum and entanglement capacities are derived for three fundamental bosonic Gaussian channels.
why_it_matters: The results provide exact energy-dependent benchmarks for judging how closely practical LOCC protocols approach ultimate bosonic communication rates.
detailed_summary: The authors determine exact PPT-assisted capacities for thermal-loss, thermal-amplification, and additive-Gaussian-noise channels. For thermal loss, the unconstrained result equals the PLOB bound throughout the non-entanglement-breaking regime. Exact capacities are also established for every prescribed mean input energy across all three channel families.
main_result: PPT-assisted quantum communication and entanglement-distribution capacities are solved exactly with and without input-energy constraints.
application_angle: These formulas set rigorous performance targets for optical and microwave quantum links and for assessing whether LOCC protocols are capacity-achieving.

title: Correlated decoding loses the surface code's effective distance below threshold
abstract: Correlated decoding improves matching and clustering surface-code decoders by reweighting one decoding subgraph conditioned on the other's correction. We show that standard reweighting can cause correlated decoders to fail on size-$(d-1)/2$ fault configurations that a distance-$d$ code should correct, reducing error suppression deep below threshold. Under circuit-level noise, a single first-pass edge can discount several correlated edges, even though their joint occurrence requires additional independent faults, so the decoder favors an over-discounted correction. Regularizing the reweighting rule restores the nominal distance scaling and a clear correlated-decoding advantage.
one_liner: Standard correlated reweighting can reduce a surface-code decoder's effective distance, while regularization restores nominal scaling.
why_it_matters: The finding exposes a hidden low-noise failure mode in practical decoders and supplies a route to retain both code distance and correlation gains.
detailed_summary: The analysis identifies fault configurations of size (d−1)/2 that defeat standard correlated decoders for a distance-d surface code. Under circuit-level noise, one first-pass edge can excessively discount several correlated edges, favoring a correction whose true fault cost is higher. Regularizing the reweighting prevents this pathology and recovers nominal distance scaling.
main_result: A regularized correlated-decoding rule restores expected distance scaling while preserving a clear decoding advantage.
application_angle: The result informs reliable decoder design for low-logical-error superconducting and other surface-code quantum processors.

title: Nambu-Goldstone Bosons and Quantum Fisher Information
abstract: The quantum Fisher matrix and geometric tensor are powerful tools for quantifying the nature of quantum systems. Unfortunately, the formalism needed to compute these quantities is opaque and has limited the development of physical intuition for their behavior, even in the ground state. For quantum systems with continuous symmetries, we know the ground state can be understood in a model-independent and intuitive way from the correlation functions of conserved currents and charges. In this paper, we demonstrate an equivalence between the quantum Fisher matrix associated with the ground states of systems with continuous symmetries and the Nambu-Goldstone. bosons produced by broken generators. We will show that the information metric defined by the Fisher matrix is the same as the Zamolodchikov metric that defines the coset space of the system. Next we show that the Uhlmann curvature associated with multi-parameter estimation is the same as the charge density matrix that defines the difference between type-A and type-B Nambu-Goldstone bosons. We demonstrate these connections in several examples and discuss the generalization to finite temperature.
one_liner: Ground-state quantum Fisher geometry is linked directly to Nambu–Goldstone modes and continuous-symmetry breaking.
why_it_matters: The framework gives physical intuition for multiparameter quantum sensitivity and connects metrological geometry to measurable symmetry and charge structure.
detailed_summary: The work equates the ground-state quantum Fisher matrix for continuously symmetric systems with the Nambu–Goldstone sector generated by broken symmetries. It identifies the information metric with the Zamolodchikov metric on the coset space. The Uhlmann curvature is further related to the charge-density matrix distinguishing type-A and type-B modes, with finite-temperature extensions discussed.
main_result: Quantum Fisher geometry and multiparameter curvature are expressed through Nambu–Goldstone modes, coset geometry, and broken-charge densities.
application_angle: These relations may guide the identification and optimization of symmetry-enhanced quantum sensors and multiparameter estimation protocols.

title: Active isolation of transmon readout with a tunable inductive bridge
abstract: Scalable superconducting quantum computation requires fast, high-fidelity readout. Currently, this is assisted through cryogenic amplification of the readout signal. In traditional dispersive readout schemes, the amplifiers that are used to provide high signal-to-noise ratio also generate thermal noise that can decohere the qubits, demanding additional ferrite-based isolators to suppress this noise. Here, we integrate a chip-scale microwave switch, the tunable inductive bridge, into the readout chain of a fixed-frequency transmon. Flux-pulsing the switch, such that it transmits only during the readout, did not make a discernable difference to qubit coherence, residual excited-state population, or readout fidelity metrics. By injecting broadband noise that mimics amplifier thermal photons, we show that the switch suppresses the resulting qubit dephasing by more than $30$~dB, consistent with its independently measured on-off ratio, establishing it as a potential chip-based integrated replacement for readout-chain isolators.
one_liner: A flux-pulsed chip-scale inductive bridge suppresses amplifier-like transmon dephasing by more than 30 dB.
why_it_matters: The switch offers a compact route to replacing bulky ferrite isolators without measurably degrading coherence, state population, or readout fidelity.
detailed_summary: A tunable inductive bridge was integrated into the dispersive readout chain of a fixed-frequency transmon and opened only during measurement. Flux pulsing produced no discernible change in coherence, residual excitation, or readout-fidelity metrics. With injected broadband noise representing amplifier thermal photons, the device reduced induced dephasing by over 30 dB, matching its measured on-off ratio.
main_result: The integrated microwave switch provides over 30 dB of active noise isolation while maintaining normal qubit and readout performance.
application_angle: Chip-scale active isolation could reduce cryogenic volume, magnetic components, and integration barriers in scalable superconducting processors.

title: Controlling Optical Quantum Interference with Plasmonic Metasurfaces
abstract: The ability to efficiently control optical quantum interference by the same device is a challenging task that promises to enable key operations in quantum information processing. Here, we tackle this problem by presenting a composite quantum plasmonic metasurface operating as an ultrathin non-unitary beamsplitter capable of achieving both single photon bosonic bunching and fermionic anti-bunching interference just by varying the incident photons frequency or changing the design dimensions. The presented metasurface combines a plasmonic grating corrugated by periodic nanoslits that can achieve extraordinary optical transmission with additional nanostripes on top forming nanocavities characterized by localized gap plasmon resonances. The photon-photon interactions are analyzed based on calculating the quantum coalescence metric which accurately portrays the obtained bunching or anti-bunching quantum interference. The presented quantum interference operation is applicable to both fundamental non-classical light interactions and in the design of more applied quantum optical logic gates used in quantum computing and communications.
one_liner: An ultrathin plasmonic metasurface switches between two-photon bunching and antibunching through frequency or geometry.
why_it_matters: A single nanoscale, non-unitary beamsplitter could compactly program distinct quantum-interference operations for photonic processing.
detailed_summary: The proposed composite metasurface combines an extraordinary-transmission nanoslit grating with nanostripes forming localized gap-plasmon cavities. Its non-unitary beamsplitter response supports either bosonic bunching or fermionic-like antibunching depending on photon frequency or device dimensions. A quantum coalescence metric is used to quantify the predicted two-photon behavior.
main_result: The design enables tunable bunching and antibunching quantum interference within the same ultrathin plasmonic device.
application_angle: The metasurface could serve as a compact element for quantum optical logic, interference control, and communication photonics.

title: Time-resolved Rydberg dynamics in molecules
abstract: We develop a general theoretical framework for the ultrafast dynamics of coherently populated autoionizing Rydberg states in molecules, whose coherent decay results in asymmetric Fano line shapes produced by interference between resonant autoionization and direct ionization. The asymmetric line shapes form in the photoelectron continuum during the autoionization lifetime of the decreasing Rydberg population. By parameterizing autoionization resonances and solving the time-dependent Schrödinger equation, we model the buildup of the Fano profile together with the decline of the coherently excited Rydberg-state population. We compare our calculated photoelectron yields with the XUV-pump--IR-probe photoemission experiment of Biswas et al., Phys. Rev. A 110, 043106 (2024), in which neutral ground-state CO$_2$ molecules are excited by an XUV pulse to the Henning sharp and diffuse Rydberg series and subsequently ionized by the delayed IR pulse. Based on our numerically modeled photoelectron yields, we analyze two complementary processes: (i) photoemission into the $X^2Π_g$ continuum of residual CO$_2^+$ ions, which exposes interferences between direct photoionization and excited-state autoionization, and (ii) IR-induced photoemission into the CO$_2^+$[$B^2Σ_u^+$] continuum, which reveals quantum beats between Rydberg states. Our close-coupling model provides a versatile, extendable framework for tracking molecular Rydberg-state relaxation and, more generally, light-driven coherent dynamics in complex quantum systems.
one_liner: A time-dependent close-coupling model resolves how molecular autoionization builds Fano profiles and Rydberg-state quantum beats.
why_it_matters: The framework connects ultrafast photoelectron observables to coherent molecular relaxation, supporting time-resolved control and diagnosis of complex quantum states.
detailed_summary: The authors parameterize autoionizing resonances and solve the time-dependent Schrödinger equation to follow coherent Rydberg populations and continuum photoelectron yields. Applied to XUV-pump–IR-probe measurements on CO2, the model reproduces the formation of asymmetric Fano profiles in the X2Πg continuum. It also identifies quantum beats between Rydberg states through IR-induced emission into the B2Σu+ ionic continuum.
platform_or_system: XUV–IR pump-probe spectroscopy of molecular CO2
main_result: The model jointly tracks Rydberg-state decay, time-dependent Fano-profile formation, and experimentally observable quantum beats.
application_angle: It provides a practical analysis framework for extracting coherent relaxation dynamics from ultrafast molecular photoemission experiments.

title: Quantum-Seeded Distributed Post-Quantum Group Signatures for 5G V2X Communications
abstract: Vehicle-to-Everything (V2X) communications rely on elliptic-curve signatures that a quantum adversary breaks and on pseudonym certificates whose anonymity rests on rotation rate, not cryptography. This work presents qDGSP, a post-quantum V2X infrastructure: a hash-based dynamic group signature scheme (DGSP, over SPHINCS+ and WOTS+) distributed between a central controller and roadside verifiers. Group keys derive deterministically from quantum key distribution (QKD) seeds served over the ETSI GS QKD 014 interface, so no group-signature secret crosses the classical channel. qDGSP-EA (Ephemeral Association) binds an ephemeral ML-DSA-65 key to one group signature per 5G cell: messages remain unlinkable across cells, linkable within one. On a testbed with emulated 5G links, median end-to-end latency stayed within the 100ms ETSI budget for every variant. The qDGSP-EA intra-cell DENM matched the NIST ML-DSA-65 baseline on the wire, and under load EA mode raised delivery from roughly 78% to 93%.
one_liner: A QKD-seeded, hash-based group-signature infrastructure delivers post-quantum authentication and controlled anonymity for 5G V2X.
why_it_matters: It combines quantum-derived keys, post-quantum signatures, and cellular-scale privacy while meeting the 100 ms latency target in an emulated 5G testbed.
detailed_summary: qDGSP distributes hash-based dynamic group signing between a central controller and roadside verifiers, with group keys deterministically derived from QKD seeds through ETSI GS QKD 014. Its ephemeral-association mode binds an ML-DSA-65 key to one group signature per 5G cell, enabling within-cell linkability but cross-cell unlinkability. In an emulated 5G testbed, all variants remained below the 100 ms ETSI latency budget, while the EA mode increased delivery under load from about 78% to 93%.
main_result: The system achieved post-quantum group authentication within the 100 ms V2X budget and improved loaded-network delivery to roughly 93%.
application_angle: The architecture targets deployable quantum-safe vehicle authentication with privacy properties compatible with cellular mobility.

title: Orchestrating Key Scarcity: Global Capacity Allocation in Hybrid QKD-PQC Networks
abstract: This article presents a Distributed Key Management System (DKMS) that provisions quantum-safe symmetric encryption keys to applications across a network. To overcome the distance and rate limitations inherent to Quantum Key Distribution (QKD), the architecture adopts a hybrid design: it utilizes multi-hop trusted relays for physical key transport, while applying an end-to-end Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) layer to ensure the relayed key material remains strictly protected from intermediate nodes. Because QKD transforms key generation into a scarce physical resource, managing unpredictable application demands poses a critical capacity allocation problem. The core contribution of this work is an SDN-driven control plane that globally orchestrates the network. Rather than relying on vulnerable hop-by-hop capacity reservations, a central controller simultaneously computes optimal filling rates and multipath routing for all per-peer key buffers. This global orchestration ensures that no application is starved and that all key buffers synchronize their filling processes. Evaluated on a Kubernetes-based digital twin across five distinct network topologies, the controller successfully filled all key buffers to capacity in under six minutes. Furthermore, under deliberately excessive demand, the network demonstrated graceful degradation, safely rejecting excess requests through controlled rate-limiting rather than experiencing catastrophic failure.
one_liner: An SDN controller globally allocates scarce QKD capacity through synchronized buffer filling, multipath routing, and controlled rate limiting.
why_it_matters: Global orchestration prevents application starvation and makes hybrid QKD-PQC networks behave predictably when physical key supply cannot meet demand.
detailed_summary: The proposed distributed key-management system transports QKD-derived material through multi-hop trusted relays while adding end-to-end PQC protection against intermediate-node exposure. A central SDN controller jointly optimizes filling rates and multipath routes for all peer-key buffers rather than reserving capacity hop by hop. Across five Kubernetes-based digital-twin topologies, every buffer reached capacity within six minutes; excessive requests were safely rejected through rate limiting.
main_result: Global optimization filled all simulated key buffers in under six minutes and maintained stable service under deliberately excessive demand.
application_angle: The controller offers an operational path for sharing limited QKD resources fairly across many applications and network routes.

title: Field demonstration of a self-contained 10 km mobile-to-ground quantum network node via common-aperture co-propagation
abstract: In this work, we demonstrate a dual-function, common-aperture free-space optical system that simultaneously supports decoy-state BB84 quantum key distribution (QKD) at 803 nm and bidirectional classical laser communication at 640/660 nm over a 10.31 km terrestrial link from a mobile platform to a stationary ground station. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first field demonstration of a fully integrated common-aperture architecture where a co-propagating classical optical link simultaneously performs full QKD post-processing and ecrypted payload transmission over a 10 km atmospheric channel. The classical link utilizes Manchester-coded on-off keying (MC-OOK) at 10 MHz, achieving a packet error rate of $\sim$ 0.4 $\%$ (estimated bit error rate (BER) of 3.13 $\times$ 10$^{-5}$) with hardware-based self-synchronization and error-packet retransmission. Over the 10.31 km link, the QKD system achieved an average quantum bit error rate (QBER) of 2.512 $\%$ and an average secret key rate of 644 bps using rate-adaptive low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes. Finally, using the distilled keys, real-time AES-256 encrypted image transmission was executed over the co-aligned classical optical channel, proving the feasibility of a completely self-contained, jam resistant mobile quantum optical network.
one_liner: A mobile common-aperture terminal combines decoy-state BB84, classical optical networking, and encrypted payload delivery over 10.31 km.
why_it_matters: The field test integrates key generation, post-processing, communications, and AES-encrypted data in one mobile-to-ground free-space optical node.
detailed_summary: The self-contained terminal co-propagates 803 nm decoy-state BB84 signals with bidirectional 640/660 nm classical channels through a shared aperture. Over a 10.31 km atmospheric link, it achieved an average QBER of 2.512% and a 644 bps secret-key rate using rate-adaptive LDPC reconciliation. The 10 MHz Manchester-coded classical link had about 0.4% packet errors, and the distilled keys supported real-time AES-256 encrypted image transfer.
main_result: The integrated 10.31 km field link generated 644 bps of secret key and used it for real-time encrypted image transmission.
