application_angle: The compact architecture supports mobile, self-contained, and potentially jam-resistant secure optical networking without a separate post-processing link.

title: Engineering \(XY\) and \(ZZ\) interactions between two remote superconducting qubits via a multimode waveguide
abstract: Waveguides provide a flexible platform for long-range interactions between superconducting qubits. Here, we study how to engineer the effective \(XY\) and \(ZZ\) interactions between two qubits via qubit frequency assignments and multimode interference determined by the mode configuration and standing-wave parities of a finite multimode waveguide. For a single-mode waveguide, we find that \(XY\) and \(ZZ\) interactions cannot be simultaneously suppressed to zero and the residual qubit-qubit coupling always exists. For example, the \(XY\) interaction may be suppressed to a negligible level when two qubits and the waveguide mode satisfy the two-photon resonant condition, but the \(ZZ\) interaction cannot be switched off. For multimode configurations within the central dispersive window, the engineered interaction types are very different for odd and even numbers of modes. Even-mode configurations can readily produce strong \(XY\) interactions, whereas odd-mode configurations can strongly suppress the \(XY\) interaction while retaining a finite \(ZZ\) interaction. Full-Hamiltonian simulations of minimal two- and three-mode configurations confirm \(XY\)-dominated SWAP dynamics and \(ZZ\)-dominated CZ-type dynamics, respectively. These results establish a frequency assignment criterion of qubits and waveguide modes for selectively engineering long-range qubit-qubit interaction types induced by the waveguide with finite multimode.
one_liner: Multimode-waveguide parity and frequency assignment selectively produce long-range XY or ZZ coupling between remote superconducting qubits.
why_it_matters: Selectable remote interactions could simplify modular superconducting processors by enabling SWAP- and CZ-type operations through the same waveguide bus.
detailed_summary: The study derives how qubit frequencies, waveguide-mode frequencies, standing-wave parity, and multimode interference determine effective XY and ZZ interactions. A single mode cannot eliminate both couplings simultaneously, whereas even-mode configurations favor strong XY exchange and odd-mode configurations can suppress XY while retaining ZZ. Full-Hamiltonian simulations of two- and three-mode cases respectively show XY-dominated SWAP dynamics and ZZ-dominated CZ-type dynamics.
platform_or_system: Remote superconducting qubits coupled by a finite multimode waveguide
main_result: Mode-parity and frequency-selection rules enable either XY-dominated state exchange or ZZ-dominated controlled-phase dynamics between remote qubits.
application_angle: The design rules provide a route to programmable long-range two-qubit interactions in distributed or modular superconducting hardware.

title: Low-nonlinearity advantage of hollow-core fiber for wavelength multiplexing of quantum entanglement and classical DWDM signals
abstract: Coexistence of classical and quantum light in optical fiber is a key requirement for scalable quantum networks. However, it is fundamentally limited by nonlinear crosstalk from intense classical signals. Hollow-core fiber (HCF), with its intrinsically low optical nonlinearity, offers a promising solution. Here, we experimentally demonstrate the coexistence of polarization-entangled photons with dense wavelength-division multiplexed (DWDM) classical signals with a total launch power of 11.2 dBm, and perform a direct comparison between equal-length single-mode fiber (SMF) and photonic-bandgap-based HCF deployed in a campus network. We observe that HCF suppresses background noise by approximately two orders of magnitude compared to SMF, while preserving high-fidelity entanglement distribution. Our results provide clear experimental evidence of the advantage of HCF and establish its potential as a transmission medium.
one_liner: Hollow-core fiber suppresses classical-channel noise by about 100-fold while carrying entangled photons alongside 11.2 dBm DWDM traffic.
why_it_matters: The campus-network experiment shows that low-nonlinearity fiber can preserve entanglement under classical launch powers that strongly contaminate standard fiber.
detailed_summary: The experiment co-transmits polarization-entangled photons and dense wavelength-division-multiplexed classical channels at 11.2 dBm total launch power. Equal-length photonic-bandgap hollow-core fiber and conventional single-mode fiber are compared in a deployed campus network. The hollow-core link reduces background noise by approximately two orders of magnitude relative to single-mode fiber while retaining high-fidelity entanglement distribution.
main_result: Hollow-core fiber provided roughly 100-fold lower coexistence noise than standard single-mode fiber while preserving entanglement fidelity.
application_angle: It could enable quantum channels to share installed network routes with high-power classical DWDM traffic using fewer isolation constraints.

title: Hybrid Lattice Surgery between Smooth Boundaries
abstract: We develop smooth hybrid lattice surgery for group surface codes, enabling joint logical measurements through merge and split operations along smooth boundaries. The code patches may correspond to identical or different finite groups, including non-Abelian groups. Our central result is that smooth merge and split realize a logical $K$-coset measurement, where $K$ is the subgroup defining the interface. This generalizes the joint logical parity measurement of ordinary surface codes. Using a tensor-network representation, we derive explicit measurement circuits and develop procedures for correcting nonidentity measurement outcomes. We illustrate the framework through a generalized controlled multiplication gate between group surface codes and protocols for preparing the $T$, $CZ$, $CCX$, and $CS$ magic states, producing resources encoded in one or more $\mathbb{Z}_2$ surface code patches. Our results show how smooth hybrid lattice surgery broadens the range of logical operations available for group surface codes.
one_liner: Smooth hybrid lattice surgery enables joint logical K-coset measurements between identical or different group surface codes.
why_it_matters: The scheme expands fault-tolerant logical operations across heterogeneous and non-Abelian codes while providing circuits for gates and magic-state preparation.
detailed_summary: The authors formulate merge and split operations along smooth interfaces between group surface-code patches, including patches based on different finite groups. They show that the protocol implements a logical K-coset measurement and derive explicit tensor-network-based measurement and outcome-correction circuits. Applications include controlled multiplication and preparation of encoded T, CZ, CCX, and CS resource states.
main_result: Smooth hybrid lattice surgery realizes correctable logical K-coset measurements and supports several encoded gates and magic-state protocols.
application_angle: It offers a route to broader fault-tolerant instruction sets and interoperable logical operations in topological quantum processors.

title: Fate of Discrete Time Crystals in Finite-Size Cavity QED Systems
abstract: It has been shown that Discrete Time Crystal (DTC) behavior may arise in the periodically driven, open Dicke model in the thermodynamic limit ($N \rightarrow \infty$). In this work, we demonstrate that finite $N$ non-mean-field fluctuations in this model can lead to decay rates and amplitudes of transient DTCs that display a non-trivial non-monotonic behavior with an increasing number of atoms. We show that the second-order cumulant expansion fails to capture the finite-size dynamics, while a stochastic version of the Truncated Wigner Approximation (TWA) is remarkably accurate, particularly in the large atom ensemble limit. Using the TWA and the Monte Carlo Wave Function (MCWF) approach, we identify three distinct dynamical regimes of transient DTC behavior in the finite-size Dicke model. We outline the mechanism behind the non-monotonic finite size dynamical decay of DTC order and discuss the implications for experiments performed on finite-sized atomic assemblies.
one_liner: Finite-size open Dicke systems exhibit three transient time-crystal regimes and non-monotonic decay as atom number increases.
why_it_matters: The results identify finite-ensemble effects and simulation methods needed to interpret discrete-time-crystal experiments in realistic cavity-QED platforms.
detailed_summary: The study analyzes periodically driven, open Dicke systems beyond the thermodynamic limit and finds non-monotonic atom-number dependence in transient time-crystal amplitudes and decay rates. Comparisons with Monte Carlo wave-function calculations show that stochastic Truncated Wigner simulations remain accurate, whereas a second-order cumulant expansion misses the finite-size dynamics. Three dynamical regimes are identified and linked to a mechanism for finite-size decay.
platform_or_system: Finite atomic ensemble in an optical cavity
main_result: Stochastic Truncated Wigner modeling accurately captures three finite-size transient time-crystal regimes and their non-monotonic decay.
application_angle: The analysis supplies experimentally relevant scaling guidance for observing driven collective phases with finite cavity-QED atom ensembles.

title: Resolving Nonlocal State Reduction via Induced Coherence in Frequency-Comb Biphoton Sources
abstract: How macroscopic definite outcomes and nonlocal correlations emerge from entangled superpositions across spacelike-separated regions without superluminal action or {\it ad hoc} wavefunction collapse remains a defining open question in the foundations of quantum mechanics. Here, we resolve this century-long paradox within \textit{linear} relativistic quantum electrodynamics by developing an open-system and measurement-defined framework realized in dual, spacelike-separated nonlinear crystals driven synchronously by a multi-mode optical frequency comb and seeded by an ultra-narrow coherent laser. Expanding the transverse electromagnetic vector potential into discrete single-photon frequency-comb supermodes, we show that tracing out the unmeasured continuous-wave idler field yields an exact spatial dephasing Lindblad master equation whose decoherence rate is governed by the non-orthogonal state overlap of single-photon-added coherent states. Connecting this open-system map to free-vector-space quotient measurement theory, we demonstrate that single-particle interference arises from the geometric projection of the composite state onto detector-defined conditional cosets rather than remote collapse, establishing strict operational equivalence across pump, seed, and signal phase scans. The resulting wave-particle-entanglement triality equality $P^2 + E^2 + V^2 = 1$ is saturated across the complete parameter space, while the atomic-clock-referenced comb structure anchors continuous-variable time-frequency displacement stabilizers directly at the hardware layer. Our work unifies induced coherence, Bohr's complementarity, and quotient measurement theory, providing a microscopic pathway toward fault-tolerant bosonic quantum information processing.
one_liner: A dual-crystal frequency-comb biphoton model links induced coherence to exact idler-induced spatial dephasing and detector-defined projection.
why_it_matters: It connects frequency-comb photonic hardware, open-system decoherence, and time-frequency stabilizers, though its broad foundational claims require scrutiny.
detailed_summary: The work considers two synchronously pumped nonlinear crystals seeded by an ultranarrow laser and expands the optical field in discrete frequency-comb supermodes. Tracing out the unmeasured continuous-wave idler produces an exact spatial-dephasing Lindblad equation governed by overlap between photon-added coherent states. The authors further derive phase-scan equivalences, a saturated P²+E²+V² relation, and hardware-referenced time-frequency displacement stabilizers.
main_result: The proposed framework derives idler-induced dephasing, induced-coherence visibility relations, and comb-referenced displacement stabilizers within linear quantum electrodynamics.
application_angle: The architecture could support phase-stable time-frequency photonic encoding and bosonic quantum-information protocols, pending independent experimental validation.

title: Single-photon time qubit: Quantum-vacuum control and complementarity of the arrow of time
abstract: Treating the arrow of time as a controllable quantum variable rather than a fixed external parameter is a central challenge in quantum physics. Recently, Bloch~\cite{Bloch2025} proposed the theoretical concept of a \emph{time qubit}, a two-level control space $\mathcal{H}_T=\mathrm{span}\{\ket{+},\ket{-}\}$ that selects between opposite Hamiltonian evolutions $\hat{H}_{\pm}=\hat{H}_0\pm\hat{V}$, but this paradigm has remained experimentally unrealized. Here we formulate the quantum-optical theory of a single-photon time qubit---uncovering quantum-vacuum control and complementarity of the arrow of time---and experimentally probe and validate its predictions using phase-resolved single-photon interferometry from two coherently seeded entangled nonlinear biphoton sources~\cite{Lee2018,Yoon2021}. First, we show theoretically and verify experimentally that a controlled $π$ pump--seed phase inversion during pair creation from the quantum vacuum flips the stimulated displacement generator $\hat{V}\to -\hat{V}$ on top of the spontaneous two-mode squeezing background $\hat{H}_0$, reversing the stimulated evolution time [$\hat{U}_{\mathrm{stim},-}(t)=\hat{U}_{\mathrm{stim},+}(-t)$] and enabling universal single-qubit $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ control and postselection-free first-order tomography on the temporal Bloch sphere. Second, we prove that spontaneous idler vacuum fluctuations record complete which-branch (temporal-direction) information whereas the shared coherent seed erases it without cascading or aligning the idler beams, establishing an exact wave--particle complementarity law $|\bm{r}|=\mathcal{V}=|α|^2/(1+|α|^2)$ for the purity of the arrow of time and enabling direct first-order measurement of the Loschmidt time-reversal echo.
one_liner: Phase-controlled seeded biphoton sources experimentally realize a single-photon time qubit with reversible stimulated evolution and tomography.
why_it_matters: The experiment turns opposite temporal evolutions into a controllable photonic qubit and exposes how vacuum noise and coherent seeding set its purity.
detailed_summary: A π pump-seed phase inversion in coherently seeded nonlinear pair generation reverses the stimulated displacement term while retaining the spontaneous two-mode-squeezing background. Phase-resolved single-photon interferometry is used to test the resulting opposite evolutions and perform postselection-free first-order tomography on a temporal Bloch sphere. The study also reports a visibility-purity law controlled by seed strength and a direct first-order Loschmidt-echo measurement.
main_result: The experiment demonstrates phase-selectable forward and reverse stimulated evolution, SU(2) time-qubit control, and first-order temporal-state tomography.
application_angle: Phase-only control of temporal photonic states may enable compact interferometric probes of reversibility and new time-domain quantum-control primitives.

title: Nanophotonic Extreme Ultraviolet Polarimeter
abstract: Nanophotonic engineering has revolutionized how we manipulate the polarization of visible light. Here, we extend such control to extreme ultraviolet radiation, the spectral region of attosecond science and semiconductor lithography, where transmissive optical elements are lacking. We implement channel waveguides that restrict incident 41-nm-wavelength light to a few modes with defined spatial profiles and propagation constants. By designing the propagation-length-dependent interference of two eigenmodes, we achieve polarization-dependent forward scattering, which we exploit to create a transmissive nanophotonic analyzer that resolves the polarization axis and spectrum of extreme ultraviolet light from a single measurement. With a 0.9°-sensitivity for polarization rotations in a 1-second measurement and single-shot capability, the device opens new experimental opportunities in ultrafast magneto-optic spectroscopy and at accelerator-based light sources.
one_liner: A 41-nm nanophotonic waveguide analyzer retrieves extreme-ultraviolet polarization and spectrum in one measurement with single-shot operation.
why_it_matters: This transmissive device brings compact polarization analysis to the EUV, where conventional transmissive optics are scarce.
detailed_summary: The device confines 41-nm radiation to a small set of waveguide modes with engineered spatial profiles and propagation constants. Length-dependent interference between two eigenmodes produces polarization-sensitive forward scattering, allowing simultaneous recovery of polarization axis and spectrum. It resolves 0.9° polarization rotations in one second and can operate on a single shot.
main_result: The nanophotonic analyzer achieves simultaneous EUV spectral and polarization readout with 0.9° rotation sensitivity and single-shot capability.
application_angle: It enables compact polarization-resolved measurements for ultrafast magneto-optic spectroscopy, attosecond experiments, and accelerator light sources.

title: Multimode Parametric Amplifier for K-Band Quantum Measurements
abstract: We demonstrate K-band nondegenerate three-wave-mixing amplification in a multimode resonator comprising an array of 500 SNAILs. Pairing K-band signal modes with lower-frequency internal idler modes enables 20 dB of gain continuously from 19.6 to 25.6 GHz with pump frequencies below 32.2 GHz. At 20 dB gain, the 3-dB bandwidth ranges from 2.6 to 11.7 MHz, and the input-referred 1-dB compression power reaches -100.9 dBm. In the 20-22 GHz band, the average added noise is 0.73 quanta. A two-mode nondegenerate parametric amplification model describes the measured gain response and gain-bandwidth behavior, while a multimode Kerr model captures the overall compression scale. Our amplifier provides a practical solution for implementing a state-of-the-art readout of superconducting qubits in the K-band.
one_liner: A 500-SNAIL multimode parametric amplifier delivers 20 dB gain across 19.6–25.6 GHz with sub-quantum average added noise in part of K-band.
why_it_matters: The amplifier directly addresses the gain, noise, bandwidth, and compression requirements of high-frequency superconducting-qubit readout.
detailed_summary: A multimode resonator containing 500 SNAIL elements pairs K-band signal modes with lower-frequency internal idlers for nondegenerate three-wave mixing. It provides continuous 20 dB gain from 19.6 to 25.6 GHz using pumps below 32.2 GHz, with 2.6–11.7 MHz bandwidth and input-referred compression up to -100.9 dBm. Between 20 and 22 GHz, the measured average added noise is 0.73 quanta.
main_result: The device demonstrates broad K-band 20 dB amplification, useful compression power, and 0.73-quanta average added noise over 20–22 GHz.
application_angle: It provides a practical low-noise front end for reading superconducting qubits and other quantum devices operating around 20–26 GHz.

title: Searching for Axion Dark Matter via Superconductor-Spin Hybrid Magnetometers
abstract: Axions are a compelling dark matter candidate suggested by theories beyond the Standard Model. The predicted axion-electron coupling and the resulting pseudomagnetic field allow for laboratory axion searches. Here we report an experimental axion search via a superconductor-spin hybrid magnetometer. A state-of-the-art broadband magnetometer with a sensitivity of sub-100 aT/Hz$^{1/2}$ at tens of kHz has been realized by coupling a ferrite spin sensor to a readout system based on a superconducting quantum interference device. The most stringent terrestrial constraints on the axion-electron coupling have been established in the frequency range 5$\sim$60 kHz. In the future, an improvement on the constraints of more than 4 orders of magnitude is foreseeable through arrays of superconductor-spin hybrid magnetometers with optimized designs. This work demonstrates the potential of superconductor-spin hybrid magnetometers in high-precision magnetic field sensing and the study of fundamental physics.
one_liner: A SQUID-coupled ferrite spin sensor searches for axion dark matter with sub-100 aT/Hz^1/2 sensitivity at tens of kilohertz.
why_it_matters: The experiment sets the strongest terrestrial axion-electron coupling limits from 5 to 60 kHz and offers a scalable route to substantially better searches.
detailed_summary: The experiment couples a ferrite spin sensor to a superconducting quantum interference device to detect the pseudomagnetic field expected from axion-electron coupling. The broadband system reaches below 100 aT/Hz^1/2 at frequencies of tens of kilohertz. Measurements establish leading terrestrial constraints on axion-electron coupling across 5–60 kHz, with optimized sensor arrays projected to improve sensitivity by more than four orders of magnitude.
main_result: The hybrid magnetometer achieved sub-100 aT/Hz^1/2 sensitivity and set the strongest terrestrial axion-electron limits in the 5–60 kHz band.
application_angle: Scalable arrays could enable markedly stronger dark-matter searches while advancing broadband ultralow-field magnetometry.

title: Narrowband nonreciprocal transmission in a Doppler-broadened multilevel atomic system
abstract: We theoretically investigate narrowband nonreciprocal transmission in a Doppler-broadened five-level M-type atomic medium. After Doppler averaging, the M-type system retains a narrow near-resonant electromagnetically induced transparency window that is narrower than that of a standard three-level $Λ$ system. This spectral narrowing is associated with the decreasing separation between the two inner dressed states as atomic velocity increases. The transparency window exhibits pronounced direction-dependent transmission, with high forward transmission and strong suppression in the reverse direction. The transparency linewidth and forward-backward probe transmission can be controlled via two independent driving fields, while the central transparency frequency is kept essentially unchanged. The resulting narrowband nonreciprocity supports high forward transmission together with strong suppression in the reverse direction, which is suitable for frequency-selective optical filtering and nonreciprocal optical transmission in thermal atomic media. Our scheme with these specific features is geared towards enabling compact vapor-cell-based nonreciprocal devices for quantum network applications.
one_liner: A Doppler-broadened five-level atomic medium produces tunable narrowband transmission with strong directional asymmetry.
why_it_matters: The scheme could provide compact vapor-cell optical isolation and frequency-selective routing for quantum-network photons.
detailed_summary: The theoretical scheme uses a five-level M-type atomic medium whose Doppler-averaged response retains a narrow electromagnetically induced transparency window. Its linewidth is smaller than in a standard three-level lambda system because the inner dressed states converge with increasing atomic velocity. Two independent drives tune the linewidth and forward-to-backward transmission contrast while leaving the central transparency frequency nearly fixed.
main_result: The model yields high forward transmission and strong reverse suppression within a narrow, independently tunable transparency window.
application_angle: The mechanism supports compact vapor-cell filters and nonreciprocal interfaces for frequency-selective quantum-network links.

title: Controlled-Z Gates via Floquet Coupling to Two Auxiliary States in Transmon Circuits
abstract: High-fidelity entangling gates are essential for quantum information processing. In transmon circuits, higher excited states provide additional pathways for engineering interactions within the computational subspace. Here we demonstrate controlled-Z (CZ) gates that exploit two noncomputational states, $\ket{02}$ and $\ket{20}$, through selective Floquet coupling. The nontrivial parametric modulation can activate both auxiliary transitions from $\ket{11}$ while suppressing the leading exchange between $\ket{01}$ and $\ket{10}$. Based on this approach, we develop two gate protocols: a nonadiabatic round trip through a bright auxiliary superposition and adiabatic evolution along a zero-energy dark state, both achieving average gate fidelities above $99.99\%$ in numerical simulations. Control of the modulation phase further extends the bright-state protocol to conventional and unconventional geometric CZ gates. Effective-model simulations show that unconventional control improves tolerance to residual $ZZ$ coupling and static qubit-frequency offsets relative to conventional control over the parameter ranges examined. Simulations including neighboring spectator qubits show that the original nonadiabatic bright-state and adiabatic dark-state CZ protocols retain high gate fidelities. This framework offers new routes toward the experimental realization of CZ gates and their geometric implementations.
one_liner: Selective Floquet coupling through two auxiliary transmon states enables simulated CZ gates with average fidelities above 99.99%.
why_it_matters: The two-path architecture suppresses unwanted qubit exchange and offers robust bright-, dark-, and geometric-gate options for superconducting processors.
detailed_summary: Parametric modulation selectively couples the computational state |11⟩ to the noncomputational states |02⟩ and |20⟩ while suppressing leading |01⟩–|10⟩ exchange. The authors design a nonadiabatic round trip through a bright superposition and an adiabatic protocol following a zero-energy dark state; both exceed 99.99% average fidelity in simulation. Phase control also realizes conventional and unconventional geometric CZ gates, with the latter showing improved tolerance to residual ZZ coupling and static frequency offsets in the examined ranges.
main_result: Two Floquet-engineered CZ protocols surpass 99.99% simulated average fidelity and remain high-fidelity when neighboring spectator qubits are included.
application_angle: The approach expands the control toolbox for robust entangling gates and geometric operations in scalable superconducting quantum processors.

title: Trapped-ion-based quantum repeater node across a 17 km metropolitan fiber
abstract: Concatenation of quantum repeater nodes has been proposed as a means to distribute entanglement efficiently across future long-distance networks. Here, we demonstrate a trapped-ion repeater node that establishes photonic entanglement over a 17 km fiber traversing a city, moving beyond laboratory-only prototypes. The node comprises two atomic ions coupled to an optical cavity. First, a detailed characterization is performed of the long fiber channel and of ion-photon entanglement distributed across it. Next, a repeater-node protocol is implemented, achieving entanglement between a local photon and a remote photon with a Bell-state fidelity of $81.6^{+1.9}_{-1.4}\%$. These results demonstrate that trapped-ion repeater-node technology can operate over existing city-scale fiber infrastructure and represent a step toward distributed quantum repeater networks.
one_liner: A two-ion cavity node distributes photonic entanglement through 17 km of deployed metropolitan fiber with 81.6% Bell-state fidelity.
why_it_matters: This moves trapped-ion repeater technology from laboratory links to existing city-scale telecom infrastructure.
detailed_summary: The repeater node contains two atomic ions coupled to an optical cavity and operates across 17 km of fiber traversing a city. After characterizing the deployed channel and remotely distributed ion-photon entanglement, the team executes a repeater-node protocol. It generates entanglement between a local photon and a remote photon with a Bell-state fidelity of 81.6%, with asymmetric uncertainty of +1.9% and −1.4%.
main_result: The node generated local–remote photonic entanglement over 17 km of metropolitan fiber with 81.6% Bell-state fidelity.
application_angle: Operation on deployed urban fiber is a practical step toward concatenated repeater nodes for long-distance quantum networks.

title: Atmospheric channel model for QKD over satellite megaconstellations
abstract: Atmospheric turbulence and channel loss represent the primary limiting factors in ground-to-satellite quantum communication systems, yet their joint impact remains insufficiently characterized across diverse operational conditions. In this work, we develop a comprehensive and open atmospheric channel model for quantum optical links along ground-to-satellite paths, integrating altitude-dependent molecular and aerosol absorptions. The model is validated with available data from missions such as Micius and Hispasat, including a secondary viability assessment for a hypothetical Starlink-based quantum communication network, where we evaluate the predicted channel behavior in terms of single-photon transmittance and power balance, alongside the channel capacity of the link for uplink and downlink exclusively. Our comparative analysis demonstrates the ability of our channel model to predict real data under simple atmospheric behavior assumptions, which offer practical guidelines for the design and optimization of future quantum satellite missions.
one_liner: An open atmospheric model jointly predicts turbulence, absorption, loss, and capacity for ground-to-satellite quantum optical links.
why_it_matters: Validation against mission data makes the model useful for engineering QKD links and assessing possible megaconstellation-based quantum networks.
detailed_summary: The model combines atmospheric turbulence and channel loss with altitude-dependent molecular and aerosol absorption along ground-to-satellite paths. It is compared with available observations from missions including Micius and Hispasat. A secondary study evaluates a hypothetical Starlink-based network through predicted single-photon transmittance, power balance, and separate uplink and downlink channel capacities.
main_result: The open model reproduces available mission data under simplified atmospheric assumptions and quantifies uplink and downlink performance across operating conditions.
application_angle: It provides design guidance for satellite-QKD terminals, mission planning, link budgets, and feasibility studies of constellation-scale quantum communication.

title: Moments of Random Permanents and Hafnians: A Replica Approach
abstract: Using contour-integral representations of the permanent and of the Hafnian, we turn the computation of their moments for random matrices into a replica calculation, analogous to that of the moments of the partition function of a mean-field spin glass. For the $2k$-th moment of $N\times N$ matrices with independent entries, the dominant saddle point is replica symmetric for $k>2$, and we obtain in closed form the exponential growth rate, the prefactor and the first $1/N$ correction, in agreement with exact enumerations. The growth rate depends only on whether the entries are real or complex; higher cumulants affect only the prefactor and the $1/N$ term. At $k=2$ the replica-symmetric solution becomes unstable, separating a power-law bulk of the distribution from a large-deviation tail, which we compute. The results apply to boson sampling with single photons and with squeezed light.
one_liner: A replica calculation derives asymptotic moments and large-deviation behavior of random permanents and hafnians relevant to boson sampling.
why_it_matters: The results sharpen predictions for output-statistics tails and scaling in single-photon and squeezed-light sampling experiments.
detailed_summary: Contour-integral representations map moments of random permanents and hafnians onto a replica calculation analogous to a mean-field spin glass. For 2k-th moments with k greater than two, a replica-symmetric saddle yields the exponential growth rate, prefactor, and first 1/N correction, matching exact enumerations. At k=2 the symmetric solution becomes unstable, separating a power-law distribution bulk from a computed large-deviation tail.
main_result: The analysis provides closed-form asymptotics for random permanent and hafnian moments and identifies a replica instability governing distribution tails at k=2.
application_angle: These statistics help characterize scaling, rare events, and validation benchmarks in single-photon and squeezed-light boson-sampling hardware.

title: Constant-Depth Quantum Barrier Option Pricing via a Static Bivariate Oracle Framework
abstract: Quantum amplitude estimation offers a theoretical quadratic speedup over classical Monte Carlo methods for financial derivative pricing. However, extending gate-based algorithms to path-dependent barrier options has historically been hampered by sequential path discretization, where tracking price paths across $d$ monitoring dates incurs a linear escalation in qubit footprint and gate depth ($\mathcal{O}(d)$), posing severe coherence challenges for near-term quantum processors. In this work, we present a constant-depth quantum pricing framework that fundamentally eliminates the temporal dependency of barrier monitoring. Leveraging the Brownian reflection principle and Girsanov theorem, we project the continuous supremum dynamics onto a static bivariate joint distribution of the terminal price $S_T$ and running supremum $M_T$. This allows decoupling dynamic boundary checks into a static bivariate oracle comprising two parallel comparators and a dual-controlled rotation gate. We prove this architecture reduces circuit depth and comparator complexity from $\mathcal{O}(d)$ to an invariant $\mathcal{O}(1)$, while supporting discrete monitoring via zero-quantum-cost boundary corrections. Transpilation benchmarks for daily monitoring ($d = 252$) show our framework slashes physical CNOT count by 98.59% (from 2262 to 32) and compresses two-qubit depth by 98.02% (from 1514 to 30 layers). Under a realistic 127-qubit IBM Eagle noise model, the shallow circuit achieves a 7.84% relative valuation error with M3 readout mitigation. Finally, the framework seamlessly extends to nonlinear exotic payoffs lacking analytical solutions, establishing a noise-resilient pathway toward practical quantum advantage in computational finance.
one_liner: A static bivariate oracle makes barrier-option pricing circuits independent of the number of monitoring dates.
why_it_matters: The approach sharply reduces two-qubit gates and depth, addressing a major coherence bottleneck for quantum amplitude estimation on near-term hardware.
detailed_summary: The framework replaces sequential path tracking with a static joint distribution of terminal price and running supremum, derived using the Brownian reflection principle and Girsanov theorem. Its oracle uses parallel comparators and a dual-controlled rotation, reducing depth and comparator complexity from O(d) to O(1). For 252 monitoring dates, transpilation reduces CNOT count from 2262 to 32 and two-qubit depth from 1514 to 30; simulation under an IBM Eagle noise model gives 7.84% relative valuation error with M3 mitigation.
platform_or_system: Gate-based quantum circuits under an IBM Eagle noise model
main_result: The proposed barrier-pricing circuit cuts physical CNOT count by 98.59% and two-qubit depth by 98.02% for daily monitoring.
application_angle: Constant-depth barrier monitoring could make amplitude-estimation-based pricing of exotic derivatives more feasible on noisy quantum processors.

title: Enhanced orbital-angular-momentum dimensionality and spatial-spectral decoupling in thin-film SPDC
abstract: Thin-film spontaneous parametric down-conversion, due to the relaxed phase-matching condition, generates photon pairs that are extremely broadband in frequency and angle and highly entangled in time/frequency and position/momentum. Here we show that it also provides a very broad orbital angular momentum (OAM) spectrum, which, in contrast to the case of bulk crystals, is decoupled from the frequency spectrum. To demonstrate it experimentally, we generate photon pairs in a $7~μ\mathrm{m}$-thick lithium niobate film and compare them with those from a $500~μ\mathrm{m}$-thick periodically poled lithium niobate crystal under identical pump conditions. The thin-film source exhibits a substantially broader OAM spectrum, with the azimuthal Schmidt number almost 9 times larger than that of the bulk source. On this highly entangled state, we perform quantum-state tomography in selected two- and four-dimensional OAM subspaces, demonstrating high-purity maximally entangled states. These results highlight thin nonlinear films as a promising platform for high-dimensional quantum-state generation with weak spatial--spectral coupling.
one_liner: A 7-μm lithium-niobate SPDC film generates broadband, high-dimensional OAM entanglement with weak spatial-spectral coupling.
why_it_matters: Thin-film SPDC provides substantially more accessible OAM dimensions while reducing coupling between spatial and spectral degrees of freedom.
detailed_summary: Photon pairs generated in a 7-μm lithium-niobate film are compared with those from a 500-μm periodically poled bulk crystal under identical pumping. The film produces an azimuthal Schmidt number nearly nine times larger and decouples the OAM spectrum from frequency more effectively. Tomography in selected two- and four-dimensional OAM subspaces verifies high-purity maximally entangled states.
main_result: The thin-film source achieves nearly ninefold higher azimuthal Schmidt dimensionality than the bulk source while supporting high-purity OAM entanglement.
application_angle: The source is promising for high-dimensional photonic encoding, quantum networking, and spatial-mode quantum information processing.

title: Optimal Quantum-Circuit Synthesis and Implementation of General Unitaries with Parallelized Bitstring-Conditioned Rotations
abstract: We theoretically introduce a quantum-circuit synthesis protocol to realize any $n$-qubit transformation $U\in U(2^n)$, up to a diagonal. The resulting circuit is directly native to and optimal in gate count and depth for systems where bitstring-conditioned rotations with tunable angle and axis, $C^{(n-1)}R(θ,φ)$, form the set of native operations. Subsequently, we suggest how this protocol can be implemented in a few-mode superconducting circuit, and experimentally demonstrate the method for the smallest nontrivial case, i.e., for two qubits. We report an average gate fidelity of 97.6 % for Haar-random two-qubit unitaries up to phase shifts in the computational basis. Importantly, these results suggest that multimode devices, such as those in the multimon or multiunimon families may become competitive with qubit-array networks for general-unitary implementations for qubit counts as low as three.
one_liner: Parallel bitstring-conditioned rotations synthesize arbitrary unitaries efficiently on few-mode superconducting circuits.
why_it_matters: Native multiqubit conditional rotations could let compact multimode processors outperform conventional qubit arrays for general transformations.
detailed_summary: The protocol realizes any n-qubit unitary up to a diagonal and is optimal in gate count and depth when bitstring-conditioned rotations are native operations. A few-mode superconducting implementation is proposed, followed by an experimental two-qubit demonstration. Haar-random two-qubit unitaries are implemented up to computational-basis phase shifts with 97.6% average gate fidelity.
platform_or_system: Few-mode superconducting multimon or multiunimon circuit
main_result: The experiment implements general two-qubit unitaries up to diagonal phases with 97.6% average fidelity.
application_angle: Efficient general-unitary synthesis may make compact multimode superconducting devices competitive for small quantum processors and control modules.

title: Quantum Limits of Blind Superresolution Imaging
abstract: Quantum estimation has shown that spatial-mode measurements can avoid Rayleigh's curse, but the fundamental precision limits are usually formulated for a known point-spread function (PSF). We show that, for two equally bright incoherent sources sharing an unknown static, shift-invariant complex-amplitude response, the local quantum information for separation is exactly the same as in the known-PSF case. In a quantum semiparametric formulation, the equality follows from the orthogonality of the separation score to the nuisance tangent space generated by all admissible PSF perturbations. We propose two receivers to access this information: momentum-resolved Hong--Ou--Mandel interference (MR-HOM), which acquires half the small-separation quantum information per signal photon without reconstructing the PSF, and a tomography-assisted symmetric logarithmic derivative receiver (TA-SLD), which asymptotically attains the full bound under explicit recovery conditions. These results provide a route toward blind superresolution without prior PSF calibration in microscopy, astronomy, and other optical imaging systems with uncertain responses.
one_liner: Blind superresolution retains the known-PSF quantum precision limit despite an unknown static optical response.
why_it_matters: The result removes prior PSF calibration as a fundamental requirement for quantum-enhanced separation estimation in realistic imaging systems.
detailed_summary: For two equally bright incoherent sources, a semiparametric analysis shows that unknown shift-invariant PSF perturbations do not reduce the local quantum information for separation. A momentum-resolved Hong–Ou–Mandel receiver accesses half of the small-separation quantum information per signal photon without reconstructing the PSF. A tomography-assisted symmetric-logarithmic-derivative receiver can asymptotically attain the full bound when the stated recovery conditions hold.
main_result: The separation quantum-information bound is unchanged by an unknown static shift-invariant PSF, and proposed receivers access half or all of it.
application_angle: Calibration-free quantum superresolution could improve microscopy, astronomy, and imaging through uncertain or drifting optical systems.

title: Parallel Teleportation via AME(5,2) States on IBM Quantum Hardware
abstract: The five-qubit Absolutely Maximally Entangled AME$(5,2)$ state, whose every pair of qubits is maximally mixed so that all its information lives in non-local correlations, could in principle serve as a single shared quantum networking resource for teleporting two unknown qubits in parallel (each via its own Bell measurement and Pauli correction). Nonetheless, its hardware implementations remain scarce despite its theoretical importance. Here, we demonstrate parallel teleportation based on a five-qubit absolutely maximally entangled state, AME$(5,2)$, on the superconducting processor ibm_pittsburgh. We construct three-qubit Clifford decoders that extract two Bell pairs using three logical two-qubit gates for each of 60 inequivalent sender-receiver assignments. Using parallelization and classical Pauli frame post-processing, we retain reference-receiver entanglement on both channels after three teleportation rounds. With XY4 dynamical decoupling and the lowest-cost decoder, the final entanglement fidelities are $0.704\pm0.028$ and $0.680\pm0.022$, where uncertainties are pointwise $99\%$ confidence-interval half-widths over eight trials. Their lower bounds exceed the separability threshold of $1/2$. The decoder with lower circuit depth generally retains higher mean fidelity, and XY4 generally improves on XX. These results establish a hardware demonstration of two-channel entanglement transmission through repeated AME-assisted teleportation and provide compact decoding circuits for reconfigurable multipartite communication.
one_liner: A five-qubit AME state enables two simultaneous teleportation channels through three repeated rounds on IBM hardware.
why_it_matters: This demonstrates reusable multipartite entanglement as a compact, reconfigurable networking resource with both channels retaining nonclassical fidelity.
detailed_summary: The experiment prepares an AME(5,2) state on ibm_pittsburgh and uses compact three-qubit Clifford decoders to extract two Bell pairs for 60 sender-receiver assignments. Parallel execution and Pauli-frame post-processing preserve both reference-receiver links over three teleportation rounds. With XY4 decoupling and the lowest-cost decoder, final entanglement fidelities reach 0.704±0.028 and 0.680±0.022, with 99% confidence bounds above the 1/2 separability threshold.
main_result: Two entanglement channels remain above the separability threshold after three rounds of AME-assisted parallel teleportation.
application_angle: Compact AME decoders could support reconfigurable multipartite communication and simultaneous routing in future quantum networks.

title: Structured light for addressable two-qubit gates in medium-sized ion crystals: modeling motional and dephasing errors
abstract: Geometric phase gates with addressed laser radiation are widely used in trapped-ion quantum computers to drive high-fidelity entangling gates on an arbitrary qubit pair of a larger ion chain. Such programmable connectivity exploits the collective phonons to mediate the desired interaction, while simultaneously achieving robustness to their thermal fluctuations by a careful calibration of the gate time with respect to the laser and vibrational-mode frequencies. Crosstalk errors can arise when the spectator qubits, which should ideally remain idle during the gate, are partially driven by the laser fields. The minimal crosstalk, which is set by the laser beam size on the spectator ions, can be achieved when the addressing beams propagate perpendicular to the ion chain. However, this results in exciting the radial phonons, and can complicate achieving high-fidelities as the ion chain grows due to the so-called spectral mode crowding. In this work, we present the theoretical description of a scheme recently implemented by Faorlin et $al.$. This scheme overcomes these complications by engineering addressable state-dependent forces along the ion-chain with laser beams that propagate perpendicular to it through the use of structured light gradients. In this way, one can excite the axial phonons and avoid the spectral mode crowding, while simultaneously minimizing the crosstalk. We present a detailed derivation of the entangling gate scheme, together with analytical closed-form expressions for the leading contribution to the gate error caused by thermal motional fluctuations and dephasing noise. Our results confirm that such fluctuations account for up to 93$\%$ of the error budget under the operating conditions of the gate implemented by Faorlin et $al.$. We identify target parameters to reduce the motional error from the reported $10^{-3}$ to the $10^{-5}$ level.
one_liner: Structured-light gradients enable low-crosstalk axial-phonon entangling gates in medium-sized trapped-ion chains.
why_it_matters: The analysis identifies the dominant physical errors and concrete parameters for improving addressed two-qubit gates from 10^-3 to 10^-5 motional error.
detailed_summary: The scheme uses beams perpendicular to the ion chain while structured-light gradients generate longitudinal state-dependent forces, coupling to axial rather than crowded radial phonon modes. The paper derives the gate dynamics and closed-form leading errors from thermal motion and dephasing. Under reported experimental conditions, these effects account for up to 93% of the error budget, and target parameters are identified for lowering motional error to 10^-5.
platform_or_system: Medium-sized trapped-ion chain with structured-light addressing
main_result: The model explains up to 93% of the demonstrated gate-error budget and specifies a path from 10^-3 to 10^-5 motional error.
application_angle: The scheme supports scalable, programmable ion-pair connectivity with reduced spectator crosstalk and less sensitivity to spectral mode crowding.

title: Dynamical Mean-Field Theory for Real Materials using Variational Quantum Compressed Time Evolution on a Quantum Computer
abstract: We design a hybrid quantum-classical computational workflow, combining density functional theory and dynamical mean-field theory, to investigate the electronic properties of CaCuO2, a parent structure of high-temperature cuprate superconductors. Our approach uses a quantum algorithm as an impurity solver that is based on variational quantum compressed time evolution to compute the time-dependent Greens function on an IBM Heron quantum device. Utilizing error mitigation techniques and a Lehmann representation fitting procedure, we extract the density of states from the signal in the accessible time regime. Despite the significant challenges rooted in the residual imprecision of currently accessible NISQ devices, we successfully resolve the characteristic features of the spectral function. However, we find that the required numerical accuracy for full DMFT self-consistency exceeds current hardware capabilities, indicating that practical real-material DMFT applications will necessitate post-NISQ hardware developments.
one_liner: A hybrid DFT+DMFT workflow uses an IBM Heron processor to recover key spectral features of CaCuO2 with a variational quantum impurity solver.
why_it_matters: It tests quantum hardware on a real-material many-body problem while identifying the accuracy gap that must close before self-consistent quantum DMFT becomes practical.
detailed_summary: The workflow combines density functional theory with dynamical mean-field theory and computes the impurity Green's function through variational quantum compressed time evolution on IBM Heron hardware. Error mitigation and Lehmann-representation fitting recover characteristic features of the CaCuO2 spectral function from the short accessible time signal. Residual hardware errors remain too large to complete a numerically stable DMFT self-consistency loop.
main_result: The experiment resolves characteristic CaCuO2 spectral features on quantum hardware but does not reach the accuracy required for full DMFT self-consistency.
application_angle: The approach is a hardware benchmark and development path for quantum-assisted electronic-structure calculations of correlated materials.

title: Observable-Level Framework for Finite-Key Security in Coherent-One-Way Quantum Key Distribution
abstract: Practical security analysis of Coherent-One-Way (COW) quantum key distribution requires optical-device modeling, finite experimental statistics, and security inference to be treated consistently without conflating assumptions. We present a modular observable-level simulation framework organized through the pipeline θ_phys -> p -> O -> S_j(O), in which physical source, channel, receiver, and detector parameters determine detector-resolved event probabilities, a finite-block layer applies an effective dead-time treatment and generates aggregate detector counts, and interchangeable security evaluators act on the same observable record. The framework is verified against analytical optical, virtual-state, and finite-key relations and evaluated against reported experimental COW-QKD operating points. The Kato finite-key calculation reproduces the refined experimentally reported secure-key rates most closely at intermediate distances, with deviations of -1.5% at 50 km and -10.3% at 75 km. Monitoring bright-port decoy counts agree within 0.9-2.4%, while remaining distance-dependent dark-port residual identifies the principal model-sensitive observable of the present physical description. Applying Kato and Azuma-Hoeffding concentration treatments to identical detector records isolates the effect of finite-key statistical inference and shows substantially tighter Kato phase-error bounds for rare-event monitoring records studied here. Holding the Kato evaluator fixed, joint optimization of coherent-state mean photon number mu and receiver splitting fraction t_B increases model-predicted secure-key rate by 7.4-20.2% relative to optimization of mu alone with t_B = 0.3. The framework therefore provides a common computational interface for experimental reproduction, controlled security-model comparison, model-based protocol optimization, and modular adversarial stress testing in COW-QKD.
one_liner: A modular observable-level COW-QKD simulator links optical hardware, finite detector records, and interchangeable finite-key security analyses.
why_it_matters: It enables controlled reproduction and optimization of practical COW-QKD systems while exposing which observables and statistical assumptions dominate security estimates.
detailed_summary: The framework maps source, channel, receiver, and detector parameters to detector-resolved probabilities and finite-block count records before applying interchangeable security evaluators. Against reported COW-QKD operating points, the Kato analysis reproduces secure-key rates within -1.5% at 50 km and -10.3% at 75 km, while bright-port decoy counts agree within 0.9-2.4%. Joint optimization of mean photon number and receiver splitting raises predicted secure-key rates by 7.4-20.2% over optimizing photon number alone at fixed splitting.
main_result: A common detector-record interface reproduces experimental trends, separates finite-key inference effects, and yields up to 20.2% higher predicted key rates through joint parameter optimization.
application_angle: The framework supports experimental validation, security-model comparison, link optimization, and adversarial stress testing for deployed COW-QKD.

title: Ensemble basis-free coherence for quantum communication
abstract: The resource theory of coherence quantifies the quantum properties of states and their role in quantum information processing. Extending coherence theory to ensembles, the natural objects in quantum communication, remains an active research direction, with their operational potential still being explored. In this work, we establish a maximally coherent ensemble in every finite dimension: the continuous ensemble of pure states distributed according to the normalized Haar measure attains the tight upper bound on basis-free relative entropy ensemble coherence. We then prove that ensemble coherence bounds the effective informational advantage of postselective measurements over the Holevo quantity for two equiprobable pure states. Finally, for the qubit B92 QKD protocol, we show that the coherence of Alice's ensemble upper-bounds the secret key rate in the asymptotic regime. These results give ensemble coherence a quantitative operational meaning in quantum communication and cryptography
one_liner: Basis-free ensemble coherence is given operational meaning through bounds on postselective information gain and the asymptotic B92 secret-key rate.
why_it_matters: The results connect a resource-theory quantity directly to communication and cryptographic performance, providing new limits for ensemble-based protocols.
detailed_summary: The authors prove that the Haar-distributed continuous ensemble of pure states maximizes basis-free relative-entropy ensemble coherence in every finite dimension. They show that this coherence bounds the effective information advantage of postselective measurements over the Holevo quantity for two equiprobable pure states. For qubit B92 QKD, Alice's ensemble coherence also upper-bounds the asymptotic secret-key rate.
main_result: Ensemble coherence is established as an upper bound on both postselective information advantage and the asymptotic B92 secret-key rate.
application_angle: These bounds can guide resource accounting and performance-limit analysis in state-ensemble quantum communication protocols.

title: CO$Φ$ - COmpiling PHotonics into dIgital quantum circuits
abstract: Photonic and qubit-based (digital) approaches to quantum computing are largely regarded as separate paradigms. This article aims to bridge these paradigms by developing a method for mapping quantum-optical systems onto qubit-based quantum circuits. The key ingredient enabling this mapping is the introduction of a truncation of the Fock space describing single-mode optical states. Within this framework, representations of basic photonic operations are developed, including the phase-rotation operator, the displacement operator, the squeezing operator, and the beam splitter. Explicit quantum circuit constructions are provided for Fock-space truncations of dimension $N=2$ and $N=4$. We discuss benchmarking of the implemented operations and identify the regime of applicability and the limitations of the proposed method. The presented results can be used to simulate quantum optical circuits on qubit-based quantum computers, with special relevance to Gaussian Boson Sampling in the low-photon-number regime. To demonstrate the practical applicability of this approach, we complement the theoretical framework with a Python-based quantum programming tool CO$Φ$ that compiles Blackbird quantum-optics programs into qubit-based OpenQASM circuits using a truncated Fock-space encoding. The compiler is available on GitHub at https://github.com/Quantum-Cosmos-Lab/cophi.
one_liner: The COΦ compiler translates truncated-Fock photonic programs into qubit-based OpenQASM circuits for low-photon-number optical simulation.
why_it_matters: It provides a concrete software bridge between photonic algorithms and gate-based quantum processors, including an accessible route to small Gaussian-boson-sampling studies.
detailed_summary: COΦ encodes each optical mode in a finite Fock space and constructs qubit circuits for phase rotation, displacement, squeezing, and beam-splitter operations. Explicit circuits are developed for local truncation dimensions N=2 and N=4, with benchmarking and applicability limits discussed. The accompanying Python tool compiles Blackbird quantum-optics programs into OpenQASM for execution or simulation on digital quantum platforms.
main_result: The work demonstrates an end-to-end compiler for mapping basic photonic circuits into digital quantum circuits at small Fock-space truncations.
application_angle: It enables low-photon-number photonic experiments and Gaussian-boson-sampling prototypes to be explored on qubit-based hardware and simulators.

title: Tuning between collective dynamics and scrambling through initial-state symmetry alignment in long-range spin models
abstract: Long-range interactions in many-body quantum systems give rise to a wide range of dynamical phenomena, from collective dynamics well described by integrable mean-field models with symmetric all-to-all couplings, to fast scrambling of quantum information from disordered long-range interactions. Here, we investigate scenarios in which both regimes emerge within a single deterministic, translation-invariant XY spin model with long-range couplings. We consider a sparse powers-of-two (PWR2) graph, where each spin interacts with a logarithmic number of neighbors, and a power-law-decaying model. By altering the initial state via local perturbations on a completely symmetric state, we show that the dynamics changes from collective to scrambling as witnessed by bipartite and multipartite entanglement measures. We characterize this collective-to-scrambling crossover using Lyapunov exponents in the semiclassical regime, and show that the spectral properties of the coupling graph adjacency matrix provide a very efficient tool to predict the onset of fast scrambling. Our results offer a unified framework for controlling the switch between collective and scrambling dynamics in a setup accessible in experiments with neutral atoms in cavities or in tweezer arrays.
one_liner: Initial-state symmetry alignment switches a deterministic long-range XY spin system between collective motion and fast quantum-information scrambling.
why_it_matters: It offers an experimentally accessible control knob for selecting collective or scrambling dynamics without changing the underlying interaction network.
detailed_summary: The study considers sparse powers-of-two and power-law coupling graphs in translation-invariant long-range XY spin models. Local perturbations of an initially symmetric state drive a crossover from collective dynamics to scrambling, diagnosed through bipartite and multipartite entanglement. Semiclassical Lyapunov exponents characterize the crossover, while the adjacency-matrix spectrum efficiently predicts the onset of fast scrambling.
main_result: State preparation alone controls a collective-to-scrambling crossover whose onset can be predicted from the interaction graph spectrum.
application_angle: The mechanism can support programmable studies of information spreading in neutral atoms coupled through cavities or arranged in tweezer arrays.

title: A Solar Optical Clock
abstract: Precision spectroscopy underpins quantum sensing, atomic timekeeping, and the search for terrestrial-mass exoplanets. Finding an Earth-Sun analog requires fractional splitting of spectral features that rivals the precision of the best laboratory spectroscopy. This corresponds to resolution of a few parts in $10^5$ of a typical stellar spectral line, or a Doppler velocity precision of less than 10 cm s$^{-1}$. Only a few astrophysical spectrometers reach this regime, and only by dispersing starlight with large gratings and averaging thousands of lines. Here, we show that comparable precision can be achieved on a single solar line by leveraging techniques used in quantum sensors and optical clocks. A laser is frequency-locked to the 1565 nm solar Fe I line by coupling to a single mode of the solar thermal field and counted against an optical frequency comb referenced to the SI second, thus creating a solar optical clock. Operating at the fundamental photon-noise limit of thermal heterodyne spectroscopy, we achieve centroid precision of one part in $10^9$ of the optical frequency, or 30 cm s$^{-1}$ in radial velocity. We recover the Sun's five-minute acoustic oscillations and the expected Rossiter-McLaughlin signal during a solar eclipse. Combining these techniques from quantum sensing with a thirty-meter-class telescope could enable our demonstrated precision on the nearest Sun-like stars in a few hours. Multiplexing such absolute frequency measurements across lines with different magnetic sensitivity and formation depth would reduce averaging time and help disentangle stellar granulation and activity from the Doppler signature of terrestrial exoplanets, providing new approaches to address some of the most demanding measurements in astrophysical spectroscopy.
one_liner: A laser locked to a single 1565 nm solar Fe I line forms a comb-referenced solar optical clock with 30 cm/s radial-velocity precision.
why_it_matters: It transfers optical-clock and quantum-sensing methods to stellar spectroscopy, offering a route toward detecting Earth-like exoplanets without relying only on large gratings.
detailed_summary: A laser is locked to a single spatial mode of the Sun's thermal field at the 1565 nm Fe I line and counted against an SI-referenced optical frequency comb. Operating at the thermal heterodyne photon-noise limit, the system reaches one-part-in-10^9 optical-frequency centroid precision, corresponding to 30 cm/s radial velocity. It resolves solar five-minute oscillations and the expected Rossiter-McLaughlin signature during an eclipse.
main_result: The solar optical clock achieves 30 cm/s precision on one spectral line and recovers known solar oscillation and eclipse-induced velocity signals.
application_angle: Scaling the technique to large telescopes and multiple lines could improve terrestrial-exoplanet searches and separation of stellar activity from Doppler motion.

title: Photonic band structure by direct second-kind free-space boundary integral equations
abstract: We present a direct boundary integral equation (BIE) formulation of the Bloch eigenvalue problem for two-dimensional photonic crystals that uses only the free-space Helmholtz Green function. The unknowns are the Cauchy data of the Bloch mode on the inclusion boundary and on two cell walls. On the inclusion boundary, the transmission conditions are imposed via Müller's formulation. The wall equations, in turn, come from a stack formulation, in which Green's formula is applied on stacks of three cells, so that the wall self-interactions and the interactions between arcs sharing endpoints cancel exactly. The resulting system is of the second kind, Fredholm of index zero, and free of corner singularities, and the walls may be curved to keep the cell boundary away from the inclusions. Its operators are assembled once per frequency and reused for all Bloch vectors. We prove that every Bloch mode yields a nonzero null vector, and that a null vector comes from a Bloch mode exactly when its cell representation vanishes outside the cell, which gives an inexpensive test for spurious null vectors. The band frequencies are computed with a high-order Nyström discretization and the search of Bruno, Santana and Trefethen, which locates them as poles of adaptive Antoulas--Anderson (AAA) rational approximants to a randomly scalarized resolvent sampled on the real frequency axis. Numerical examples validate the method against exact and published band structures and include a challenging triangular lattice of air pores in a dielectric, whose cell requires curved walls.
one_liner: A second-kind free-space boundary-integral solver computes Bloch bands in challenging 2D photonic crystals.
why_it_matters: The formulation enables accurate, reusable-frequency band calculations for complex photonic-crystal geometries while providing a cheap test for spurious modes.
detailed_summary: The method formulates the 2D photonic-crystal Bloch eigenproblem using free-space Helmholtz kernels, Müller transmission conditions, and three-cell stack equations. Its second-kind system avoids corner singularities, supports curved cell walls, and reuses frequency-dependent operators across Bloch vectors. High-order Nyström discretization and AAA resolvent-pole searches reproduce exact and published bands, including a difficult triangular air-pore lattice.
main_result: The authors obtain accurate band structures with a second-kind integral formulation and an inexpensive criterion for rejecting spurious null vectors.
application_angle: The solver can accelerate reliable design and optimization of photonic-crystal waveguides, cavities, and band-gap devices.

title: Efficient Ground-State Manifold Amplification for Rydberg Atom Arrays via Houdayer Cluster Updates
abstract: We demonstrate a hybrid quantum-classical approach for exploring ground-state manifolds of maximum independent set problems, in which quantum hardware supplies the initial solutions and an entirely classical post-processing algorithm expands them, increasing the solution diversity of quantum hardware measurements by up to several orders of magnitude. Quantum optimization devices, while capable of generating high-quality solutions, can suffer from fundamental sampling limitations. This is particularly problematic for applications that strongly depend on a large variety of uncorrelated optimal solutions. We apply the Houdayer cluster update algorithm to systematically expand quantum-generated solution sets through classical post-processing. We validate our approach on a test bed of 43 problem instances from QuEra's Aquila analog annealing device, achieving diversity amplification factors, defined as the increase in the number of distinct solutions at a given set size, of up to 11923x with a median of 24.3x across different problem scales and hardness parameters. Because exact ground-state degeneracies are known for these instances, the recovered fraction of the manifold can be measured rather than bounded: post-processing recovers a median of 21% of the ground-state manifold, and provably all of it for six instances. We also demonstrate that, in some cases, the classical post-processing can discover independent sets larger than those found by the quantum hardware, thus improving on solution quality and not just diversity. While the method is non-ergodic and cannot guarantee complete manifold coverage, it consistently discovers a larger number of high-quality, and in some cases strictly better, configurations than quantum sampling alone. This work demonstrates how simple classical post-processing can enhance the utility of quantum optimization results.
one_liner: Houdayer cluster updates amplify distinct Rydberg-array ground-state solutions by as much as 11,923×.
why_it_matters: Classical post-processing substantially expands—and sometimes improves—the useful solution set returned by analog quantum optimization hardware.
detailed_summary: Quantum samples from 43 maximum-independent-set instances run on QuEra's Aquila are expanded using classical Houdayer cluster updates. The distinct-solution amplification reaches 11,923×, with a median of 24.3×, while the recovered ground-state-manifold fraction has a median of 21%. Six instances are fully recovered, and some post-processed configurations exceed the best independent-set size measured directly by the hardware.
main_result: Hybrid post-processing increases ground-state diversity by up to 11,923× and occasionally finds better solutions than the original hardware samples.
application_angle: The approach improves quantum-optimizer output for tasks requiring many diverse optimal configurations without modifying the device.

title: NeST: ultra-high-rate qLDPC codes with sub-$50μ$s stabiliser cycles via spin shuttling
abstract: Quantum low-density parity-check codes now reach encoding rates up to 50% at useful distances. Their checks however are long-range group actions, not local neighbourhoods, and that connectivity has so far been supplied by neutral atoms. Silicon spin qubits offer the same primitive --- coherent transport of qubit blocks --- through electron shuttling, and on microsecond rather than millisecond timescales. They however travel along fabricated tracks rather than free space: permutations an atom array obtains by moving tweezers must here become collision-free motions on a physical lattice. We here present the first code and spin-qubit hardware co-design. We build an architecture whose geometry mimics that of a family of non-abelian groups, broad enough to host codes of excellent parameters: a hierarchy of nested conveyor-belt loops on a plain square lattice of shuttling tracks, in which every group multiplication becomes a rigid, globally controlled motion of whole qubit trains. We call it NeST, for Nested Shuttling Tracks. A code search over the family returns rate-20% mitten codes up to $[[1400,280,\leq 28]]$, and circuit-level simulations including shuttling dephasing give thresholds above $10^{-3}$ with sub-$50μ$s stabiliser cycles, two to three orders of magnitude faster than neutral-atom implementations. Via extrapolations, we estimate that this largest code may reach a logical error probability per qubit per round of $10^{-14}$, assuming a ten-fold improvement on early shuttling demonstrations, with other physical errors at p=0.1%. Logic is compatible with NeST too: for the [[150,30,10]] code we build a code-surgery gadget in which every qubit again moves only by rigid belt motions, at no qubit cost and a 29% increase in gate layers. This demonstrates that ultra-low-overhead fault tolerance and a fast clock speed are not competing goals, and that silicon spin qubits can supply both.
one_liner: Nested silicon spin-shuttling tracks enable high-rate qLDPC designs with simulated stabilizer cycles below 50 μs.
why_it_matters: The hardware-code co-design combines qLDPC encoding rates near 20% with a fast silicon clock and structured long-range connectivity.
detailed_summary: NeST maps non-abelian group operations onto rigid, collision-free motions of qubit trains through nested conveyor-belt loops on square shuttling tracks. A code search identifies 20%-rate mitten codes up to [[1400,280,≤28]], while circuit-level simulations including shuttling dephasing predict thresholds above 10^-3 and stabilizer cycles under 50 μs. A [[150,30,10]] code-surgery construction adds no qubits and increases gate layers by 29%.
main_result: The co-designed architecture supports simulated sub-50 μs qLDPC stabilizer cycles, thresholds above 10^-3, and belt-motion-compatible code surgery.
application_angle: NeST offers a fabrication-oriented route to fast, low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum processors based on silicon spin qubits.

title: Entanglement Distribution in Quantum Switch Networks: Memory Limits and Achievability
abstract: We study the minimum persistent memory required to distribute a graph state through a quantum switch. Specifically, consider a central switch that assists $n$ remote users in distributing a graph state, using independently generated user-switch Bell pairs. Since Bell-pair generation is probabilistic, different links generally succeed at different times. When a Bell-pair is generated, the qubits may need to be stored in memory while waiting for other links to succeed. Recently, new protocols have been proposed to reduce this storage overhead by processing and releasing some switch qubits before all Bell links are available. However, these protocols do not characterize the minimum persistent switch memory required at each stage. Moreover, the local-cover method in the state-of-the-art Piecemaker protocol is computationally expensive for general target graphs. In this work, we characterize the minimum persistent switch memory required after any subset of users' Bell links are generated and processed. We then develop an online stabilizer-transition protocol that attains this limit, which can be implemented in polynomial time in the number of qubits $n$. Remarkably, this optimal protocol can provide substantial memory reductions over existing heuristic approaches. In particular, for the path graph $P_n$ over $n$ users, Piecemaker protocol requires at least $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ qubits of peak persistent memory for \textit{every Bell-links generation order}, whereas under the order $(1,2,\ldots,n)$, our protocol requires only one persistent switch qubit. Finally, the same stabilizer-transition framework also provides a direct forward construction for sequential graph-state generation using the minimum number of quantum emitters, equal to the maximum of the height function.
one_liner: An online stabilizer protocol attains the minimum persistent memory needed for graph-state distribution through a quantum switch.
why_it_matters: Optimal early processing can sharply reduce costly switch memory while retaining polynomial-time operation for general target graph states.
detailed_summary: The work characterizes the minimum persistent switch memory after any subset of probabilistic user-switch Bell links has arrived and been processed. A polynomial-time online stabilizer-transition protocol achieves this stage-by-stage limit. For an ordered path graph, it needs only one persistent switch qubit, whereas Piecemaker requires at least floor(n/2) for every link-generation order.
main_result: The proposed online protocol provably achieves minimum persistent switch memory and can reduce path-graph storage from floor(n/2) qubits to one.
application_angle: Lower memory demand could make asynchronous multipartite entanglement distribution more practical in quantum-network switches and repeater nodes.

title: CoDecoder: Make Quantum Decoders Up to 100x Faster and Even More Accurate
abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computers need fast and accurate error decoding. We present CoDecoder, a small neural frontend that composes with an existing decoder to improve accuracy and reduce mean decoding time. It predicts each shot's logical outcome, retains confident predictions and routes the remaining shots to the unchanged fallback. A logical-operator-aware output head scores shifted logical operators, combining equivalent logical lines on surface codes and deciding logical qubits jointly on bivariate-bicycle (BB) codes. Fused GPU inference and efficient routing reduce the overhead paid on every shot. In registered tests under circuit-level noise, composition reduces failures by 6.4-31.4% relative to correlated matching on surface codes of distance 7-17 and by 22-50% relative to full-DEM Relay-BP on two BB codes, with 2.3-124-fold speed-ups across these comparisons. With our re-implementations of the neural decoder Cascade, composition reduces decoding time in all four settings. A joint decision of both decoders on the routed shots keeps this speed and makes the composition more accurate than Cascade in all four, with 14-18% fewer failures on the [[72,12,6]] code. On the [[72,12,6]] BB code, a conventional head with independent logical outputs fails 3.8-5.0 times as often as our joint class score under matched training conditions. Per-shot analysis shows how composition gains accuracy. On retained shots, the frontend corrects more fallback errors than it introduces, even when it is less accurate overall.
one_liner: A neural routing frontend makes established quantum decoders up to 124× faster while also reducing logical failures.
why_it_matters: CoDecoder improves latency and accuracy without replacing the trusted fallback decoder, supporting real-time fault-tolerant control.
detailed_summary: CoDecoder predicts each shot's logical outcome, accepts confident predictions, and routes uncertain cases to an unchanged conventional decoder. Circuit-level tests report 2.3–124× speedups alongside 6.4–31.4% fewer failures than correlated matching on surface codes and 22–50% fewer than full-DEM Relay-BP on two BB codes. Its logical-operator-aware joint head is especially important for the [[72,12,6]] BB code.
main_result: Composing the learned frontend with conventional decoders simultaneously reduces mean latency and logical failures across tested surface and BB codes.
application_angle: The routing design can help meet stringent real-time decoding deadlines while retaining conventional algorithms as a fallback.

title: Bias-Preserving Entanglement of Kerr-Cat Qubits with an ATS Coupler
abstract: Kerr-cat qubits offer a hardware-efficient route to fault-tolerant quantum computing by suppressing bit-flip errors exponentially, while phase-flip errors increase only linearly with the mean photon number. To maintain this protection, entangling operations must be bias-preserving, ensuring that phase-flip errors occurring during the gate do not propagate into bit-flip errors. In this paper, we propose an asymmetrically threaded SQUID (ATS) parametric coupler to implement high-fidelity, bias-preserving entangling gates between Kerr-cat qubits. By engineering a photon-number asymmetry between the control and target modes, we enable fast gate operations that suppress non-adiabatic leakage without complex pulse shaping. Through numerical simulations of the full circuit Hamiltonian, we demonstrate a bias-preserving CX gate achieving 99.69% fidelity in the absence of photon loss for a gate duration of 50 ns.
