Under a single-photon loss rate of 100 kHz, our protocol yields a noise bias of 9922, exceeding the noise bias of a naive non-bias-preserving CX implementation by approximately a factor of 570. These results support the ATS coupler as a valuable building block for concatenated cat-qubit architectures.
one_liner: An ATS parametric coupler enables a simulated 50 ns, 99.69%-fidelity bias-preserving CX gate between Kerr-cat qubits.
why_it_matters: The design maintains cat-qubit noise bias during entanglement, addressing a central requirement for hardware-efficient fault tolerance.
detailed_summary: The proposed asymmetrically threaded SQUID coupler engineers photon-number asymmetry between control and target Kerr-cat modes. Full-circuit Hamiltonian simulations yield a 99.69%-fidelity CX gate in 50 ns without photon loss and without complex pulse shaping. At a 100 kHz single-photon loss rate, the simulated noise bias is 9,922, about 570 times that of a naive non-bias-preserving CX.
platform_or_system: superconducting Kerr-cat qubits with ATS coupler
main_result: Numerical simulations predict a fast, high-fidelity CX gate that preserves a noise bias near 10^4 under photon loss.
application_angle: The coupler could serve as an entangling primitive for concatenated cat-qubit processors with strongly biased error channels.

title: Lamb shift of rotational energy levels in quantum gravity
abstract: One of the major challenges of modern foundational physics is the combination of quantum physics and general relativity into a theory of quantum gravity. A severe obstacle are the required extremely high energy scales for direct tests of quantum gravity effects. In recent years, attention has shifted towards near-future experimental predictions of effective or phenomenological models, such as gravitationally induced entanglement or interactions of linearized gravity with non-relativistic measurement devices. These developments motivate us to study the coupling between the quantized metric perturbation and an anisotropic quantum rigid rotor. The intuitive motivation for our study is that a sufficiently heavy rotor consists of a very large number of component systems. Although quantum gravitational effects are completely negligible at the scale of a single atom or molecule, the effects can get amplified by the sheer number of constituents. The resulting effective model describes the gravitational analogue of the angulon quasiparticle excitations discussed in condensed matter physics, suggesting a pathway for future analogue experiments. As a first concrete test of our model, we derive the gravitational Lamb shift for the energy eigenstates of the rotor, which become dressed by a cloud of virtual gravitons. Although the effect is very small, it could provide a concrete test for whether gravity is truly quantum.
one_liner: A quantized gravitational field dresses an anisotropic quantum rotor with virtual gravitons, producing a gravitational Lamb shift.
why_it_matters: The model identifies a concrete, though extremely small, spectroscopic signature of quantum gravity and suggests an analogue-simulation route.
detailed_summary: The authors couple an anisotropic quantum rigid rotor to quantized metric perturbations, obtaining a gravitational analogue of the angulon quasiparticle. Rotor eigenstates are dressed by virtual gravitons, leading to a calculated gravitational Lamb shift. The proposed constituent-number amplification motivates future spectroscopy or analogue experiments, although the predicted effect remains very small.
main_result: The work derives a gravitational Lamb shift of rotor energy levels caused by dressing with virtual gravitons.
application_angle: Precision rotational spectroscopy or analogue quantum simulation could probe the model and inform tests of gravity's quantum character.

title: Second-Order Nonlinear Microresonators on Thin-Film Lithium Tantalate
abstract: Nonlinear frequency conversion enables coherent light generation in spectral regions that conventional lasers cannot reach directly and is foundational to the generation of squeezed states and correlated photon pairs. Implementing these nonlinear processes in microresonators lowers the required optical power by orders of magnitude but requires two conditions to be met simultaneously across wide optical bandwidths: phase matching between the interacting fields, and an appropriate coupling condition to the resonator both in the fundamental and second harmonic band. While the former can be addressed by quasi-phase matching through periodic poling, coupling two widely separated spectral bands to the resonator is nontrivial because of the wavelength dependence of mode overlap. Here, we demonstrate parametric oscillation and efficient second-harmonic generation in periodically poled racetracks on thin-film lithium tantalate on insulator. The proposed resonators feature bus-ring coupling engineered independently in the two spectral bands via a long synchronous directional coupler. Quasi-phase matching is achieved using sidewall poling that is also wavelength-calibrated and locally adapted to compensate for thickness nonuniformities. Together, these two design elements enable second-order parametric oscillation with an on-chip threshold of 181 uW and 9.8% conversion efficiency, with signal and idler tunable over tens of nanometers by a few hundred megahertz of pump detuning. Our design strategy can be flexibly applied to efficient second-harmonic generation, reaching 25% absolute conversion efficiency at milliwatt pump powers. These results show how the coupling condition is a design variable in second-order nonlinear resonators and establish thin-film lithium tantalate as a competitive platform for efficient and low-power frequency conversion.
one_liner: Periodically poled thin-film lithium-tantalate racetracks deliver low-threshold parametric oscillation and efficient second-harmonic generation.
why_it_matters: Independent dual-band coupling and locally adapted poling enable compact, low-power frequency converters for quantum and classical photonics.
detailed_summary: The devices combine a long synchronous directional coupler with wavelength-calibrated sidewall poling that compensates local film-thickness variations. They achieve second-order parametric oscillation at a 181 µW on-chip threshold with 9.8% conversion efficiency, while pump detuning tunes signal and idler over tens of nanometers. Related resonators reach 25% absolute second-harmonic conversion at milliwatt pump powers.
platform_or_system: periodically poled thin-film lithium-tantalate racetrack resonators
main_result: The platform achieves 181 µW-threshold parametric oscillation and up to 25% absolute second-harmonic conversion efficiency.
application_angle: The architecture supports efficient chip-scale sources for wavelength conversion, squeezed light, and correlated photon-pair generation.

title: Engineering Low-Latency, High-Throughput Quantum Decoders on NVIDIA GPUs
abstract: We design and optimize a quantum error correction (QEC) decoder for NVIDIA GPUs, combining Relay belief propagation, a state-of-the-art message-passing algorithm, with order-zero ordered statistics post-processing. Our implementation uses CUDA Graphs to control GPU execution, stops updates for converged samples, and collects unresolved samples in queues for post-processing. We optimize sparse traversal through coalesced message accesses, prefetching, and register reuse, and accelerate binary post-processing with warp-level collectives. In addition, mixed FP16-FP32 arithmetic and INT8 quantization reduce message storage and traffic while retaining accuracy using accumulators at higher precision. We evaluate surface, hypergraph product, and bivariate bicycle code workloads on NVIDIA A100 and GH200 data-center GPUs and a commodity RTX 5080. On the bivariate bicycle code at error probability 0.003, INT8 halves amortized decoding time relative to independently tuned FP32 with a negligible logical error rate increase on RTX 5080. With independent syndrome batches submitted back-to-back to concurrent decoder instances, RTX 5080 delivers 91% of GH200's highest measured throughput with an 8.9x shorter median submission-to-correction latency. The combination of performance optimization, mixed precision, INT8 quantization, and concurrent decoder instances opens a path toward QEC decoder clusters built from commodity GPUs.
one_liner: An optimized GPU decoder combines belief propagation, ordered-statistics post-processing, quantization, and concurrent execution for fast QEC.
why_it_matters: Commodity GPUs approach data-center throughput while sharply reducing correction latency, offering a practical route to scalable QEC decoding clusters.
detailed_summary: The CUDA implementation combines Relay belief propagation with order-zero ordered-statistics post-processing and halts updates for converged syndromes. Coalesced sparse access, prefetching, warp collectives, mixed precision, INT8 messages, and concurrent decoder instances reduce memory traffic and latency. On a bivariate bicycle code at physical error probability 0.003, INT8 halves amortized decoding time on an RTX 5080 with negligible logical-error degradation; the card reaches 91% of GH200 throughput with 8.9× shorter median submission-to-correction latency.
main_result: A commodity RTX 5080 delivers near-GH200 decoding throughput with substantially lower median end-to-end correction latency.
application_angle: The design could provide cost-effective classical decoding infrastructure for real-time control of fault-tolerant quantum processors.

title: Microlens-Integrated Grating Couplers for Efficient Free-Space Coupling in Silicon Photonics
abstract: Grating-coupler arrays are used to couple free-space light into photonic chips, but the space required for tapers and routing waveguides limits their optical fill factor. Microlens arrays can increase the effective fill factor by collecting light over a larger area and focusing it onto each grating. Separately fabricated lens arrays, however, require assembly and precise alignment to the chip. Here we integrate refractive microlenses directly with high-efficiency, normal-incidence grating couplers using two-photon polymerization. Each lens has a 100 x 100 um2 aperture and focuses incident light onto the grating. Writing the lens body at coarse resolution and the optical surface at fine resolution reduces the print time from 9 h to 19 min per lens. Under illumination by a Gaussian beam with a 276 um mode-field diameter, a printed lens increases the measured coupled power by a factor of 33 (15.2 dB) relative to the same grating before printing. Loss normalization gives an estimated lens-to-mode efficiency of 68%. The lenses show no measurable change in coupling after three 3 h thermal cycles at 150C. These results support direct printing as an approach to increasing free-space collection while simplifying lens integration in photonic systems.
one_liner: Directly printed microlenses boost free-space coupling into normal-incidence silicon-photonic grating couplers by 15.2 dB.
why_it_matters: Monolithic lens printing raises collection area without precision assembly and remains stable through repeated 150 °C thermal cycling.
detailed_summary: Refractive microlenses with 100 × 100 µm² apertures are printed directly over normal-incidence grating couplers by two-photon polymerization. A coarse lens body and finely written optical surface reduce fabrication time from 9 hours to 19 minutes per lens. With a 276 µm mode-field-diameter Gaussian beam, the lens increases coupled power by 33× and yields an estimated 68% lens-to-mode efficiency, with no measurable degradation after three 3-hour cycles at 150 °C.
main_result: The integrated lens provides a 33× coupling-power enhancement and an estimated 68% lens-to-mode efficiency.
application_angle: The approach can simplify robust optical packaging and improve free-space interfaces for photonic processors and quantum-communication receivers.

title: Lieb-Robinson bounds via the Combes-Thomas estimate
abstract: This paper studies quantum spin systems: networks of spins coupled by local interactions. The Lieb-Robinson bound predicts that in these systems, information propagates at an essentially finite speed. We produce a new proof of this result. Our approach relies on a spectral bound on entries of resolvents of band matrices, the Combes-Thomas estimate, rather than on the standard path-counting argument.
one_liner: A new proof of Lieb–Robinson bounds derives finite-speed information propagation from the Combes–Thomas resolvent estimate.
why_it_matters: The spectral approach offers a potentially reusable mathematical tool for bounding dynamics in locally interacting quantum systems.
detailed_summary: The paper studies locally interacting quantum-spin networks and their effective causal structure. It proves a Lieb–Robinson bound using the Combes–Thomas estimate for off-diagonal decay of band-matrix resolvents rather than the usual combinatorial path-counting method. The result supplies a spectral route to finite-velocity bounds for quantum information propagation.
main_result: The authors establish Lieb–Robinson locality bounds through a Combes–Thomas spectral-resolvent argument.
application_angle: The method can support rigorous analysis of locality, control, and error propagation in many-body quantum processors and simulators.

title: Can Quantum Layers offer Performance and Security Advantages in Vision-Language Models?
abstract: As quantum computing moves from the noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) era toward early fault-tolerant quantum computing (EFTQC), quantum-enhanced AI is shifting from a conceptual idea to experimental research. Quantum components are expected to extend the capabilities of existing AI systems, yet it remains unclear how such components will help within large multimodal models. In this study, we try to answer that question for vision-language models (VLMs) using classically simulated quantum layers. With LLaVA-OneVision as the backbone, we evaluate 4- and 8-qubit basic-ring and strongly entangling circuits at four insertion and four replacement locations. Insertion adds quantum layers to the classical model, while replacement substitutes them for classical components. Using the same setup, we compare performance and computational cost between classical and quantum-classical hybrid models. On the Visual Spatial Reasoning dataset, inserting a quantum layer after the visual projector reaches 80.7% development accuracy, 2.28 percentage-points above classical full fine-tuning. Replacing the final decoder feed-forward sublayer retains 79.22% accuracy with 13.07 million fewer trainable parameters. Quantum insertion can thus improve accuracy, and selective replacement can reduce parameters. These benefits depend strongly on where the quantum layer is inserted or which classical component it replaces: earlier replacements lower accuracy, and fewer parameters do not reliably shorten training or reduce computation. To assess potential security benefits, we evaluated the robustness of quantum-classical hybrid models under six attack settings. Overall, our study maps where quantum layers help and hurt within VLMs, offering a starting point for hybrid VLM design; whether these gains generalize remains open. The code is available at https://github.com/TITANS-Lab-Artifacts/QuantumVLM.
one_liner: Simulated 4- and 8-qubit layers can improve spatial-reasoning accuracy or reduce trainable parameters in a vision-language model.
why_it_matters: The study maps where hybrid quantum layers help or hurt, while showing that the reported gains remain simulation-based and placement-dependent.
detailed_summary: Using LLaVA-OneVision, the authors simulate basic-ring and strongly entangling 4- and 8-qubit circuits at several insertion and replacement points. Inserting a quantum layer after the visual projector reaches 80.7% development accuracy, 2.28 percentage points above classical full fine-tuning. Replacing the final decoder feed-forward sublayer retains 79.22% accuracy with 13.07 million fewer trainable parameters, but parameter reductions do not consistently reduce training cost; robustness is also evaluated under six attack settings.
platform_or_system: classically simulated hybrid quantum LLaVA-OneVision model
main_result: Carefully placed simulated quantum layers improve benchmark accuracy or reduce trainable parameters, with benefits strongly dependent on location.
application_angle: The results guide future placement of quantum accelerators in multimodal AI, but require validation on quantum hardware and broader datasets.

title: Digital Quantum Simulation of Dynamics in Interacting Fields
abstract: Matter under extreme conditions behaves as a non-equilibrium, strongly-interacting quantum system. Such systems are in the non-perturbative regime of quantum chromodynamics (QCD), where their time evolution is classically intractable. Quantum computing offers a promising alternative, but present-day devices are limited in qubit count and circuit depth, so efficient formulations and algorithms are key to scaling toward experimentally relevant QCD simulations. A scalable framework is established for simulating energy loss and hadronization in 1+1-dimensional SU(2) lattice gauge theory, in which a heavy quark traverses a lattice of light quarks. Classical lattice QCD methods are translated into physics-informed circuits to prepare the interacting ground state. The evolution is run on IBM's quantum processor ibm_pittsburgh, where the charge distribution and energy loss are measured. A further study develops the quantum simulation of the fully gauge-fixed SU(2) Hamiltonian in a mixed basis, a formulation that is expected to remain efficient at all gauge couplings. Digitizing the continuous gauge fields with as few as three qubits per plaquette reproduces low-energy observables with $10^{-3}$ precision. Scaling to larger systems is limited by resource overhead, which motivates truncations that preserve the relevant observables. Sequency Hierarchy Truncation (SeqHT) exploits the hierarchy in basis-operator contributions. Demonstrated on the adiabatic preparation of the $λφ^4$ ground state on ibm_sherbrooke, SeqHT reduces circuit depth by ~30%, suppressing hardware noise in the extracted observables. All simulations in this dissertation are validated on quantum hardware against classical benchmarks. These studies advance quantum simulations of real-time QCD dynamics.
one_liner: IBM quantum processors simulate interacting lattice fields, with physics-informed preparation and truncation reducing hardware costs.
why_it_matters: Hardware-validated methods for shallower, resource-efficient gauge-field simulations could bring real-time QCD dynamics closer to useful quantum computation.
detailed_summary: The work maps interacting 1+1-dimensional SU(2) lattice gauge dynamics onto quantum circuits and measures charge distributions and heavy-quark energy loss on ibm_pittsburgh. A mixed-basis gauge-field digitization using three qubits per plaquette reproduces low-energy observables to 10^-3 precision. Sequency Hierarchy Truncation reduces circuit depth by about 30% in lambda-phi-four ground-state preparation on ibm_sherbrooke, improving noisy-hardware observables against classical benchmarks.
main_result: The study demonstrates hardware-validated interacting-field simulations and a truncation method that cuts circuit depth by roughly 30%.
application_angle: The techniques target scalable quantum simulation of non-equilibrium QCD processes such as energy loss and hadronization.

title: Quasi-Phase-Matched Second Harmonic Generation in Poling-Free Lithium Niobate Microrings with Surface Molecular Pattern
abstract: Thin film lithium niobate (TFLN) is a promising integrated photonic platform owing to its large quadratic nonlinearity enabling vital applications such as second-harmonic generation (SHG), optical parametric amplification, and spontaneous parametric down-conversion. However, to achieve high SH conversion efficiency, quasi-phase matching (QPM) through periodic electrical poling is typically required, which remains challenging in certain applications like multiple-ring coupled devices. Here, we demonstrate a surface molecule patterning strategy to enable QPM in a poling-free TFLN microring for SHG. An on-chip normalized conversion efficiency of approximately 11.5%/W is obtained in the poling-free TFLN microring with surface molecular pattern, showing an approximate 400-fold improvement compared to the same microring without surface molecular pattern. This approach offers a versatile route to engineer interfacial nonlinear interactions for nonlinear optics and quantum photonics applications and may be extended to multiple-ring coupled resonators and other platforms.
one_liner: Surface molecular patterning enables quasi-phase-matched second-harmonic generation in a poling-free thin-film lithium-niobate microring.
why_it_matters: Avoiding electrical poling simplifies nonlinear resonator fabrication and may enable coupled-ring sources and frequency converters for quantum photonic chips.
detailed_summary: The authors pattern surface molecules on a thin-film lithium-niobate microring to engineer quasi-phase matching without periodic ferroelectric poling. The device reaches an on-chip normalized SHG efficiency of about 11.5%/W, approximately 400 times that of the same ring without the molecular pattern. The interfacial approach is compatible with geometries where conventional poling is difficult, including coupled resonators.
main_result: A poling-free microring achieves approximately 11.5%/W normalized SHG efficiency and a roughly 400-fold enhancement.
application_angle: The method offers a fabrication-flexible route to integrated frequency conversion and nonlinear sources for quantum photonics.

title: Photon Correlations Control Quantum Fisher Information in Coherent Multidimensional Spectroscopy
abstract: Coherent multidimensional spectroscopy probes interactions and dynamics of molecular systems through nonlinear optical signals. Quantum light excitation has been explored as a means of controlling these signals, raising the question of how excitation-light correlations affect the precision of molecular parameter estimation from the emitted signal. In this work, we show that photon-number correlations and two-photon coherence play distinct roles in encoding molecular information in the emitted rephasing signal. In the weak-emission regime and within the single Schmidt pair approximation, we derive a normally ordered information law in which the joint photon-number moment and the squared magnitude of the two-photon coherence weight the amplitude and phase sensitivities of the molecular response, respectively. For matched temporal modes and mean photon numbers in each input mode, two-mode squeezed vacuum enhances both weights relative to coherent excitation, whereas independent displaced squeezing preserves the amplitude weight but reduces the phase weight. The background population and its parameter dependence also affect the total quantum Fisher information, which therefore cannot be inferred from the coherent mean-field signal alone. We derive a leading-order bound on its enhancement over coherent excitation when the background population is nonnegative and common to the compared sources. These findings provide criteria for selecting excitation sources according to how the target molecular parameter affects the amplitude and phase of the response.
one_liner: Photon-number correlations and two-photon coherence separately govern amplitude and phase information in multidimensional spectroscopy.
why_it_matters: The derived information law provides source-selection rules for quantum-enhanced estimation of molecular parameters beyond coherent-light spectroscopy.
detailed_summary: In the weak-emission, single-Schmidt-pair regime, the authors derive a normally ordered law linking molecular-response information to photon statistics. Joint photon-number moments weight amplitude sensitivity, while squared two-photon coherence weights phase sensitivity. Two-mode squeezed vacuum enhances both terms relative to matched coherent excitation, whereas independent displaced squeezing retains the amplitude weight but weakens the phase contribution.
main_result: The work derives how distinct optical correlations control quantum Fisher information for molecular amplitude and phase parameters.
application_angle: The criteria can guide the design of quantum light sources optimized for precision molecular spectroscopy and chemical sensing.

title: Extending AMIRAL's blind deconvolution of Adaptive Optics corrected images with Markov chain Monte Carlo methods
abstract: Adaptive optics (AO) corrected image restoration is particularly difficult, as it suffers from the lack of knowledge on the point spread function (PSF) in addition to usual difficulties. An efficient approach is to marginalize the object out of the problem and to estimate the PSF and (object and noise) hyperparameters only, before deconvolving the object using these estimates. Recent works have applied this marginal blind deconvolution method, combined to a parametric model of the PSF, to a series of AO corrected astronomical and satellite images. In this communication, we propose a new restoration method, which consists in choosing the Minimum Mean Square Error (MMSE) estimator and computing the latter thanks to a Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm. We validate our method by means of realistic simulations, in two very different contexts: an astronomical observation on VLT/SPHERE and a ground-based LEO satellite observation on a 1.52m telescope. Finally, we present results on experimental images for both applications.
one_liner: An MCMC-based MMSE method restores adaptive-optics images while jointly accounting for uncertain point-spread functions and hyperparameters.
why_it_matters: Improved blind deconvolution can sharpen ground-based astronomical and satellite images when adaptive optics leaves the PSF poorly known.
detailed_summary: The method marginalizes the unknown object and samples the posterior distribution of the parametric PSF and noise/object hyperparameters using Markov chain Monte Carlo. It then forms a minimum-mean-square-error restoration rather than relying only on point estimates. Validation covers realistic VLT/SPHERE astronomy and ground-based low-Earth-orbit satellite simulations, followed by demonstrations on experimental images in both settings.
main_result: The authors demonstrate MCMC-computed MMSE blind restoration on simulated and experimental adaptive-optics images.
application_angle: The approach supports more reliable astronomical analysis and ground-based identification or monitoring of orbiting objects.

title: Quantum-Enhanced Matterwave Interferometry in a Ring Waveguide
abstract: We propose a quantum-enhanced matter-wave interferometry protocol based on fractional-revival dynamics of a Bose-Einstein condensate in a ring, combined with a controlled interaction quench. Using the Truncated Wigner Approximation, we show that nonlinear evolution to the quarter revival generates modest spin squeezing of $-2.03\pm0.28\;$dB, which subsequently degrades under further nonlinear evolution. In contrast, starting from a non-interacting condensate, a controlled interaction quench applied after the initial quarter-revival beam-splitter operation generates substantially stronger spin squeezing of $-14.57\pm0.27\;$dB. We further show that phase control at $t=3T_r/8$ rotates the squeezed quadrature onto the phase-sensitive direction $\hat{J}_y$, producing a phase-squeezed state at $t=T_r/2$. The subsequent quarter-revival evolution converts this phase-squeezed state into a number-squeezed state, enabling population-difference readout. The resulting sequence provides a route to quantum-enhanced interferometry using the intrinsic fractional-revival dynamics of a ring together with controlled interaction and phase operations.
one_liner: A controlled interaction quench in a ring-trapped condensate is predicted to generate 14.57 dB of squeezing for enhanced interferometry.
why_it_matters: The protocol turns intrinsic fractional revivals into a strong metrological resource with population-difference readout in a compact matter-wave geometry.
detailed_summary: Truncated-Wigner simulations show that unmodified quarter-revival dynamics produces only 2.03 dB of spin squeezing, which later degrades. Beginning with a non-interacting condensate and quenching the interaction after the first beam-splitter operation increases the predicted squeezing to 14.57 dB. A phase operation rotates the squeezed quadrature into the phase-sensitive direction, and later revival dynamics converts it to number squeezing for population readout.
main_result: The proposed quench-and-phase sequence generates 14.57 dB of simulated squeezing and converts it into a directly readable population signal.
application_angle: The sequence could improve rotation, inertial, or phase sensing with ring-based atom interferometers.

title: Zero-group-velocity modes in textured steel plates: experiments and elastic modeling
abstract: Zero-group-velocity (ZGV) resonances are investigated as a non-contact ultrasonic probe of elastic anisotropy in textured steel plates. Directional laser-ultrasonic measurements were performed on 70% cold-rolled Ti-stabilized interstitial-free steel plates in the full-hard and recrystallized condition. Experimental results were compared with predictions based on effective elastic stiffness tensors derived from X-ray diffraction measurements. Classical Voigt-Reuss-Hill estimates and microstructure-resolved finite-element homogenization reproduce the measured angular dependence of the ZGV frequencies well for both states, with the finite-element KUBC/SUBC bounds considerably narrower than the classical Voigt-Reuss bounds. For the full-hard state, agreement with the texture-based model is obtained only after a recovery treatment. This indicates that dislocations present in the full-hard material contribute to its elastic response, an interpretation that is further supported by theoretical estimations. An identifiability analysis shows that the directional ZGV measurements provide access to at least three independently observable combinations of the stiffness tensor components, and concluding suggestions for application in recrystallization monitoring are provided.
one_liner: Directional zero-group-velocity resonances provide a contact-free ultrasonic measurement of elastic anisotropy in textured steel plates.
why_it_matters: The technique could enable nondestructive monitoring of texture, recovery, and recrystallization during steel processing.
detailed_summary: Directional laser-ultrasonic measurements probe ZGV resonances in cold-rolled Ti-stabilized interstitial-free steel before and after recrystallization. Elastic tensors inferred from X-ray texture data, using both Voigt-Reuss-Hill estimates and microstructure-resolved finite-element homogenization, reproduce the measured angular trends. The full-hard sample agrees only after recovery, implicating dislocations, while identifiability analysis finds at least three independently measurable stiffness combinations.
main_result: Measured ZGV angular spectra resolve elastic anisotropy and at least three independent combinations of stiffness components.
application_angle: Non-contact ZGV monitoring could track recovery and recrystallization in industrial steel without sectioning or sensor attachment.

title: Semiclassical molecular dynamics simulations of electromagnetically induced transparency cooling of 2D and 3D ion crystals in a Penning trap
abstract: Motional modes of trapped-ion crystals in Penning traps can now be cooled to near their ground states via electromagnetically induced transparency (EIT) cooling. Numerical simulations are valuable tools for interpreting EIT cooling results and optimizing experimental protocols, but existing molecular dynamics codes are limited to the simulation of Doppler cooling. In this work, we fill this gap by implementing a semiclassical model of EIT cooling in a novel MD code. By simultaneously evolving the ions' internal quantum states and classical motion, we are able to calculate the instantaneous EIT laser forces acting on the ions. We first validate our code by comparing the single-ion cooling rate to fully quantum simulation results. Next, we analyze cooling of the drumhead modes in planar ion crystals, quantifying the effects of planar ion motion and a finite laser beam width. Finally, we demonstrate efficient EIT cooling of the axial modes in 3D ellipsoidal crystals containing up to 500 ions. Such crystals are a promising platform for future quantum sensing experiments with enhanced sensitivity. We find that the mode spectra of 3D crystals can be engineered to enable sympathetic cooling of the low-frequency $\boldsymbol{E}\times\boldsymbol{B}$ modes. This numerical framework provides a powerful tool for modeling sub-Doppler cooling techniques and for optimizing future quantum sensing and quantum information experiments.
one_liner: A semiclassical molecular-dynamics framework models EIT cooling of Penning-trap ion crystals containing up to 500 ions.
why_it_matters: It enables realistic optimization of sub-Doppler cooling for large ion crystals intended for sensitive quantum measurements and quantum-information experiments.
detailed_summary: The code jointly evolves classical ion motion and internal quantum states to calculate instantaneous EIT laser forces. Its single-ion cooling rates agree with fully quantum simulations, and it captures planar motion and finite-beam effects in 2D crystals. Simulations show efficient axial-mode cooling in 3D crystals with up to 500 ions and identify spectral engineering routes for sympathetic cooling of low-frequency E×B modes.
main_result: The framework quantitatively models EIT cooling from single ions to 500-ion 3D crystals and reveals how mode-spectrum engineering can cool low-frequency modes.
application_angle: The simulator can guide cooling-protocol and crystal-geometry design for large trapped-ion quantum sensors and processors.

title: Observation of Size-dependent Optical Modes and Confinement in Fin Cavities using Angle-Resolved Cathodoluminescence
abstract: We observe novel optical fringes and emission coherence in laterally formed semiconductor fins using wavelength- and angle-resolved cathodoluminescence (WARCL). These findings demonstrate that cavity mode and emission confinement are directly governed by cavity geometry including cavity dimensions, facet angles, and orientation. In flat fins narrowing the width from 3000 nm to 200 nm sharpens fringe intensity, indicating stronger mode confinement and increased coherence. Finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) simulations confirm that the observed fringes originate from internal reflections among the fin facets, consistent with a Fabry-Pérot (FP) cavity model where the cavity length determines the fringe spacing. FDTD also reveals a transition from multi-mode to single-longitudinal-mode behavior in 200-nm fins, consistent with experimentally observed fringe narrowing. Increasing fin length from 10 μm to 30 μm compresses fringe spacing via longer round-trip paths. Conversely, tilting the fin end-facet from 90° to 45° reduces the effective light path length, increasing the incoherent optical emission. Remarkably, this loss can be offset by adjusting the fin length-to-height ratio. Results suggest WARCL is a robust in-situ method for direct characterization of individual dielectric nanocavities, mapping their modal profiles and light directionality as a function of geometry for custom design of nanoscale optical sources and waveguides.
one_liner: Angle-resolved cathodoluminescence maps geometry-dependent confinement, coherence, and modal transitions in semiconductor fin cavities.
why_it_matters: The method directly connects nanocavity geometry to modal structure and directionality, supporting tailored nanoscale emitters and waveguides.
detailed_summary: Wavelength- and angle-resolved cathodoluminescence reveals optical fringes produced by internal reflections among semiconductor-fin facets. Narrowing the fin from 3000 to 200 nm strengthens confinement and yields behavior consistent with a transition toward a single longitudinal mode. FDTD calculations reproduce the observations and show how fin length, facet angle, and length-to-height ratio control fringe spacing and coherence.
main_result: The study experimentally resolves size-dependent cavity modes and shows that fin geometry directly controls optical confinement, coherence, and emission directionality.
application_angle: WARCL provides an in-situ tool for designing and characterizing individual nanocavities used in compact optical sources and waveguides.

title: Teaching quantum mechanics in secondary schools: A qubit-first learning path to Bell's inequalities
abstract: Teaching quantum mechanics at the secondary school level remains a major educational challenge. Traditional historical approaches often present the theory as a sequence of disconnected phenomena, requiring extensive prior knowledge of classical physics before students can appreciate the conceptual structure of quantum physics. In this work, we present the design, implementation, and evaluation of a curriculum based on the two state (qubit first) approach, in which the fundamental postulates of quantum mechanics are introduced through mathematically accessible two level systems and realized with light polarization. The curriculum integrates theoretical instruction, laboratory activities, a coherent progression grounded in the interactive simulations, and inquiry based learning into a coherent pathway that progresses from quantum states and superposition to entanglement and the experimental violation of Bell's inequalities. A distinctive feature of the project is the experimental realization of the violation of Bell's inequalities obtained in a newly established quantum optics laboratory in an Italian high school, where students performed, for the first time in Italy, an authentic Bell test using polarization-entangled photons. The same educational framework was adopted for in service teacher professional development courses. Learning outcomes were evaluated through mixed methods. Preliminary analysis indicates significant improvements in conceptual understanding, confidence in using mathematical formalism, and appreciation of the relationship between theory, experimentation, and the foundations of quantum mechanics. The proposed curriculum shows that two-state formalism and supported by real laboratory experiences enables secondary-school students to engage more meaningfully with both the conceptual foundations of quantum mechanics and their experimental verification.
one_liner: High-school students followed a qubit-first curriculum and performed an authentic Bell test with polarization-entangled photons.
why_it_matters: It demonstrates that advanced quantum concepts and genuine entanglement experiments can be made accessible in secondary-school laboratories.
detailed_summary: The curriculum introduces quantum postulates through two-level systems and light polarization, progressing from superposition to entanglement and Bell inequalities. Students in a newly established Italian high-school quantum-optics laboratory performed an authentic Bell test using polarization-entangled photons. Preliminary mixed-method evaluation reports gains in conceptual understanding, mathematical confidence, and appreciation of experimental verification.
main_result: Secondary-school students successfully carried out a polarization-entangled-photon Bell test within a structured qubit-first curriculum.
application_angle: The approach offers a replicable pathway for building practical quantum-literacy and workforce-training programs around accessible photonic experiments.

title: Broadband Mid-Wave Infrared Imaging Enabled by All-Silicon Hyperboloid Metalens
abstract: The mid-wave infrared (MWIR, 3-5 microns) is indispensable for thermal sensing, gas detection, long-range imaging, and free-space optical communications. Meta-optics offer a compact, lightweight, and potentially low-cost alternative to conventional refractive optics, making them attractive for size, weight, and power (SWaP)-constrained systems. However, their strong chromatic dispersion has largely restricted imaging to narrow spectral bands. Here, we demonstrate broadband imaging across the full 3-5 micron MWIR band using a single-layer silicon metasurface coupled with computational reconstruction. Remarkably, the reconstruction model is adapted using only four image captures, overcoming large training data requirements and enabling broadband image recovery despite the strongly wavelength-dependent optical response. In contrast to approaches that engineer complex, dispersion-optimized metalens profiles for broadband operation, our method leverages the wavelength-dependent information encoded by a simple 2cm diameter hyperboloid metalens. We show that this metasurface captures sufficient broadband intensity information for computational reconstruction across the entire MWIR band. These results establish a simple route toward broadband computational meta-optics without requiring broadband achromatic metalens designs, offering a promising platform for compact MWIR imaging systems.
one_liner: A single-layer silicon metalens plus four-shot model adaptation enables computational imaging across the full 3–5 µm MWIR band.
why_it_matters: It offers a compact broadband alternative to complex achromatic optics for thermal sensing, gas detection, remote imaging, and optical links.
detailed_summary: A 2 cm all-silicon hyperboloid metalens encodes wavelength-dependent intensity information across the 3–5 µm band. A computational model adapted using only four captured images reconstructs broadband scenes despite the lens's strong chromatic response. The approach avoids complex dispersion-engineered achromatic metasurface profiles while retaining full-band imaging capability.
main_result: The system demonstrates reconstructed imaging across the entire 3–5 µm MWIR band using a simple metalens and only four adaptation captures.
application_angle: The compact architecture targets SWaP-constrained thermal cameras, gas sensors, long-range imagers, and free-space optical communication terminals.

title: Lean-QuantumAlg: A Framework for AI Agents to Produce Quantum Algorithms that Humans Can Trust
abstract: AI agents are increasingly capable of constructing quantum algorithms and proofs, yet machine-checked proofs alone cannot guarantee that the intended problem is solved or that resource claims match the verified computation. Here we introduce Lean-QuantumAlg, a Lean 4 framework for trustworthy AI-assisted development of quantum algorithms. Its Algorithm-Solves-Problem contract binds correctness, success probability, borrowed-state restoration and quantum and classical resource bounds to a single execution, while separating the guarantees that Lean checks from the problem specifications and execution models that humans review. We demonstrate the framework on nine AI-formalized quantum algorithms, from Grover search to quantum attacks on RSA-2048 and P-256, with less than 1% of each algorithm's imported source code requiring statement-level human review once the shared framework has been audited. By integrating reusable mathematical foundations, certified algorithmic primitives and execution-grounded verification, Lean-QuantumAlg provides a basis for AI agents to construct and certify quantum algorithms, opening a path toward scalable AI-driven discovery of quantum algorithms.
one_liner: Lean-QuantumAlg binds quantum-algorithm correctness, success probability, state restoration, and resource bounds into one verified contract.
why_it_matters: It could make AI-generated quantum algorithms more auditable by separating machine-checked guarantees from human-reviewed specifications and models.
detailed_summary: Lean-QuantumAlg defines an Algorithm-Solves-Problem contract covering correctness, success probability, borrowed-state restoration, and quantum and classical resources for one execution. The framework is demonstrated on nine AI-formalized algorithms ranging from Grover search to quantum attacks on RSA-2048 and P-256. After auditing the shared framework, less than 1% of each imported algorithm source reportedly requires statement-level human review.
main_result: The framework machine-checks integrated functional and resource guarantees for nine AI-formalized quantum algorithms with limited algorithm-specific human review.
application_angle: It supports trustworthy AI-assisted development and resource assessment of algorithms intended for future quantum-computing platforms.

title: Meter-scale quantum interconnects between large quantum processors
abstract: Modular quantum architecture requires long-distance quantum interconnects to stitch together individual processor modules. Such interconnects, long-distance couplers or L-couplers, must support coherent quantum operation over meter-scale distances and scale to multiple connections between any two modules. Here we demonstrate four L-couplers operating between two 120-qubit IBM Nighthawk R1 superconducting qubit processors. Each L-coupler joins two Nighthawk lattice qubits through two frequency-tunable L-qubits, two RF-SQUID based "i2m" couplers, and 80 cm of superconducting aluminum coax. Each cable installs perpendicular to the processor surface, to enable denser connections, and is joined to the chip by an indium-to-indium room temperature pressure bond made after both modules were mounted. L-coupler modes near 5 GHz, with internal quality factors of 0.86 to 1.09e6, carry relay-based state transfer at a mean network benchmarking fidelity of 99.00%, with a best link of 99.29 +/- 0.07%. We then realize distant CZ gates between lattice qubits in separate modules at a mean fidelity of 94.75%, with a best link of 96.42 +/- 0.28%, and use them to generate entangled states across the two processors, including a demonstration of simultaneous Bell pair generation using two adjacent L-couplers. These four high-fidelity L-couplers establish a practical path to scalable quantum interconnects for modular quantum computing.
one_liner: Four 80 cm superconducting links connect two 120-qubit processors with 99.00% mean state-transfer and 94.75% mean remote-CZ fidelity.
why_it_matters: The demonstration addresses a central scaling bottleneck by enabling multiple coherent, meter-scale links between large superconducting processors.
detailed_summary: Four long-distance couplers connect two IBM Nighthawk R1 120-qubit processors through tunable link qubits, RF-SQUID couplers, and 80 cm aluminum coaxial cables. Link modes near 5 GHz have internal quality factors of 0.86–1.09 million and achieve 99.00% mean network-benchmarking fidelity for relay-based state transfer. Remote CZ gates reach 94.75% mean fidelity, enabling cross-module entanglement and simultaneous Bell-pair generation on adjacent links.
platform_or_system: Modular superconducting-qubit processors with coaxial interconnects
main_result: The four meter-scale-class links demonstrate high-fidelity state transfer, remote CZ gates, and simultaneous entanglement generation between separate 120-qubit processors.
application_angle: The perpendicular, pressure-bonded interconnect design provides a practical route to densely connected modular superconducting quantum computers.

title: High-fidelity and robust controlled-Z gates for superconducting transmon qubits. I. Intrinsic errors and decoherence
abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires quantum gates that combine short duration, high fidelity, and robustness to noise. As quantum processors scale, robustness becomes increasingly important because exhaustive characterization and frequent recalibration of individual gates become impractical. We present a comprehensive optimal-control framework for controlled-Z (CZ) gates between directly coupled, frequency-tunable transmons that systematically accounts for intrinsic Hamiltonian errors and realistic decoherence mechanisms, including energy relaxation and dephasing. Using smooth, single-shot flux pulses, we obtain 12-ns CZ gates---close to the theoretical speed limit of 11.6 ns---with intrinsic errors suppressed to the $2\times10^{-5}$ level. We construct dephasing noise models, calibrated against published experimental measurements, that capture fast dephasing from room-temperature control electronics and slow dephasing from $1/f$ flux noise. Using these models, we identify dephasing sweet spots that suppress sensitivity to dephasing noise. We further exploit transmon asymmetry as a design parameter to access distinct noise-resilient operating regimes. These results establish an experimentally applicable framework for balancing gate speed, fidelity, and noise robustness while reducing characterization and recalibration overhead.
one_liner: Optimal-control flux pulses deliver 12 ns controlled-Z gates for tunable transmons with intrinsic error near 2×10⁻⁵.
why_it_matters: The framework jointly optimizes speed, fidelity, and dephasing robustness, potentially reducing calibration overhead in scalable superconducting processors.
detailed_summary: The authors optimize smooth, single-shot flux pulses for directly coupled, frequency-tunable transmons while including intrinsic Hamiltonian errors, relaxation, and dephasing. The resulting 12 ns CZ gate approaches the 11.6 ns theoretical speed limit and suppresses intrinsic errors to about 2×10⁻⁵. Experiment-calibrated models of electronic and 1/f flux noise reveal dephasing sweet spots and show how transmon asymmetry can access distinct noise-resilient regimes.
main_result: The study obtains a near-speed-limit 12 ns CZ gate with intrinsic error around 2×10⁻⁵ and identifies noise-resilient operating points.
application_angle: The approach supports faster, more robust superconducting processors with less per-gate characterization and recalibration.

title: A random sampling method to test the weak Eigenstate Thermalization Hypothesis
abstract: We introduce a random sampling method for testing the weak Eigenstate Thermalization Hypothesis (wETH) that is particularly useful for large, sparse Hamiltonians. We test the method on a well-studied Rydberg atom system that exhibits both two- and three-body dipole-dipole interactions. Our results show that our method allows for the study of system sizes significantly beyond the limits of exact diagonalization. We find that the fluctuations in eigenstate expectation values decay as the Hilbert space dimension $D^{-1/2}$, consistent with wETH and in agreement with previous numerical results.
one_liner: Random sampling tests weak eigenstate thermalization in interacting Rydberg systems beyond exact-diagonalization sizes.
why_it_matters: The method provides a scalable numerical diagnostic for thermalization in large sparse Hamiltonians relevant to programmable quantum simulators.
detailed_summary: A random-sampling method is introduced to test the weak Eigenstate Thermalization Hypothesis without full exact diagonalization. It is applied to a Rydberg-atom model containing both two- and three-body dipole-dipole interactions and reaches substantially larger system sizes. Eigenstate-observable fluctuations scale as D⁻¹ᐟ², consistent with weak ETH and earlier numerical results.
main_result: The method accesses system sizes beyond exact diagonalization and recovers the weak-ETH fluctuation scaling D⁻¹ᐟ².
application_angle: It enables scalable benchmarking of thermalization and ergodicity in experimentally relevant many-body quantum simulators.

title: Electrically Pumped Quadratic-Soliton Mode-Locked Laser in Lithium Niobate Nanophotonics
abstract: Femtosecond mode-locked lasers are the workhorse of modern photonics, enabling optical atomic clocks, frequency combs, precision spectroscopy, and ultrafast signal processing. Bringing them onto nanophotonic chips promises miniaturized ultrafast systems, yet combining femtosecond pulse generation with electrical pumping remains a major challenge, rooted in a trade-off between the speed and energy efficiency of mode-locking mechanisms. Kerr-based mechanisms offer nearly instantaneous response but typically require high intracavity peak powers that are difficult to achieve with nanophotonic-compatible semiconductor gain. Conversely, semiconductor saturable absorbers enable strong nonlinear responses at low energies but are limited by their slow carrier dynamics. Here we break this trade-off by introducing quadratic-soliton mode-locking based on a quadratic nonlinear interferometer (QNLI): an effective saturable absorber built from cascaded second-order nonlinearity in periodically poled lithium niobate nanophotonics, with a measured sub-20 fs response time. Through hybrid integration with an electrically pumped semiconductor gain element, we demonstrate a self-starting quadratic-soliton mode-locked laser with femtojoule pulse energies, operating in single- and multiple-soliton states. Quadratic solitons arise through the QNLI's dissipative and dispersive nonlinear response, which we confirm with a modified complex Ginzburg-Landau equation in agreement with measurements. By combining soliton formation with intracavity electro-optic modulation, we generate 750 fs pulses with flat-top spectra. Our engineerable, ultra-energy-efficient, electrically powered laser provides the critical source for fully integrated ultrafast photonic circuits in lithium niobate nanophotonics that natively offers electro-optic control, quadratic wavelength conversion, pulse compression, and spectral broadening.
one_liner: An electrically pumped lithium-niobate laser achieves self-starting quadratic-soliton mode locking with a sub-20 fs nonlinear response.
why_it_matters: It addresses a central integration barrier for compact femtosecond sources by combining ultrafast response, femtojoule operation, and electrical pumping.
detailed_summary: The device combines a periodically poled lithium-niobate quadratic nonlinear interferometer with an electrically pumped semiconductor gain element. Cascaded second-order nonlinearity produces an effective saturable absorber with a measured response below 20 fs, enabling self-starting single- and multiple-soliton operation at femtojoule pulse energies. Intracavity electro-optic modulation produces 750 fs pulses with flat-top spectra, while a modified complex Ginzburg-Landau model reproduces the measured behavior.
main_result: The authors demonstrate an electrically pumped, self-starting quadratic-soliton laser producing femtojoule pulses and 750 fs electro-optically shaped output.
application_angle: The source could underpin fully integrated frequency combs, spectroscopy systems, optical clocks, and ultrafast lithium-niobate photonic circuits.

title: Injection is all you need: parallel universal logic in high-rate concatenated self-dual codes
abstract: We propose a quantum architecture that achieves addressable and parallel universal fault-tolerant logical in high-rate codes. The codes are obtained from the flexible concatenation of small-distance high-rate self-dual CSS codes. Addressable and parallel universal logic on the resulting $K$ logical qubits is injected by fault-tolerantly preparing and then consuming diverse logical $K$-qubit CSS stabilizer states and logical $\lvert H \rangle^{\otimes K}$ global magic states. Flag-at-origin is used to prepare the stabilizer resource states while a concatenated cultivation protocol prepares the global magic states. These resource states are consumed by Steane-QEC or Knill-QEC teleportation gadgets, which simultaneously perform quantum error correction. Any quantum algorithm with $T$-depth $D_T$ can be executed by consuming $12D_T$ or fewer resource states. We benchmark the fault-tolerant preparation of the resource states for several two-level concatenations of the $[[k+4,k,2]]$ H codes and the Hamming $[[15,7,3]]$ code. In particular, we find that the concatenated cultivation offers at least one order of magnitude spacetime reduction compared to cultivation in the surface code.
one_liner: Resource-state injection enables addressable, parallel universal fault-tolerant logic in high-rate concatenated self-dual codes.
why_it_matters: The architecture targets lower fault-tolerant overhead, with modeled magic-state preparation using at least tenfold less spacetime than surface-code cultivation.
detailed_summary: The proposal concatenates small-distance, high-rate self-dual CSS codes and injects universal operations through logical CSS stabilizer states and global |H⟩⊗K magic states. Steane- or Knill-QEC teleportation gadgets consume these resources while simultaneously correcting errors, allowing addressable parallel logic across K logical qubits. An algorithm of T-depth D_T requires at most 12D_T resource states, and benchmarks indicate at least an order-of-magnitude spacetime reduction over surface-code cultivation for selected code constructions.
main_result: The architecture realizes parallel universal logical operations and reports at least a tenfold spacetime advantage for magic-state cultivation in benchmarked cases.
application_angle: It offers a potential route to higher-throughput fault-tolerant processors and encoded quantum-network nodes with reduced resource overhead.

title: Pure dephasing destroys two-photon amplitude, not nonlinear phase
abstract: A two-level emitter chirally coupled to a waveguide imprints a $π$ conditional phase on a two-photon pulse, a key component assumed in quantum photonic neural network architectures, but whether it survives the pure dephasing of a solid-state emitter is unknown, since no two-photon scattering treatment includes it. We derive the dephased two-photon amplitude in closed form and validate it against an independent Fock-state master equation. The conditional phase is pinned at exactly $π$ at every dephasing rate examined: dephasing destroys the amplitude carrying the nonlinear phase rather than rotating it. The one- and two-photon channels are not attenuated equally, so dephasing does not simply scale the node down but reweights it between photon-number sectors---an error no phase setting can train away. The standard factorization of two-photon correlators, exact for arbitrary loss, fails at first order in $γ_φ$, discarding $16$--$81\%$ of pairs over $γ_φ/γ=0.1$--$1$.
one_liner: Pure dephasing preserves the π two-photon conditional phase of a chiral emitter but suppresses its nonlinear amplitude.
why_it_matters: The identified photon-number-dependent error cannot be corrected by phase retuning, directly affecting solid-state photonic gates and neural-network nodes.
detailed_summary: The authors derive a closed-form two-photon scattering amplitude for a two-level emitter chirally coupled to a waveguide and validate it using a Fock-state master equation. Across the examined dephasing rates, the conditional phase remains exactly π, while the amplitude carrying that phase is diminished. Because one- and two-photon sectors are reweighted differently, dephasing creates an error that phase optimization cannot remove; standard correlator factorization misses 16–81% of photon pairs over γφ/γ=0.1–1.
main_result: Pure dephasing leaves the nonlinear π phase unchanged but selectively destroys two-photon amplitude and invalidates standard correlator factorization.
application_angle: The result provides a realistic error model for solid-state photon-photon gates, quantum-network components, and photonic neural processors.

title: Phonon-assisted free-electron recoil control and mechanical sensing
abstract: Mechanical vibrations are fundamental to a wide range of physical phenomena and technologies, yet their ability to actively shape free-electron dynamics remains largely unexplored. Here we theoretically show how an optomechanical membrane provides a phonon-assisted optical interface for controlling free-electron recoil and sensing localized forces. Transverse membrane motion scatters cavity light into high-momentum evanescent sidebands that enable phase-matched interaction with electrons traveling in vacuum. Beyond supplying momentum for phase matching, the vibration amplitude controls the electron-light interaction strength and redistributes electron populations among recoil orders. External forces that perturb the vibration are thereby encoded in the electron recoil spectrum. Under the modeled conditions, electron readout of localized stochastic forces can yield a higher signal-to-noise ratio than a Gaussian optical homodyne benchmark at equal detected probe rates. These results provide a theoretical basis for mechanically reconfigurable free-electron optics and mode-selective mechanical sensing.
one_liner: A vibrating optomechanical membrane can control free-electron recoil while encoding localized forces into the electron spectrum.
why_it_matters: The scheme links free-electron optics with mode-selective force sensing and may outperform optical homodyne readout at equal detected probe rates.
detailed_summary: The theoretical scheme uses transverse motion of an optomechanical membrane to scatter cavity light into high-momentum evanescent sidebands that phase-match to electrons traveling in vacuum. Mechanical amplitude controls the electron-light coupling and redistributes populations among discrete recoil orders, so perturbing forces become visible in the recoil spectrum. Under the modeled conditions, electron readout of localized stochastic forces exceeds the signal-to-noise ratio of a Gaussian optical homodyne benchmark at equal detected probe rates.
main_result: The model demonstrates phonon-controlled electron recoil and predicts enhanced readout of localized stochastic forces under specified conditions.
application_angle: The concept could enable mechanically reconfigurable electron optics and spatially selective nanoscale force or vibration sensing.

title: Transversal syndrome extraction: A unifying construction for measuring the error syndromes of any stabilizer code
abstract: Fault-tolerant syndrome extraction is fundamental to stabilizer-code-based quantum error correction, yet existing general protocols incur substantial costs in either circuit depth or width. In this work, we design ancilla stabilizer states for a general transversal circuit to construct a family of fault-tolerant syndrome-extraction gadgets that interpolate between Shor and Steane syndrome extraction for any stabilizer code. The result is a configurable trade-off between circuit depth and width.
one_liner: A transversal syndrome-extraction framework yields tunable depth-width trade-offs for any stabilizer code.
why_it_matters: Configurable gadgets could adapt fault-tolerant error correction to hardware with different connectivity, ancilla, and coherence constraints.
detailed_summary: The authors construct ancilla stabilizer states enabling a general transversal circuit for fault-tolerant syndrome measurement. The resulting gadget family applies to any stabilizer code and continuously interpolates between Shor- and Steane-style extraction. Its configuration exposes an explicit trade-off between circuit depth and qubit width.
main_result: A universal family of fault-tolerant syndrome-extraction gadgets provides configurable circuit-depth and qubit-width trade-offs.
application_angle: The construction supports hardware-aware selection of error-correction circuits under limited ancilla counts or coherence times.

title: Normal-Form Characterization of Adaptivity and Entanglement in Pauli-Based Computation
abstract: Pauli-based computation (PBC) is a measurement-based model of quantum computation that samples from output distributions of universal Clifford+$T$ circuits. Here, we provide a normal form (NF) that completely characterizes its adaptive and entanglement structures. These insights unify PBC with one-way quantum computing as dual or `time-reversed' counterparts. We use the NF to advance strategies for distributed computation and investigate magic-state injection rates. We also demonstrate an exponential improvement in the detection of unnecessary magic-state qubits, allowing their efficient removal. Our NF further enables ahead-of-time circuit compilation using PBC, reducing CNOT gate count and quantum memory of random quantum circuits on average by 50% and 40%, respectively, beating other state-of-the-art compilers.
one_liner: A normal form exposes adaptivity and entanglement in Pauli-based computation and improves compilation efficiency.
why_it_matters: The framework could reduce gates, memory, and magic-state overhead in fault-tolerant and distributed quantum computing.
detailed_summary: The proposed normal form completely characterizes adaptive measurement and entanglement structures in Pauli-based computation, relating it to one-way quantum computing as a time-reversed counterpart. It enables efficient detection and removal of unnecessary magic-state qubits. For random circuits, ahead-of-time compilation reduces CNOT count by about 50% and quantum memory by about 40% on average.
main_result: The normal form enables exponentially better detection of redundant magic states and average reductions of 50% in CNOTs and 40% in memory.
application_angle: The method offers practical resource savings for compiled fault-tolerant circuits and distributed measurement-based computation.

title: Delta-Doped GeV$^-$ in diamond with isotope resolvable optical spectra
abstract: Group IV color centers in diamond -- silicon, germanium, tin, and lead-vacancy centers -- are a promising platform for quantum networking. Typical Group-IV creation utilizes ion implantation during diamond growth that leaves the color centers with a broad depth distribution and damage-induced strain inhomogeneity. Deterministic placement and damage reduction in Group IV generation are essential for improving this platform. In this letter, we report on the localization of germanium-vacancy (GeV$^-$) to a $<$ 10 nm layer via the timed injection of GeH$_4$ during microwave plasma chemical vapor deposition. In this layer we have realized 17 ppm of Ge and a strain-free environment for the GeV$^-$. Subsequent electron irradiation and annealing have generated a sheet density of 0.12 GeV$^-$/$μ$m$^2$. The minimal damage from color center generation mitigates spectral inhomogeneity and allows spectral resolution of isotopic clusters, with the best cluster having an inhomogeneous distribution of 2.14 GHz and an average linewidth of $47 \pm 11$ MHz. Our study gives insight into formation dynamics of GeV$^-$ in delta-doped systems and estimates our vacancy to GeV$^-$ yield to be $\geq$ 90%, establishing an athermal nearest-neighbor formation model. We further characterized the spin $T_2^*$ and set a lower bound of 730 ns, limited by a paramagnetic defect.
one_liner: Delta doping confines GeV− centers to under 10 nm and produces isotope-resolved, low-inhomogeneity optical spectra.
why_it_matters: Precise depth control and narrow optical distributions address key fabrication barriers for diamond quantum-network nodes.
detailed_summary: Timed GeH4 injection during microwave-plasma CVD confines germanium to a layer thinner than 10 nm with 17 ppm Ge and low strain. Electron irradiation and annealing yield 0.12 GeV− centers per μm², with an estimated vacancy-to-center conversion of at least 90%. The best isotope cluster shows 2.14 GHz inhomogeneous broadening, 47 ± 11 MHz average linewidth, and spin T2* of at least 730 ns.
main_result: The process creates shallow, low-strain GeV− ensembles with isotope-resolved spectra, narrow linewidths, and at least 90% estimated vacancy conversion.
application_angle: The fabrication route can improve reproducibility and optical indistinguishability of diamond emitters for quantum-network interfaces.

title: Memory--Transport Competition in Physical Two-Bath Quantum Reset Dynamics
abstract: Coherence preservation and environmental renewal offer competing ways of controlling quantum memory and transport. We show that a seemingly natural protocol which exactly replaces the bath occupations while preserving arbitrary system--bath coherences need not correspond to a physical fermionic state. We instead construct a two-reservoir protocol with independent, number-conserving thermal attenuators, for which complete positivity and fermionic admissibility hold by construction. Physical attenuation necessarily modifies bath populations as well as cross correlations; the coherence control is not an independent hard-reset knob. Quadratic dynamics reduces the stroboscopic problem to an exact matrix fixed-point equation without a weak-coupling or Markov approximation. Analytically, coherence retention enhances the leading short-cycle transfer rate, including the complete-erasure limit; no general endpoint-vanishing theorem exists. An exact stationary continuity theorem forces the through-current to vanish whenever either reservoir is left entirely unrefreshed, although no analogous theorem suppresses it at complete erasure. For biased structured reservoirs, exact finite-chain calculations display distinct coherence-, current-, and signed energy-transfer operating points; a resolved high-retention boundary layer exposes strong finite-size sensitivity of the coherence peak. The model provides a microscopic, fermion-admissible benchmark for the interplay of reservoir coherence, particle transport, and energetic exchange.
one_liner: A physical two-reservoir reset model reveals exact constraints linking retained coherence, transport, and energy exchange.
why_it_matters: The benchmark prevents unphysical reset assumptions and clarifies how reservoir refresh protocols affect quantum-device transport.
detailed_summary: The work shows that replacing bath occupations while preserving arbitrary system-bath coherences can produce an invalid fermionic state. It instead uses independent number-conserving thermal attenuators, ensuring complete positivity and fermionic admissibility, and solves the quadratic stroboscopic dynamics through an exact matrix fixed point. Exact results show coherence-enhanced short-cycle transfer, vanishing stationary current when either bath is wholly unrefreshed, and strong finite-size sensitivity near high retention.
platform_or_system: Quadratic fermionic system with two reservoirs
main_result: A fully physical reset protocol yields exact transport laws and distinct operating points for coherence, current, and signed energy transfer.
application_angle: The model provides a rigorous design and validation benchmark for reservoir-engineered quantum transport and reset hardware.

title: Distributed dual-comb spectroscopy
abstract: We propose distributed dual-comb spectroscopy, a quantum-enhanced sensing architecture that simultaneously exploits spatial- and spectral-domain entanglement to improve the extraction of global spectroscopic information across broadband frequency ranges. Our scheme consists of a network of Mach-Zehnder interferometers interrogating spatially separated samples, each driven by a classical frequency comb at the bright port. A single two-mode squeezed frequency comb is distributed through a passive beam-splitter array into $K$ entangled combs, establishing multipartite correlations across sensors while preserving intrinsic spectral entanglement. The protocol is compatible with both heterodyne detection and division detection, and enables parallel estimation of weighted-average absorption features over multiple frequency components. Compared with spatially separable quantum strategies requiring $K$ independently engineered nonclassical comb sources, our approach achieves enhanced signal-to-noise performance using only a single quantum resource distributed across the network. These results establish a scalable route toward broadband distributed quantum spectroscopy with simultaneous spatial and spectral advantage.
one_liner: One distributed squeezed frequency comb enables quantum-enhanced dual-comb spectroscopy across multiple remote samples.
why_it_matters: A single shared nonclassical source could make broadband quantum sensor networks more scalable than per-node source architectures.
detailed_summary: The proposal distributes a two-mode squeezed frequency comb through a passive beam-splitter network to create K spatially entangled combs while retaining spectral entanglement. Mach-Zehnder sensors interrogate separated samples using classical combs at their bright ports. Heterodyne or division detection then estimates weighted-average absorption features across many frequencies with improved signal-to-noise ratio relative to spatially separable quantum strategies.
main_result: The architecture provides simultaneous spatial and spectral quantum advantage using one shared squeezed-comb source across K sensors.
application_angle: It offers a scalable route to broadband monitoring of spatially distributed chemical or material samples.

title: Photon localization: Local measurements, localized states, and causality
abstract: We review what it means for a relativistic particle to be localized and argue that the most useful approach is through local measurement. This perspective ties localization directly to relativistic causality and measurable outcomes in spacetime. Strict localization in quantum field theory is formalized by states that give the same expectation value as vacuum for all local observables outside some spacetime region. With this formalism, single photons cannot be strictly localized, but coherent states can. The structure and interpretation of local observables and local operator algebras are discussed in connection with the Reeh-Schlieder theorem. Since probabilities of local measurement outcomes cannot vanish in vacuum, particle detection events must be phrased carefully. Key characteristics of strictly localized states are surveyed alongside concrete strategies for constructing them. The relationship between localization, causality, and on-demand sources is analyzed, finding that strictly localized states can represent localized, propagating information in quantum field theory. Explicit examples of localized photonic states are presented with an emphasis on quantum optics, including states that approximate single photons and (entangled) Bell states.
one_liner: A measurement-centered treatment clarifies photon localization, causality, and realizable localized photonic states.
why_it_matters: The analysis sharpens what on-demand photonic sources can physically localize and transmit without violating relativistic causality.
detailed_summary: The review defines strict localization through agreement with vacuum for every local observable outside a spacetime region. Under this definition, single photons cannot be strictly localized, whereas coherent states can. It connects local measurement probabilities, operator algebras, and the Reeh-Schlieder theorem, then presents explicit photonic states approximating localized single photons and entangled Bell states.
main_result: The work establishes a causal measurement framework for localization and identifies photonic states capable of carrying strictly localized information.
application_angle: These results inform the interpretation and design limits of triggered photon sources, photonic links, and localized quantum-state preparation.

title: Laser with $7\times10^{-18}$ stability
abstract: We report a laser with record frequency stability, based on a 21 cm cryogenic silicon cavity. For best short-term stability, the cavity operates at 6 K to minimize Brownian thermal noise and achieves a fractional stability of $7\times10^{-18}$ between 2 to 50 s of averaging time and 2.5 mHz linewidth. For best long-term stability the cavity operates at 16 K, where silicon has a zero-crossing of thermal expansion. Slightly increased thermal noise limits the performance to $9\times10^{-18}$, consistent with the expected temperature scaling, but the long-term performance is improved. The laser then has a linewidth of 2.9 mHz and long-term frequency drift less than 4 μHz s$^{-1}$. The laser is used to enhance the performance of a state-of-the-art Sr lattice clock, operating with Rabi and Ramsey interrogation times beyond 10 s.
one_liner: A 21 cm cryogenic silicon-cavity laser reaches 7×10^-18 fractional stability and a 2.5 mHz linewidth.
why_it_matters: This ultrastable laser enables optical-clock interrogation beyond 10 s and improves precision spectroscopy and frequency metrology.
detailed_summary: A 21 cm silicon reference cavity operated at 6 K suppresses Brownian thermal noise, yielding 7×10^-18 fractional frequency stability over 2–50 s and a 2.5 mHz linewidth. At silicon's 16 K thermal-expansion zero crossing, the system achieves 9×10^-18 stability, a 2.9 mHz linewidth, and drift below 4 μHz/s. The laser supports Rabi and Ramsey interrogation exceeding 10 s in a state-of-the-art strontium lattice clock.
platform_or_system: Cryogenic silicon-cavity laser and Sr lattice clock
main_result: The system achieves record 7×10^-18 laser stability and millihertz linewidth while enabling optical-clock interrogation beyond 10 s.
application_angle: It can improve optical clocks, precision spectroscopy, relativistic geodesy, and searches for weak variations in fundamental physics.

title: Efficient third-harmonic generation in high-Q tantalum pentoxide microcavities
abstract: Nonlinear harmonic generation in microcavities offers a compelling route toward energy efficient on-chip short-wavelength coherent light sources, enabled by tight optical confinement within compact mode volumes and flexible dispersion engineering. Tantalum pentoxide (Ta2O5) photonic platforms are particularly promising for realizing such nonlinear processes: their broad transparency window (280-8000 nm) supports broadband operation, their large bandgap suppresses two-photon absorption, and their thick-film deposition capability enables dispersion management--features that can collectively enhance the performance of nonlinear light sources. Here, we demonstrate, to the best of our knowledge, the first efficient third-harmonic generation (THG) in high-Q Ta2O5 microcavities. These microcavities feature smooth surfaces and high loaded Q factors up to 2.67X10^6, thereby facilitating nonlinear interactions. Through dispersion engineering, efficient THG is realized in both suspended microdisks and monolithic microrings under telecom-band continuous-wave laser pumping, as confirmed by optical spectra, visible-light microscopy, and the near-cubic pump-power dependence of the conversion efficiency. This work lays a foundation for chip-scale f-3f self-referencing of frequency combs and next-generation integrated nonlinear photonics.
one_liner: High-Q Ta2O5 microdisks and microrings efficiently generate visible third harmonics from telecom-band continuous-wave pumps.
why_it_matters: The result advances compact, low-power short-wavelength sources and integrated f–3f frequency-comb self-referencing.
detailed_summary: The authors demonstrate efficient third-harmonic generation in suspended Ta2O5 microdisks and monolithic microrings pumped by telecom-band continuous-wave lasers.
