Smooth surfaces and loaded quality factors up to 2.67×10^6 strengthen the nonlinear interaction, while dispersion engineering supports harmonic conversion. Optical spectra, visible microscopy, and near-cubic power scaling verify the third-order process.
main_result: Dispersion-engineered Ta2O5 microcavities deliver efficient third-harmonic generation under telecom-band continuous-wave pumping.
application_angle: The platform could provide chip-scale visible coherent sources and enable f–3f self-referencing of integrated frequency combs.

title: FVQKD: A Formal Verification of Quantum Key Distribution Security in Rocq
abstract: Quantum key distribution (QKD), whose security is derived from quantum mechanics rather than computational assumptions, is moving into standardization and commercial deployment. Yet its security guarantees rest on technically delicate proofs checked by hand. Formal verification closes this gap, establishing a two-factor assurance: unconditional security from physical principles, and machine-checked proofs against reasoning errors. We present FVQKD, a Rocq library for machine-checking QKD security proofs. Its first result is a complete, end-to-end machine-checked proof of composable, finite-key security for BB84. The mechanization reconstructs the complete proof infrastructure from first principles, including the smooth entropy framework, the entropic uncertainty relation, and the Quantum Leftover Hash Lemma. It uncovers necessary side conditions that the published argument leaves unstated, one of which reveals a missing proof branch, and it grounds the information-theoretic bound in a formal semantics of protocol execution, which the pen-and-paper analysis lacks. The proof is entirely admit-free, relying only on the Rocq kernel and standard foundational axioms. To our knowledge, this is the first end-to-end formal verification of a QKD security proof. Built on MathComp, MathComp-Analysis, and CoqQ, the development provides quantum-information infrastructure designed for reuse across broader QKD variants and quantum cryptography applications.
one_liner: FVQKD provides an admit-free Rocq proof of composable finite-key security for BB84 from protocol semantics to key extraction.
why_it_matters: Machine checking exposes hidden assumptions and a missing proof branch, strengthening assurance for standardized and deployed QKD systems.
detailed_summary: FVQKD mechanizes an end-to-end composable finite-key security proof for BB84 in Rocq. The library reconstructs smooth-entropy tools, the entropic uncertainty relation, and the Quantum Leftover Hash Lemma, then connects the bound to formal protocol-execution semantics. The verification identifies unstated side conditions and a missing branch in the published hand proof, while using no admitted propositions.
main_result: The work delivers the first claimed end-to-end, machine-checked, admit-free QKD security proof and uncovers gaps in the manual argument.
application_angle: Reusable formal infrastructure can reduce proof risk in QKD standardization, certification, protocol extensions, and commercial deployment.

title: High-fidelity and robust controlled-Z gates for superconducting transmon qubits. II. System-parameter uncertainties and overall errors
abstract: In the companion paper (Part I), we developed an optimal-control framework to suppress intrinsic and decoherence-induced errors in controlled-Z (CZ) gates between directly coupled, frequency-tunable transmons. Here, we extend this framework to incorporate uncertainties in coupling strength, anharmonicities, and zero-flux qubit frequencies, enabling the design of high-fidelity gates robust against noise and parameter uncertainties. We classify these uncertainties by whether they perturb the off-diagonal coupling strengths or the diagonal detunings of the Hamiltonian, and we identify distinct suppression mechanisms for each class. Coupling errors are mitigated through dynamical decoupling induced by strong detuning modulation. For a 30-ns gate, this strategy reduces the coupling error to $6.21\times10^{-7}$ and tolerates coupling-strength uncertainties up to $2π\times4$ MHz while keeping total gate infidelity below $10^{-3}$. Detuning errors are minimized near a symmetric-detuning operating point that balances the two dominant leakage-mediated interactions. A 24-ns gate operated near this point tolerates individual uncertainties of up to $2π\times5$ MHz in each relevant diagonal parameter under the same infidelity threshold. We further optimize gate performance under realistic conditions where intrinsic errors, decoherence, and parameter uncertainties coexist across six representative stages of progressively improving hardware performance. The resulting stage-specific controls achieve lower infidelity and greater robustness. Together with the companion study (Part I), this framework offers a practical approach to balance speed, fidelity, and robustness while reducing the need for exhaustive characterization and frequent recalibration in large-scale superconducting quantum processors.
one_liner: Robust optimal-control pulses keep fast transmon CZ-gate infidelity below 10^-3 despite multi-megahertz parameter uncertainty.
why_it_matters: Tolerance to imperfect device characterization can reduce calibration overhead while preserving fast, high-fidelity superconducting gates.
detailed_summary: The framework incorporates uncertainty in coupling strength, anharmonicity, and zero-flux qubit frequencies when optimizing CZ gates between tunable transmons. Strong detuning modulation dynamically suppresses coupling errors, giving a 6.21×10^-7 coupling error for a 30 ns gate and tolerating coupling uncertainty up to 2π×4 MHz below 10^-3 total infidelity. A symmetric-detuning point enables a 24 ns gate to tolerate individual diagonal-parameter uncertainties up to 2π×5 MHz under the same threshold.
main_result: Optimized 24–30 ns CZ controls remain below 10^-3 infidelity across realistic multi-megahertz Hamiltonian-parameter uncertainties.
application_angle: More robust gates could reduce exhaustive characterization and frequent recalibration in large superconducting quantum processors.

title: Time-reversal-based quantum metrology in a central-spin architecture: from SATIN to butterfly echo
abstract: We investigate quantum-enhanced time-reversal-based metrology using the central spin model, in which a single ancilla spin of magnitude $S_{\rm cen}$ mediates interactions between $N$ bath spins through a star-graph topology. We demonstrate that the SATIN (Signal Amplification Through Time-reversal Interaction) echo protocol can be implemented in this setup to achieve a Fisher information of $N^2/e$ with the collective $\langle J_y\rangle$ readout, corresponding to a $4.34\,\mathrm{dB}$ offset from the Heisenberg limit. Furthermore, we establish that this platform provides a pathway to perform the butterfly echo protocol by conjugating each evolution step with a random collective bath rotation, thereby achieving axis-agnostic Heisenberg-scaled sensing. Crucially, with a small $N-$independent number of random steps, the butterfly echo reaches a Fisher information of $N^2/4$ ($6\,\mathrm{dB}$ below the Heisenberg limit) for any unknown encoding axis, with the plateau gain tracking the Haar limit. Finally, we demonstrate that the central-spin magnitude $S_{\rm cen}$ provides a powerful knob to reduce the optimal protocol timescale without altering the metrological ceiling or the circuit depth required to reach isotropy. The proposed scheme is relevant to cavity QED and NMR quantum processors, where the central spin architecture arises naturally.
one_liner: Central-spin time-reversal protocols provide near-Heisenberg collective sensing and axis-agnostic enhancement with few random steps.
why_it_matters: The scheme combines strong quantum enhancement, unknown-axis sensing, and tunable protocol speed in cavity-QED and NMR-compatible hardware.
detailed_summary: In a star-coupled central-spin model, the SATIN echo reaches Fisher information N^2/e using collective Jy readout, corresponding to a 4.34 dB offset from the Heisenberg limit. Random collective bath rotations convert the protocol into a butterfly echo that becomes axis agnostic and reaches N^2/4 Fisher information with only a small, N-independent number of steps. Increasing the central-spin magnitude shortens the optimal timescale without changing the metrological ceiling or isotropization depth.
platform_or_system: Central-spin bath in cavity QED or NMR
main_result: The proposed echoes achieve Heisenberg-scaled sensing, including axis-agnostic Fisher information N^2/4 with constant-depth randomization.
application_angle: The architecture offers a route to robust quantum-enhanced sensing when the signal axis is unknown or interrogation time is constrained.

title: Demand-Driven Routing Space for Lattice-Surgery Compilation
abstract: Lattice-surgery compilation places logical qubits on a grid of surface-code tiles and routes their interactions. Sparse static layouts limit routing contention but reserve space that often remains idle. Reducing this reservation requires balancing area savings against additional gate serialization and qubit movement. In this paper, we present a co-designed dynamic architecture and compiler that allocates routing space according to circuit demand. The architecture preserves a fixed virtual qubit floorplan while allowing its physical spacing to change between execution stages. The compiler coordinates placement, scheduling, and routing to implement lattice surgeries using fewer physical qubits. Across our application benchmarks, our method reduces space-time volume by 55.6% in geometric mean and compiles 75.5 times faster than the evaluated DasCot configuration. A circuit-synthesis case study shows how our compiler exposes optimization tradeoffs.
one_liner: Demand-driven lattice-surgery routing cuts geometric-mean space-time volume by 55.6% while greatly accelerating compilation.
why_it_matters: Dynamic allocation reduces the physical-qubit cost of fault-tolerant computation without abandoning a stable logical floorplan.
detailed_summary: The proposed architecture preserves a fixed virtual logical-qubit floorplan while varying physical spacing between execution stages according to routing demand. Its compiler jointly coordinates placement, scheduling, movement, and lattice-surgery routing to avoid reserving mostly idle communication space. Across application benchmarks, it reduces geometric-mean space-time volume by 55.6% and compiles 75.5 times faster than the evaluated DasCot configuration.
main_result: Demand-driven routing achieves a 55.6% geometric-mean space-time reduction and a 75.5× compilation speedup over the evaluated baseline.
application_angle: The approach can lower physical-qubit and runtime requirements for practical fault-tolerant quantum computers.

title: Reconfigurable Free-Space Optical Interconnects
abstract: Free-space optical interconnects can support many low-data-rate channels while avoiding the cost, energy consumption, and packaging constraints of optical waveguide- or fiber-based systems that are widely used today. We propose a free-space optical interconnect system based on reconfigurable micromirror arrays, and show that it scales favorably due to its two-dimensional scaling. We discuss the channel count scaling model, compare our demonstration with theory, and project a channel count above 10,000 to achieve 100 Tbps with slow channels (e.g., <10 Gbps). In a proof-of-concept system with a piston-motion micromirror array, we demonstrate nine channels that are simultaneously optimized. The optimization enables -21.7 dB of average worst-case crosstalk for a channel pitch equal to twice the beam radius, a smaller channel spacing than that required in flat tip-tilt mirrors. The optimization flow is further investigated for different channel spacings, simultaneous illumination, and different numbers of outputs, which generally achieve smaller worst-case crosstalk than the flat tip-tilt mirror case. Overall, the work demonstrates the advantage of piston-motion micromirrors in the proposed optical interconnects.
one_liner: Reconfigurable piston micromirror arrays simultaneously optimize dense free-space optical links with low interchannel crosstalk.
why_it_matters: The two-dimensional architecture could provide more than 10,000 low-rate channels and an aggregate 100 Tbps without dense waveguide or fiber packaging.
detailed_summary: The proposed interconnect uses piston-motion micromirror arrays to reconfigure many parallel free-space optical channels. A nine-channel prototype achieved -21.7 dB average worst-case crosstalk at a pitch of twice the beam radius, outperforming the analyzed flat tip-tilt configuration. A two-dimensional scaling model projects over 10,000 channels for 100 Tbps aggregate throughput using sub-10-Gbps links.
main_result: Nine channels were simultaneously optimized with -21.7 dB average worst-case crosstalk, while the scaling model projects more than 10,000 channels.
application_angle: The approach targets high-bandwidth, energy-efficient chip and system interconnects with relaxed optical-packaging constraints.

title: A simple proof of unitary parallelization via port-based teleportation
abstract: Port-based teleportation (PBT) is a variant of quantum teleportation that does not require corrections on the teleported state: starting with $N$ shared EPR states, Alice can teleport a qudit to Bob by performing a measurement on her system and informing Bob which of his $N$ `ports' to retrieve the state, up to infidelity decaying with $N$. Existing quantum circuits of PBT rely on representation theory tools and the mixed Schur transform. In this note, we report an elementary efficient circuit for PBT, which has depth $\operatorname{polylog}(N,d)$. As a corollary, this gives a simple proof that all $n$-qubit unitaries can be parallelized to $\operatorname{poly}(n)$ depth, recovering a recent result due to Nehoran--Slote--Yuen and OpenAI.
one_liner: An elementary port-based teleportation circuit achieves polylogarithmic depth in the number of ports and qudit dimension.
why_it_matters: The construction simplifies port-based teleportation and yields a direct route to parallelizing arbitrary n-qubit unitaries to polynomial depth.
detailed_summary: Port-based teleportation transfers a qudit using one of N shared EPR ports without requiring a correction on the recovered state, at an infidelity that decreases with N. The paper gives an elementary efficient circuit of depth polylog(N,d), avoiding the mixed Schur-transform machinery used by earlier constructions. As a corollary, it recovers polynomial-depth parallelization of arbitrary n-qubit unitaries.
main_result: The authors construct a port-based teleportation circuit with depth polylogarithmic in N and d and derive polynomial-depth unitary parallelization.
application_angle: Shallower teleportation primitives could reduce latency in distributed quantum processing and measurement-based implementations.

title: Exceptional point structure and chiral state transfer in a rate-operator-engineered $\mathcal{PT}$-symmetric Bose-Hubbard dimer
abstract: The rate operator quantum jumps (ROQJ) is a general method to unravel a master equation describing the dynamics of an open quantum system into stochastic pure state trajectories. By post-selecting on no jumps occurring, one obtains a trajectory generated by a non-Hermitian Hamiltonian. The ROQJ allows for versatile modification of this non-Hermitian evolution, with each non-Hermitian Hamiltonian corresponding to a different continuous measurement scheme. We apply the ROQJ to modify the non-Hermitian dynamics of the open three-particle Bose-Hubbard dimer model under environmental non-local dephasing to construct a $PT$-symmetric non-Hermitian Hamiltonians with a general two parameter $PT$-symmetric imaginary diagonal part, which generalizes the well-known gain-loss Bose-Hubbard dimer. We characterize the symmetry structure of the spectrum for different on-site interaction strengths. For vanishing on-site interaction, we find the unbroken $PT$-symmetry region enclosed by order two exceptional lines of different character and four order four exceptional points, two of which are not found in the usual gain-loss Bose-Hubbard dimer. Additionally, we find regions with degenerate imaginary parts of the eigenvalues, also not found in the gain-loss Bose-Hubbard dimer. In this parameter space, we use time-dependent rate operator transformations to investigate state transfer under slowly varying parameter loops. Loops encircling an order four exceptional point exhibit chiral state transfer. Because the loops cross exceptional lines, the final states are superpositions of eigenstates. Chiral state transfer is also found with non-zero homogeneous on-site interaction when the loop crosses over broken $PT$-symmetry regions of different character. Using inhomogeneous on-site interactions, we find direction dependent state transfer between eigenstates without crossing or encircling exceptional points.
one_liner: Measurement-engineered non-Hermitian Bose-Hubbard dynamics reveal higher-order exceptional points and directional state transfer.
why_it_matters: The work expands the controllable topology of PT-symmetric many-body systems and identifies several routes to chiral or direction-dependent state conversion.
detailed_summary: Rate-operator quantum-jump engineering maps continuous-measurement choices onto tunable non-Hermitian Hamiltonians for an open three-particle Bose-Hubbard dimer. Without on-site interaction, the spectrum contains second-order exceptional lines and four fourth-order exceptional points, including two absent from the standard gain-loss dimer. Parameter loops produce chiral transfer, while inhomogeneous interactions enable direction-dependent eigenstate transfer without crossing or encircling exceptional points.
main_result: Engineered measurement dynamics produce new fourth-order exceptional points and controllable chiral or direction-dependent state transfer.
application_angle: The protocol provides design principles for non-Hermitian state routing in controllable bosonic and photonic quantum simulators.

title: In situ enhanced detectability of axions' responses in a microwave cavity
abstract: Microwave cavities in strong magnetic fields are among the most sensitive detectors for axion dark matter detection. Its sensitivity, however, is fundamentally limited by the second order nature of axion photon energy conversion, which yields an extremely weak signal. Here we propose a feasible approach to break this limitation, by pre-exciting the target cavity mode to generate a first order power response signal in situ. The resulting signal amplitude scales linearly with the axion-photon coupling parameter, which is in sharp contrast to the quadratic scaling of conventional schemes, and is detectable via standard quadrature balanced homodyne detection system, even though its phase remains stochastic. Numerical simulations demonstrate that this pre-excited seed field can effectively suppress thermal noise, and thus the detection sensitivity of the system can approach the lower quantum noise limit. Consequently, the sensitivities predicted by the KSVZ and DFSZ models could be surpassed. This proposal might offer a pathway to a major leap in axion dark matter searches, as it is within reach of current technology.
one_liner: Pre-exciting an axion haloscope cavity converts its response from quadratic to linear scaling in axion-photon coupling.
why_it_matters: The proposed homodyne-readable response could approach the quantum-noise floor and extend cavity searches beyond benchmark KSVZ and DFSZ sensitivities.
detailed_summary: The proposal seeds the target mode of a magnetized microwave cavity so that axion-induced interference generates a power response linear in the axion-photon coupling, rather than the conventional quadratic response. Balanced homodyne detection extracts the quadrature signal despite its stochastic phase. Numerical simulations indicate suppression of thermal noise and sensitivity approaching the lower quantum-noise limit.
main_result: Simulations predict a linear-in-coupling axion response measurable by balanced homodyne detection near the quantum-noise limit.
application_angle: The scheme could upgrade existing cavity haloscopes using currently accessible microwave excitation and quadrature-detection technology.

title: All-photonic millimeter-wave and terahertz signal core at room and cryogenic temperatures
abstract: Millimeter-wave and terahertz technologies offer new opportunities for high-capacity communications, sensing, and quantum systems, but electronic signal chains above 100 GHz are limited by weak sources, noisy receivers, and lossy interconnects. Photonic approaches mitigate these constraints by enabling chip-scale high-frequency components, yet existing implementations generally retain lossy off-chip electrical or free-space links, hindering dense and compact integration for cryogenic or space-constrained settings. Here, we show a monolithic lithium tantalate photonic chip, termed a signal core, which generates, modulates, routes, and detects continuous-wave signals at discrete frequencies between 100 GHz and 2.5 THz. The architecture integrates high-frequency functional modules on chip and uses exclusively fiber-based optical interfaces. Bidirectional coherent electro-optic conversion enables signal generation, detection, and nanosecond-scale amplitude and phase modulation, while micro-coplanar striplines interconnect the modules into an end-to-end signal chain on a single chip. Our modules achieve single-photon electro-optic coupling rates of g_0/2π=10 kHz and peak drive-power-normalized photon-flux conversion efficiencies of 1.0%/mW for generation and 0.5%/mW for detection. It also operates at 4 K in a dilution refrigerator through the same fiber-only optical links. Together, these capabilities establish an all-photonic platform for millimeter-wave-to-terahertz systems and offer a broadly applicable architecture for applications constrained by electrical-interconnect loss, heat load, and footprint.
one_liner: A monolithic lithium-tantalate chip performs generation, modulation, routing, and detection from 100 GHz to 2.5 THz.
why_it_matters: Fiber-only interfaces and operation at both room temperature and 4 K address loss, heat-load, and footprint constraints in high-frequency systems.
detailed_summary: The monolithic signal core integrates coherent electro-optic generation, detection, routing, and nanosecond-scale amplitude and phase modulation across discrete frequencies from 100 GHz to 2.5 THz. Micro-coplanar striplines connect the modules on chip, while all external access is optical fiber. It reaches g0/2π = 10 kHz and peak drive-normalized photon-flux efficiencies of 1.0%/mW for generation and 0.5%/mW for detection, and remains operational at 4 K.
main_result: The chip realizes an end-to-end, fiber-interfaced 100-GHz-to-2.5-THz signal chain at room temperature and 4 K.
application_angle: It enables compact high-frequency links for communications, sensing, and cryogenic quantum systems where electrical wiring is lossy or thermally costly.

title: A sharp gradient-corrected Lieb--Thirring inequality in one dimension with applications to density functional theory
abstract: We first prove a sharp Lieb-Thirring inequality with semi-classical constant and gradient correction in one dimension. In the periodic setting, the corresponding inequality also includes a parity dependent shell-correction term, which appears to be new. Moreover, we also characterize the optimizers of these inequalities. In particular, the optimizing density profiles form a two-dimensional manifold, which we call here the Poincaré density manifold. We then apply these results to study the Thomas--Fermi--von Weizsäcker (TFW) approximation of the kinetic energy in Density Functional Theory. More precisely, we first obtain an explicit and non-asymptotic bound on the global and local error made by the TFW approximation. These bounds are controlled by the distance of the normalized density profile from the Poincaré density manifold times the number of particles. In particular, these bounds show that the TFW approximation is exact on the Poincaré manifold. We then show that, in the periodic setting, the distance between the Kohn-Sham potential and the inverse TFW potential in the natural dual Sobolev space can also be controlled by explicit density dependent constants times the distance to the Poincaré manifold. As a corollary, we prove that for a fixed density profile, the Kohn-Sham potential converges towards the inverse Thomas--Fermi potential in the high-density limit $N \rightarrow \infty$ with asymptotic rate of order $N^{-2}$. This rate is shown to be optimal.
one_liner: A sharp one-dimensional Lieb-Thirring bound quantifies gradient and shell corrections to density-functional kinetic-energy models.
why_it_matters: Explicit error bounds identify when Thomas-Fermi-von Weizsäcker theory is exact and establish optimal high-density convergence of inverse potentials.
detailed_summary: The authors prove a sharp one-dimensional Lieb-Thirring inequality with the semiclassical constant and a gradient correction; the periodic result also contains a parity-dependent shell term. Optimizing densities form a two-dimensional Poincaré density manifold on which the Thomas-Fermi-von Weizsäcker kinetic-energy approximation is exact. They derive explicit global and local errors and show that the Kohn-Sham potential approaches the inverse Thomas-Fermi potential at the optimal N^-2 rate for fixed density profiles.
main_result: The work establishes sharp gradient-corrected bounds, characterizes all optimizers, and proves an optimal N^-2 high-density potential-convergence rate.
application_angle: The bounds provide rigorous accuracy diagnostics for reduced-cost density-functional modeling of one-dimensional quantum materials and devices.

title: A Personal History in Quantum Foundations: an Oral History Interview
abstract: This oral history interview provides Yakir Aharonov's personal and conceptual recollections from the 1950s to the 2000s, focusing on his academic trajectory, some of his major contributions to quantum foundations, and his perspective on the development of the field. The interview traces Aharonov's academic career through the Technion, University of Bristol, Brandeis University, Yeshiva University, University of South Carolina, Tel Aviv University, George Mason University, and Chapman University. The interview also traces the development of Aharonov's work and collaborations on the EPR paradox, time-energy uncertainty relations, quantum measurement theory, quantum frames of reference, the two-state vector formalism, weak values, protective measurements, and several other contributions. It includes recollections of meetings and discussions with David Bohm, Niels Bohr, John Clauser, Paul Dirac, Rudolf Peierls, Aage Petersen, and Abner Shimony. Also mentioned: David Albert, Jeeva Anandan, Peter Bergmann, Gideon Carmi, Avshalom Elitzur, Dave Finkelstein, Vladimir Fock, Itzhak Kalugai, Ed Lerner, Joel Lebowitz, Stanley Mandelstam, Yuval Ne'eman, Sandu Popescu, Maurice Pryce, Daniel Rohrlich, Nathan Rosen, Joseph Safko, Paul Singer, Daniele Struppa, Leonard Susskind, Lev Vaidman, Chien-Shiung Wu.
one_liner: An oral history traces Yakir Aharonov’s career and the development of influential ideas in quantum foundations and measurement.
why_it_matters: The interview preserves first-hand context on weak values, protective measurements, and other concepts that later influenced quantum sensing protocols.
detailed_summary: This oral-history interview documents Yakir Aharonov’s scientific career from the 1950s through the 2000s. It recounts the development of the two-state vector formalism, weak values, protective measurements, time-energy uncertainty relations, and related foundational work. Its relevance to sensing is historical and conceptual rather than an experimental demonstration.
main_result: The paper records a first-person history of major developments in quantum foundations and measurement theory.
application_angle: It provides historical context for measurement concepts that underpin weak-value and related quantum-sensing approaches.

title: Efficient Modeling of 3D-Printed Freeform Waveguides with a Transformation Optics-Based Beam Propagation Method
abstract: An efficient numerical method is introduced for simulating wave propagation in 3D-printed freeform waveguides, referred to as photonic wire bonds (PWBs). This approach integrates transformation optics (TO) with curvilinear meshing to map the original 3D freeform PWB structure onto a straight waveguide, which possesses anisotropic material characteristics. The resulting waveguide is then analyzed using an anisotropic full-vectorial beam propagation method (BPM). To validate the performance and effectiveness of the proposed TO-BPM algorithm, a comparison is made with the finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) technique. Our approach reduces the simulation time by more than two orders of magnitude, depending on the degree of trajectory bending, in combination with a mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) of 3.9% in power transmission simulation relative to the FDTD.
one_liner: A transformation-optics beam-propagation method simulates curved 3D-printed photonic wire bonds over 100 times faster than FDTD.
why_it_matters: Fast full-vector modeling could accelerate design optimization of freeform chip-to-chip optical interconnects while retaining useful transmission accuracy.
detailed_summary: The method maps a three-dimensional curved photonic wire bond onto a straight waveguide with anisotropic material parameters using transformation optics and curvilinear meshing. An anisotropic full-vectorial beam-propagation solver then calculates propagation and transmission. Against FDTD, it achieves more than two orders of magnitude shorter simulation time, depending on bend severity, with a 3.9% mean absolute percentage error in transmitted power.
main_result: The TO-BPM approach delivers over 100-fold simulation speedup with 3.9% transmission MAPE relative to FDTD.
application_angle: The method enables faster iterative design of compact freeform optical links for photonic packaging and chip interconnection.

title: Noise redistribution by stabilizer codes: an organizing view of concatenated three-qubit codes
abstract: We present an organizing framework for concatenated quantum error correction based on the observation that the syndrome projection of a stabilizer code reshapes the noise channel in a code-determined manner. For any stabilizer code, one level of QEC maps the physical noise to a block-diagonal logical channel whose diagonal Pauli weights are fixed by the code geometry. Coherences between different syndrome classes vanish, and no physical Pauli twirl is required to reach this block-diagonal form. Concatenation can then be viewed as the iteration of the same redistribution step: the dominant logical error after one level selects the code used at the next. We instantiate the framework with the two smallest stabilizer codes, the bit-flip and phase-flip codes, and apply it to amplitude damping. The redistribution rules give the concatenation protocol $C_2(\hatσ_y) C_1(\hatσ_x)$, whose ideal-recovery fidelity scales as $f_l=1-\mathcal O(γ^2)$. Solving the crossover condition $F_l>F_{l-1}$ in the ideal-gate limit yields a critical damping parameter $γ_c\approx0.30$; in terms of the initial channel fidelity, $f=1-1.72755γ^2$. Under the same ideal-recovery assumption, we compare the overall gate accuracy rate with that of the five-qubit code. The scope of the framework, in particular for coherent and correlated noise, is stated explicitly.
one_liner: A stabilizer-code framework treats concatenated error correction as iterative redistribution of physical noise into logical Pauli channels.
why_it_matters: The approach offers a code-guided way to select concatenation order for non-Pauli noise and quantify when added correction levels improve fidelity.
detailed_summary: The framework shows that syndrome projection maps arbitrary physical noise to a code-dependent block-diagonal logical channel without requiring a physical Pauli twirl. Concatenation is interpreted as repeated noise redistribution, with the dominant logical error determining the next code. For amplitude damping, concatenated phase- and bit-flip three-qubit codes yield ideal-recovery infidelity of order γ² and a crossover threshold near γ=0.30.
main_result: Code-guided concatenation suppresses amplitude-damping infidelity to order γ² under ideal recovery, with improvement predicted below γ≈0.30.
application_angle: The framework can guide low-overhead error-correction design for quantum processors dominated by relaxation or other structured noise.

title: Lifetime of the singly charged $^{229}$Th nuclear isomer
abstract: The nucleus of thorium-229 ($^{229}$Th) has an exceptionally low-energy isomeric state ($^{229\mathrm{m}}$Th). Because its excitation energy is close to the energy levels of valence electrons, the lifetime of $^{229\mathrm{m}}$Th varies substantially depending on its electronic state. Although internal conversion and radiative decay were recently observed, the electronic bridge decay of $^{229\mathrm{m}}$Th, a higher-order decay process through an electronic transition, has not yet been confirmed. A promising candidate to search for this decay channel is singly charged $^{229\mathrm{m}}$Th$^+$ in the electronic ground state. Here we produce $^{229\mathrm{m}}$Th$^+$ by a charge exchange reaction in an ion trap and detect the isomers through measuring the electrons emitted from internal conversion processes. We determined the half-life of $^{229\mathrm{m}}$Th$^+$ to be 0.46(8) s. Our result differs by several orders of magnitude from the half-lives of internal conversion and radiative decay, indirectly suggesting the existence of the electronic bridge decay of $^{229\mathrm{m}}$Th. This will enable the direct observation and further investigation of the electronic bridge process, which will contribute to understanding nuclear-electron interactions and accelerating nuclear deexcitation in the operation of a thorium-based nuclear clock.
one_liner: Ion-trap measurements determine a 0.46(8) s half-life for singly charged thorium-229 nuclear isomers.
why_it_matters: The anomalous lifetime indirectly supports electronic-bridge decay and informs charge-state engineering for thorium nuclear clocks.
detailed_summary: The experiment produces singly charged metastable thorium-229 ions through charge exchange in an ion trap. Isomers are identified through electrons emitted by internal-conversion processes, yielding a measured half-life of 0.46(8) s. Its large difference from known internal-conversion and radiative lifetimes indirectly indicates an electronic-bridge decay contribution.
main_result: The singly charged thorium-229 isomer has a measured half-life of 0.46(8) s, indirectly suggesting electronic-bridge decay.
application_angle: Characterizing electronic-state-dependent decay is important for controlling nuclear excitation and de-excitation in thorium-based clocks.

title: Local Dephasing Sustains Continuous Time Crystals in a Spin-1/2 Ensemble
abstract: Local pure dephasing suppresses single-spin coherence, yet we show that it sustains continuous time-crystalline order in a fully connected ferromagnetic spin-$1/2$ ensemble with local decay. An exact operator identity reveals the mechanism: dephasing raises the interaction energy, while energy relaxation on a finite timescale converts this charging into delayed feedback. Within homogeneous mean-field theory, we prove that dephasing is necessary for periodic motion in this model and that feedback exactly balances transverse damping over each cycle. Beyond mean field, the identity fixes the relative amplitude and phase of energy and longitudinal magnetization in oscillatory Liouvillian modes. Liouvillian spectra and stationary two-time correlations characterize temporal order through decay rates that decrease algebraically with system size, frequencies approaching nonzero mean-field values, and comparable per-spin oscillatory weights. Semiclassical trajectories further reveal recurrent switching between a limit-cycle region and two symmetry-related stationary regions: fluctuations interrupt and reactivate collective oscillations, and oscillatory episodes provide an intermediate channel between stationary regions. These results establish local dephasing as a resource for autonomous collective motion and show how the resulting temporal order can participate in metastable dynamics.
one_liner: Local dephasing is shown to sustain continuous time-crystalline oscillations in a fully connected dissipative spin-1/2 ensemble.
why_it_matters: Turning dephasing into a resource for autonomous collective motion could inform robust nonequilibrium quantum devices and oscillator-based sensors.
detailed_summary: An exact operator identity shows that local dephasing raises interaction energy, while delayed relaxation converts this charging into feedback that sustains oscillations. Homogeneous mean-field theory makes dephasing necessary for periodic motion and predicts exact cycle-averaged compensation of transverse damping. Liouvillian spectra, two-time correlations, and semiclassical trajectories show algebraically improving coherence with system size and fluctuation-driven switching among oscillatory and stationary regions.
main_result: Local dephasing generates feedback that stabilizes finite-frequency continuous time-crystalline motion despite single-spin coherence loss.
application_angle: The mechanism suggests autonomous collective oscillators that exploit, rather than merely tolerate, dephasing in quantum hardware and sensing.

title: Fock-space relativistic coupled-cluster study of systematic shifts and fine-structure constant sensitivity in {\rm Cf$^{17+}$}, {\rm Cm$^{15+}$} and {\rm Bk$^{16+}$} highly charged ions
abstract: Highly charged ions (HCIs) are among the most promising candidates proposed for the development of next-generation optical clocks and the precision tests of fundamental physics. In this work, we investigate the clock-relevant properties of $\rm Cf^{17+}$, $\rm Cm^{15+}$ and $\rm Bk^{16+}$ HCIs using Fock-space relativistic coupled-cluster (FSRCC) theory. The corrections from Breit interaction, QED effects and perturbative triples are incorporated to improve the accuracy of results further. We compute excitation energies, transition amplitudes, lifetimes, hyperfine structure constants, electric quadrupole moments, and electric dipole polarizabilities for low-lying states of these ions. These properties are further used to characterize important clock transitions and estimate key systematic frequency shifts. Our calculations reveal that the proposed clock transitions exhibit strongly suppressed systematic frequency shifts. We also compute the sensitivity coefficients, $q$, and enhancement factors, $K_α$, for the proposed clock transition as a probe to variation in the fine-structure constant, $α$. Our calculations predict exceptionally large $K_α$ of $-55.3$ and $57.5$ for $5f_{5/2} \rightarrow 6p_{1/2}$ transition in $\rm Cf^{17+}$ and $6p_{1/2} \rightarrow 5f_{5/2}$ transition in $\rm Bk^{16+}$, respectively. These giant $K_α$s place the proposed transitions among the most sensitive optical probes for the laboratory searches for $α$ variation. Further, a comparative analysis of proposed transitions in $\rm Cm^{15+}$ and $\rm Bk^{16+}$ shows that, $5f_{5/2} \rightarrow 5f_{7/2}$ transition possess smaller systematic shifts and is therefore attractive for precision frequency metrology, whereas $6p_{1/2} \rightarrow 5f_{5/2}$ transition exhibit significantly enhanced sensitivity to $α$ variation.
one_liner: Relativistic coupled-cluster calculations identify highly charged ion transitions with low clock shifts and extreme sensitivity to α variation.
why_it_matters: Cf17+, Cm15+, and Bk16+ offer complementary transitions for next-generation optical clocks and laboratory tests of fundamental constants.
detailed_summary: Fock-space relativistic coupled-cluster calculations include Breit, QED, and perturbative-triples corrections for low-lying states of Cf17+, Cm15+, and Bk16+. Computed energies, amplitudes, lifetimes, hyperfine constants, quadrupole moments, and polarizabilities are used to estimate clock shifts. The predicted enhancement factors reach −55.3 for Cf17+ and 57.5 for Bk16+, while selected fine-structure transitions offer smaller systematic shifts.
platform_or_system: Cf17+, Cm15+, and Bk16+ highly charged ions
main_result: The study predicts strongly shift-suppressed clock transitions and α-sensitivity enhancement factors as large as |Kα|=57.5.
application_angle: These transitions could support precision optical clocks and sensitive searches for temporal or environmental variation of the fine-structure constant.

title: Second- and third-order nonlinearities in silicon nitride waveguides via heterogeneous integration of lithium niobate membranes
abstract: Thick, dispersion-engineered silicon nitride is a leading platform for integrated third-order nonlinear optics, supporting supercontinuum and frequency comb generation. However, it lacks the second-order nonlinearity required by many applications. Here we bond pre-fabricated x-cut thin-film lithium niobate membranes onto finished silicon nitride waveguides as a back-end step, compatible with commercially fabricated waveguides. A single silicon nitride waveguide generates an octave-spanning supercontinuum and, through the lithium niobate membrane, concurrent second-harmonic, sum- and difference-frequency generation. These results open new possibilities for thick silicon nitride photonics, from visible light generation to on-chip $f$-$2f$ comb self-referencing, a key step towards miniaturised timing and navigation quantum technologies.
one_liner: Bonded lithium-niobate membranes add second-order nonlinear conversion to dispersion-engineered silicon-nitride waveguides.
why_it_matters: The back-end-compatible process combines octave-spanning comb generation and frequency conversion on one commercially manufacturable photonic platform.
detailed_summary: Pre-fabricated x-cut thin-film lithium-niobate membranes are bonded onto finished, thick silicon-nitride waveguides as a back-end integration step. One waveguide produces an octave-spanning supercontinuum through third-order nonlinearity while concurrently supporting second-harmonic, sum-frequency, and difference-frequency generation in the membrane. The architecture therefore combines χ(2) and χ(3) processes without replacing the established silicon-nitride fabrication flow.
main_result: A single heterogeneous waveguide simultaneously generates an octave-spanning supercontinuum and multiple second-order frequency-conversion products.
application_angle: The platform could enable integrated visible sources and on-chip f–2f comb self-referencing for compact timing, navigation, and quantum-photonic systems.

title: Reset-Enhanced Dissipative Quantum Metrology
abstract: Quantum metrology is ultimately shaped not only by measurements, but also by the dissipative dynamics that prepare and maintain the probe. Nevertheless, a general mechanism for enhancing both steady-state and transient precision in open quantum systems has been lacking. Here we show that adding a simple reset channel provides such a mechanism: reset acts as a minimal dissipative control that can enhance metrological precision without modifying the intrinsic Hamiltonian or applying continuous coherent driving. We derive a unified quantum-Fisher-information (QFI) reset-rate response identity, showing how reset enhances steady-state and transient estimation while revealing a sharp transient distinction. For static-parameter estimation in diagonal dynamics, reset leaves the leading short-time QFI unchanged; for the separate task of elapsed-time estimation, it generates an immediate drift contribution that can scale quadratically with the reset rate in the short-time limit. For frequency estimation, the enhancement is instead dominated by a genuinely quantum eigenvector contribution. These results establish reset as a simple dissipative resource for open-system quantum metrology.
one_liner: A reset channel is shown to enhance steady-state and transient precision in open-system quantum metrology.
why_it_matters: Reset offers experimentally simple dissipative control that can improve sensing without changing the probe Hamiltonian or requiring continuous coherent drive.
detailed_summary: The work derives a unified identity describing how quantum Fisher information responds to reset rate in both steady-state and transient regimes. For diagonal dynamics, reset preserves the leading short-time QFI for static parameters, whereas elapsed-time estimation gains an immediate drift term that can scale quadratically with reset rate. Frequency-estimation gains instead arise mainly from a quantum eigenvector contribution.
main_result: A simple reset process can enhance multiple metrological tasks, with distinct mechanisms governing static-parameter, elapsed-time, and frequency estimation.
application_angle: Reset-based control may improve noisy quantum sensors using dissipative operations that are simpler than Hamiltonian redesign or continuous coherent driving.

title: High-fidelity entanglement of two spectrally-distinct solid state emitters
abstract: Solid state quantum emitters with electronic spin properties can be entangled using optical interferometric which-path erasure techniques that rely on identical frequencies and linewidths of the emitters. This promises a powerful, fast and scalable platform for quantum technologies. Using current protocols, a pair of emitters embedded in a waveguide interferometer can be deterministically prepared in a maximally entangled state. However, the amount of entanglement diminishes rapidly with increasing separation of the emission lines and variations in the linewidths of the emitters. Solid state emitters such as quantum dots are subject to intrinsic variations in the fabrication process. Therefore, manufacturing the required number of identical emitters on a chip is not scalable. In this Letter, we present a method that uses readily available pairs of entangled photons to entangle solid state emitters with large transition frequency separations and linewidth variations, circumventing the need to fabricate optically identical emitters. We demonstrate a concurrence of C = 0.95 for typical quantum dots using narrowband photon inputs.
one_liner: Entangled photon pairs enable high-fidelity entanglement between solid-state emitters with mismatched frequencies and linewidths.
why_it_matters: The protocol relaxes the requirement for optically identical emitters, addressing a major fabrication and scaling obstacle for solid-state quantum networks.
detailed_summary: The proposed protocol uses entangled photon pairs to erase distinguishing information between solid-state emitters despite substantial transition-frequency and linewidth mismatch. This replaces the usual reliance on mutually indistinguishable emitter photons in an interferometric entanglement scheme. For representative quantum-dot parameters and narrowband photon inputs, the calculated concurrence reaches 0.95.
main_result: The method achieves a predicted concurrence of 0.95 for typical quantum dots without requiring matched optical transitions or linewidths.
application_angle: Tolerance to emitter variability could improve the manufacturability and scalability of chip-based quantum-network nodes and distributed quantum processors.

title: The Impact of Markovian Errors on Random Circuits
abstract: Randomized benchmarking (RB) returns a single decay parameter or gate error rate, but when the noise is gate-dependent that parameter is notoriously difficult to interpret. We study RB and related random-circuit benchmarks under small gate-local Markovian noise by factorizing each noisy gate into its ideal action followed by the exponential of a small error generator and then perturbing the RB $\mathscr{L}$ matrix, which models the RB decay. For any low-error gate set that satisfies the requirements of RB (it is a sequence-asymptotic unitary 2-design), we show that Pauli-stochastic error rates contribute linearly to the RB decay parameter, while Hamiltonian error rates contribute through a gauge-invariant quadratic form. Pauli-correlation and active generators are absent from the linear term and enter only at higher order. For the single-qubit native gate set $\{X_{π/2},Y_{π/2}\}$ we derive this quadratic form explicitly in terms of three first-order gauge-invariant (FOGI) coordinates: the two intrinsic over-rotations and one relational axis-tilt error. The resulting formula explains the dependence of DRB on the sampling distribution and the compilation dependence of CRB. These results turn RB decay rates into interpretable functions of experimentally meaningful elementary error rates.
one_liner: Perturbative formulas connect randomized-benchmarking decay directly to experimentally meaningful Markovian gate-error components.
why_it_matters: The framework makes RB results more diagnostic by separating linear stochastic errors from gauge-invariant quadratic coherent-error contributions.
detailed_summary: The authors perturb the randomized-benchmarking transfer matrix for low-error gate sets that asymptotically form unitary 2-designs. Pauli-stochastic rates enter the decay parameter linearly, while Hamiltonian errors contribute through a gauge-invariant quadratic form; Pauli correlations and active generators appear only at higher order. For the native single-qubit set {Xπ/2,Yπ/2}, the quadratic term is expressed using two intrinsic over-rotations and one relational axis-tilt coordinate.
main_result: Randomized-benchmarking decay is decomposed into interpretable stochastic and coherent error contributions, including an explicit single-qubit native-gate formula.
application_angle: The formulas can help hardware teams diagnose calibration errors and interpret how sampling distributions and compilation choices affect benchmark results.

title: One-shot entanglement generation and distillation via Petz recovery and binary hypothesis testing
abstract: How much entanglement can two distant laboratories share when their connection is noisy? We relate this question to deciding which of two quantum hypotheses is present. Our one-shot bounds apply to entanglement generation over a quantum channel and to one-way entanglement distillation from a shared state. We use Cheng's trace inequality to bound the infidelity of a Petz decoder in terms of a binary hypothesis testing cost. Applying the inequality before averaging over codes reduces the error analysis to computing a second moment of random subspaces. The proof covers every integer target dimension and treats rank-deficient states explicitly. A corollary expresses the achievable entanglement through hypothesis-testing coherent information, with a single logarithmic error slack and exact integer rounding. We also prove an error-preserving conversion from entanglement generation codes to entanglement transmission codes: the target dimension decreases by only a constant factor at fixed error, and the decoder is the original decoder followed by local processing. Consequently, for both entanglement generation and entanglement transmission, arbitrary pure reference-input states yield the same coherent-information rate, second-order Gaussian correction at the original error tolerance, and explicit achievable logarithmic remainder. For commuting testing hypotheses, the logarithmic remainder improves to a constant. These results give a direct route from binary distinguishability to explicit recovery guarantees and finite-resource quantum communication rates.
one_liner: Petz recovery and binary hypothesis testing yield explicit one-shot bounds for entanglement generation and one-way distillation.
why_it_matters: The bounds translate finite-resource distinguishability into practical recovery guarantees, including second-order rates and controlled logarithmic corrections.
detailed_summary: The analysis bounds Petz-decoder infidelity using a binary hypothesis-testing cost and reduces random-code error analysis to a second moment of random subspaces. It covers every integer target dimension and rank-deficient states, producing achievable rates through hypothesis-testing coherent information with explicit rounding and error slack. An error-preserving conversion also connects entanglement-generation codes to transmission codes with only a constant-factor reduction in target dimension.
main_result: The work establishes explicit one-shot recovery and rate bounds for entanglement generation, transmission, and one-way distillation.
application_angle: These bounds support quantitative design of finite-resource quantum links, repeaters, and entanglement-distribution protocols under realistic channel noise.

title: Problem-aware sampling for bias and variance reduction in randomised Hamiltonian simulation
abstract: Randomised quantum simulation algorithms such as qDRIFT reduce circuit depth by replacing deterministic product formulas with stochastic compilations, but achieving high accuracy can require many steps. In vanilla qDRIFT, Hamiltonian terms are sampled with probabilities proportional to their coefficient magnitudes. We propose StateDRIFT, a variant of qDRIFT which optimises its sampling distribution to estimate time-evolved quantities using knowledge of the initial state and target observable, with a provable truncation bound that keeps qDRIFT's guarantees. The distribution at each depth is chosen by solving an optimisation problem targeting bias and/or variance. StateDRIFT can significantly reduce the bias and variance of estimators, and hence circuit depth, which we test on short-time dynamics of lattice models and molecules under Jordan-Wigner up to 18 qubits. For example, with BeH2 StateDRIFT can reduce the number of two-qubit gates required to achieve a given accuracy from 11,201 to 983. StateDRIFT involves measuring observables and commutators on the initial state, so we propose two practical ways to estimate these: classical surrogates such as tensor networks, and classical shadows, which recover most or all of the saving from exact oracles in the systems tested.
one_liner: StateDRIFT adapts qDRIFT sampling to the initial state and observable, sharply reducing simulation bias, variance, and gate count.
why_it_matters: Problem-aware stochastic compilation could make useful Hamiltonian simulations substantially cheaper on noisy, depth-limited quantum processors.
detailed_summary: StateDRIFT optimizes the Hamiltonian-term sampling distribution at each circuit depth using information about the initial state and target observable while retaining a provable qDRIFT-style truncation bound. Tests cover short-time lattice and molecular dynamics after Jordan–Wigner mapping for systems up to 18 qubits. For BeH2, the reported two-qubit-gate requirement falls from 11,201 to 983 at fixed accuracy, and practical estimates based on tensor-network surrogates or classical shadows retain most of the benefit.
main_result: Problem-aware sampling reduces estimator bias and variance, including an order-of-magnitude two-qubit-gate reduction for the tested BeH2 case.
application_angle: The method can extend the reach of near-term quantum simulation by lowering circuit depth while allowing its optimization data to come from practical classical or measurement-based estimators.

title: Screening strongly correlated materials in solid oxide cells with quantum simulation
abstract: We develop an end-to-end framework for assessing a quantum-computing application in industrial materials science: the screening of strongly correlated oxygen-electrode materials for SOFCs and SOECs. We formulate the materials problem in terms of interface observables including oxygen-vacancy formation energies, vacancy migration barriers, and electronic conductivity. We describe how these observables can be obtained using a diagrammatic GW-based embedding, either GW+DMFT or self-energy embedding theory (SEET), applied to a DFT-screened shortlist. The atomistic electrode/electrolyte interface defines the electronic structure problem from which the correlated impurity models are constructed. Quantum impurity solvers would provide the finite-temperature impurity Green's functions required by the embedding. The computational challenges that classical solvers may encounter as the interacting active space grows, together with the polynomial scaling of quantum Hamiltonian simulation for efficiently represented discretized models, open an opportunity for quantum advantage. We identify the benchmarks needed to assess this opportunity through convergence of vacancy and migration energetics and comparison with the best applicable classical solvers. We provide illustrative logical qubit counts and identify the thermal state preparation, simulation, measurement, and repeated-solve costs needed for a complete resource assessment. We connect microscopic observables to macroscopic engineering metrics using a continuum model for mixed ionic--electronic conducting oxygen electrodes that couples oxygen surface exchange, solid-state oxygen transport, electrode microstructure, and finite electrode thickness. Finally, we estimate the potential worldwide business value of improved electrode materials under SOFC and SOEC deployment scenarios informed by public technical targets and electrolyser deployment data.
one_liner: An end-to-end framework maps quantum impurity simulation of correlated oxide interfaces to solid-oxide-cell performance and business value.
why_it_matters: It defines concrete observables, benchmarks, resource requirements, and engineering metrics for evaluating a potentially valuable industrial quantum-computing application.
detailed_summary: The framework begins with DFT-screened electrode/electrolyte interfaces and constructs correlated impurity models for GW+DMFT or SEET embedding. Quantum solvers would estimate finite-temperature Green's functions used to calculate vacancy formation energies, migration barriers, and electronic conductivity. The study specifies classical benchmarks, illustrative logical-qubit requirements, and costs for thermal-state preparation, simulation, measurement, and repeated solves, then connects microscopic outputs to continuum electrode performance.
platform_or_system: Fault-tolerant quantum impurity simulation for oxide interfaces
main_result: The work establishes a benchmark and resource-assessment pipeline for testing quantum advantage in screening strongly correlated solid-oxide-cell electrodes.
application_angle: The framework targets discovery of improved SOFC and SOEC electrode materials with measurable effects on efficiency, deployment, and commercial value.

title: What does quantum parameter estimation estimate? A no-go result for true quantity values
abstract: We examine the conditions under which quantum parameter estimation is compatible with the concept of a ``true'' quantity value: a unique value of the estimated quantity that exists prior to and independently of measurement. While quantum parameter estimation typically assumes that the quantity to be estimated is a parameter, we argue that this assumption can be lifted, opening the way to a more general formulation of estimation that may apply even in situations where the quantity to be estimated is no longer a parameter, but instead a quantum variable susceptible to quantum fluctuations. We identify three assumptions that characterize the way estimation is often presented in the quantum metrology literature, namely, as a procedure for inferring an unknown ``true value", which is assumed to be unique and to exist prior to and independently of measurement. Using our more general framework, we prove a no-go theorem showing that the preceding assumptions are jointly incompatible with two further assumptions: the completeness of the quantum state (no `hidden variables'), and the presence of entanglement between the probe systems and the system under measurement. We note that the presence of such entanglement is a generic prediction of standard quantum theory. Consequently, if one is not willing to accept hidden variables, nor willing to modify standard quantum theory by introducing a new physical mechanism that destroys entanglement at some scale or regime, then a realist account of estimation is ultimately impossible.
one_liner: A no-go theorem challenges interpreting quantum parameter estimation as recovery of a unique, pre-existing true value.
why_it_matters: It clarifies the conceptual limits of quantum sensing when probes become entangled with the measured system, distinguishing parameter inference from intrinsic-value measurement.
detailed_summary: The authors generalize estimation so the inferred quantity may be a fluctuating quantum variable rather than a fixed external parameter. They prove that a unique, measurement-independent true value is incompatible with both quantum-state completeness and probe-system entanglement under the stated assumptions. Because such entanglement is generic in standard quantum theory, a realist interpretation requires hidden variables or an additional mechanism that destroys entanglement.
main_result: The paper proves that several common true-value assumptions cannot jointly hold with complete quantum states and probe-system entanglement.
application_angle: The result guides how quantum-sensor outputs should be interpreted when measurement backaction and entanglement make the target quantity intrinsically quantum.

title: Confinement of hybridized light modes in nonlinear-optical superpotentials
abstract: In this work, we present a spatial and temporal light trapping mechanism induced by coherent frequency conversion. We consider a wave-mixing process, where a pumped nonlinearity mediates a frequency-domain beamsplitter interaction between two signal modes. When these wave modes are counterpropagating, temporally trapped eigenmodes emerge at the zero of the nonlinearity profile. We establish that such spatio-temporal trapping has a direct connection to supersymmetric quantum mechanics, which ensures the existence and robustness of the trapped modes and allows us to derive analytic solutions of the bound eigenmodes. Backwards sum-frequency conversion may thus enable a unique class of active photonic memory devices, whose design parameters are compatible with the state of the art in integrated nonlinear photonics. We propose proof-of-principle experiments to study this nonlinear-optical trapping effect on thin-film lithium niobate. In addition, as a case study, we show how the temporal trap can be used alongside parametric gain. Our work unveils potential applications ranging from classical integrated photonics to multimode quantum nonlinear photonics.
one_liner: Coherent frequency conversion can confine counterpropagating optical modes in robust spatiotemporal traps defined by a nonlinear profile.
why_it_matters: The mechanism offers an active, analytically designable route to integrated photonic memories and multimode quantum nonlinear-optical devices.
detailed_summary: A pumped nonlinearity mediates a frequency-domain beamsplitter interaction between two counterpropagating signal modes. Temporally localized eigenmodes form at a zero of the nonlinear coupling profile, with supersymmetric quantum mechanics guaranteeing their existence and robustness and enabling analytic bound-state solutions. The authors propose thin-film lithium-niobate experiments and analyze operation of the temporal trap alongside parametric gain.
main_result: The study derives robust spatiotemporally trapped hybrid light modes produced by backward coherent frequency conversion.
application_angle: The proposed trap could support compact active photonic memories, controllable pulse storage, and multimode quantum-frequency processing.

title: The Entire Quantum Computer on a Classical Leash
abstract: We show that a classical client with no quantum hardware can use a single untrusted and potentially malicious quantum server as if it were its own trusted quantum computer. Through the server, the client can privately choose and run quantum computations, prepare quantum states, and process quantum states supplied by other parties. It can also keep quantum memory on the server, hidden from the server itself, and use that memory in later computations so its quantum state persists across rounds of interaction. Together, these capabilities let a purely classical party act as a quantum party in a variety of interactive protocols. We expect this virtual quantum computer to be a broadly useful tool. As immediate applications, we resolve two known open problems: (1) classical verification of quantum sampling with negligible computational soundness error, and (2) remote state preparation of arbitrary efficiently preparable quantum states. Underlying all of these results is a general-purpose, maliciously secure two-party computation protocol between a classical client and a quantum server, which we construct assuming only the post-quantum hardness of learning with errors.
one_liner: A classical client can privately operate a persistent virtual quantum computer through one untrusted quantum server.
why_it_matters: The protocol expands secure delegated quantum computing to state preparation, external-state processing, and reusable hidden quantum memory without client quantum hardware.
detailed_summary: The construction gives a purely classical client private control over computations, state preparation, externally supplied quantum states, and persistent quantum memory held by a potentially malicious server. Its foundation is a general maliciously secure classical-client/quantum-server two-party computation protocol based only on post-quantum learning-with-errors hardness. The framework also yields classical verification of quantum sampling with negligible computational soundness error and remote preparation of arbitrary efficiently preparable states.
main_result: The protocol realizes a private, persistent virtual quantum computer for a classical client using one untrusted quantum server.
application_angle: It enables secure cloud access to quantum computation and quantum-network protocols without requiring clients to own or operate quantum devices.

title: A Topology-Aware Quantum-Classical Framework for Multi-Target Active Debris Removal using Gaussian Boson Sampling
abstract: The continued growth of orbital debris threatens the safety and sustainability of near-Earth space, making Active Debris Removal (ADR) an important mitigation strategy. Selecting $k$ targets from $N$ candidates yields a combinatorial search space of size $\binom{N}{k}$, making joint target selection and mission sequencing computationally demanding. We present a topology-aware quantum-classical framework integrating orbital mechanics, weighted orbital-transfer graphs, Gaussian Boson Sampling (GBS), and multi-objective evolutionary optimization. Seven target-prioritization strategies represent physical consequence, orbital persistence, conjunction risk, network centrality, community structure, inferred source families, and random selection. GBS generates candidate target subsets from the weighted graph, which are then evaluated using PyGMO-based evolutionary optimization to identify servicing sequences that jointly minimize total velocity increment ($Δv$) and mission duration, accounting for modeled timing, propulsion, and mass feasibility. We evaluate the framework across three benchmark environments, SOCRATES Minefield, Collision Cloud, and Random, with candidate-pool sizes $N\in\{15,18,22,25\}$ and target cardinalities $k\in\{3,5\}$. The experiments characterize how benchmark topology, prioritization strategy, and problem scale relate to sampling behavior and downstream mission performance. By separating candidate-subset generation from detailed trajectory optimization, the framework offers a topology-aware approach to focusing computational effort on a limited set of candidate ADR missions.
one_liner: A hybrid framework uses Gaussian boson sampling to propose orbital-debris target sets before classical multi-objective route optimization.
why_it_matters: It tests photonic quantum sampling as a candidate-generation tool for a real combinatorial mission-planning problem across varied graph topologies.
detailed_summary: The method encodes orbital-transfer relationships as weighted graphs and uses Gaussian boson sampling to generate subsets of debris targets. PyGMO evolutionary optimization then searches servicing orders that jointly reduce total delta-v and mission duration while enforcing modeled timing, propulsion, and mass feasibility. Evaluations span three synthetic environments, four candidate-pool sizes, two target cardinalities, and seven physically or structurally motivated prioritization strategies.
main_result: The framework demonstrates topology-aware GBS candidate generation coupled to classical optimization for multi-target debris-removal planning.
application_angle: The approach could focus expensive trajectory optimization on promising debris-removal missions, although the abstract does not claim operational quantum advantage.

title: Thermal-noise-limited stabilization of a self-injection-locked diode laser using a miniature Fabry-Perot cavity
abstract: We present an ultrastable laser system based on miniature core components: a self-injection-locked laser comprising a distributed-feedback laser diode and an integrated microring resonator, together with a 3-ml vacuum-gap Fabry-Perot cavity. By carefully addressing technical noise sources, in particular residual amplitude modulation, we demonstrate a thermal-noise-limited fractional frequency instability of $5\cdot10^{-15}$ for averaging times between 1 and 10 s, which is among the lowest reported for compact cavity-stabilized lasers. This performance is achieved with conventional multilayer mirrors and a moderate cavity finesse of $10^5$. Such stability of the output frequency, combined with the small size of the core components and a possibility to generate a Kerr frequency comb in the very same microring resonator, provides a path towards fully integrated photonic frequency references for transportable optical clocks and low-noise microwave synthesis.
one_liner: A miniature cavity stabilizes a self-injection-locked diode laser at a thermal-noise-limited fractional instability of 5×10⁻¹⁵.
why_it_matters: It combines leading compact-laser stability with small core components and a microring that could also generate a Kerr frequency comb.
detailed_summary: The system combines a distributed-feedback diode self-injection-locked to an integrated microring with a 3-ml vacuum-gap Fabry-Perot reference cavity. After suppressing technical noise, especially residual amplitude modulation, it reaches a fractional frequency instability of 5×10⁻¹⁵ for averaging times from 1 to 10 seconds. This thermal-noise-limited performance uses conventional multilayer mirrors and a moderate cavity finesse of 10⁵.
platform_or_system: Microring-locked diode laser with miniature Fabry-Perot cavity
main_result: The compact laser system achieves thermal-noise-limited 5×10⁻¹⁵ fractional frequency instability over 1–10-second averaging times.
application_angle: Its stability and compact architecture support transportable optical clocks, integrated photonic frequency references, and low-noise microwave synthesis.

title: Optimal Control of a Fluxonium Circuit with the Q-PRONTO Numerical Method
abstract: Optimizing the control of large quantum systems is a resource-intensive task, where the convergence rate of the underlying iterative schemes is crucial. The recently developed Quantum Projection Operator-Based Newton Method for Trajectory Optimization (Q-PRONTO) offers a unique quadratic convergence for controlling quantum states, while most model-based solvers guarantee only an approximately linear convergence rate. As a proof of concept, here, we design and benchmark single-qubit gates optimized by Q-PRONTO based on the circuit Hamiltonian of a fluxonium superconducting qubit. To ensure that we can apply a long string of arbitrary pulses to the circuit, we modify the firmware associated with the Quantum Instrumentation Control Kit (QICK) by altering its memory allocation. We characterize the performance of the optimal solutions using standard randomized benchmarking and achieve a total error per gate of $6.6\times10^{-4}$.
one_liner: Q-PRONTO-optimized fluxonium gates achieve a randomized-benchmarking error per gate of 6.6×10⁻⁴.
why_it_matters: Quadratically convergent optimal control could reduce pulse-design cost while delivering high-fidelity gates on superconducting quantum hardware.
detailed_summary: The authors apply the Q-PRONTO trajectory-optimization method to single-qubit gates using a circuit-level fluxonium Hamiltonian. They modify QICK firmware memory allocation to support long sequences of arbitrary control pulses. Standard randomized benchmarking measures a total error per gate of 6.6×10⁻⁴.
platform_or_system: Fluxonium superconducting qubit with QICK control
main_result: Optimized fluxonium gates were experimentally benchmarked at a total error per gate of 6.6×10⁻⁴.
application_angle: The method offers a route to faster pulse optimization and reliable execution of long gate sequences in superconducting processors.

title: Graphical Rigidity of Continuous Variable Graph States under Gaussian Local Transformations
abstract: Multimode entangled pure Gaussian states are an essential resource for continuous variable (CV) quantum information processing. Menicucci et al. [2011] have shown how to describe them as graphs with complex adjacency matrices. Among such complex graph states (CGSs), quantum optics experimental setups straightforwardly display correlations described by purely imaginary graph states (iRGSs) whereas theoretical literature favors off-diagonal real graph state (RGS) descriptions, which actually reflect the entanglement structure in the infinite squeezing limit [Gonzalez-Arciniegas et al. 2021]. We study them beyond this ideal case, thus establishing in the finite squeezing regime an equivalence criterion for the generic case of CGSs through a graph propagating set of conditions which either finds a Gaussian Local Unitary (GLU) converting one state to another or gives a proof of impossibility if such a GLU does not exist. In the experimentally relevant case of the conversion between iRGSs and RGSs, the set of conditions results in simple relations between the topologies of the equivalent real and imaginary graphs. Finally, we show that the canonical forms of iRGSs and RGSs imply that the topology of the CV real and imaginary graph states are too rigid to admit any exact qumode local-addition analogue to the qubit complementation or qudit local-addition, thus demonstrating the non-existence of any exact qumode local-addition for these states. We however define an approximate one when the squeezing is strong enough.
one_liner: A graph-based criterion decides whether finite-squeezing Gaussian graph states are locally Gaussian-equivalent.
why_it_matters: The framework connects experimentally natural optical graph states to theoretical graph descriptions and identifies limits on local graph rewrites.
detailed_summary: The work derives propagating graph conditions that either construct a Gaussian local unitary between generic complex graph states or certify that none exists. For purely imaginary and real graph states, the conditions reduce to simple topology relations. Exact qumode local-addition operations are ruled out for their canonical forms, although an approximation is defined at strong squeezing.
main_result: The authors establish a finite-squeezing equivalence test and prove the absence of an exact local-addition analogue for canonical CV graph states.
application_angle: These criteria can guide optical cluster-state conversion and clarify which graph transformations are physically achievable with local Gaussian operations.

title: Fidelity Dynamics of a Jaynes--Cummings Qubit under Markovian and Non-Markovian Coupling Noise
abstract: We analytically investigate the fidelity dynamics of a Jaynes--Cummings qubit coupled to a single-mode cavity in the presence of stochastic fluctuations of the qubit--cavity coupling. Such fluctuations naturally arise in cavity- and circuit-QED platforms due to fabrication imperfections, control-field noise, mechanical vibrations, and environmental disturbances. Since the qubit--cavity coupling governs the rate of coherent energy and information exchange, understanding the effects of its fluctuations is essential for assessing the performance of quantum communication, quantum sensing, and quantum information-processing protocols. We consider both Gaussian white noise and Ornstein--Uhlenbeck noise with finite correlation time as models for the coupling fluctuations. Exploiting the closed dynamics within each excitation manifold, we derive exact analytical expressions for the noise-averaged density matrix and the fidelity relative to the ideal noiseless evolution. We show that the fidelity is determined by a single decoherence factor governed by the integrated noise correlation function, establishing a direct connection between microscopic coupling fluctuations and macroscopic coherence loss. In the white-noise limit, the fidelity decays exponentially, whereas finite noise correlation times produce nonexponential decay and slower coherence loss. We further show that the crossover between Markovian-like and non-Markovian regimes is controlled by the ratio of the noise correlation rate to the coherent coupling strength, and that decoherence increases with photon number because of the enhanced effective qubit--cavity coupling. These results provide a unified analytical framework for quantifying decoherence induced by stochastic coupling fluctuations and for evaluating the robustness of cavity-QED protocols under correlated noise.
one_liner: Exact formulas link stochastic qubit–cavity coupling noise to fidelity loss in the Jaynes–Cummings model.
why_it_matters: The analysis supplies quantitative noise tolerances for cavity-QED operations used in sensing, communication, and quantum processing.
detailed_summary: The authors solve the noise-averaged Jaynes–Cummings dynamics within each excitation manifold for Gaussian white and Ornstein–Uhlenbeck coupling fluctuations. Fidelity is governed by one decoherence factor determined by the integrated noise correlation function. White noise yields exponential decay, while finite correlation time slows coherence loss; higher photon number increases decoherence.
platform_or_system: Single-mode cavity coupled to a qubit
main_result: An exact analytical framework captures the crossover from exponential Markovian decay to slower correlated-noise fidelity loss.
application_angle: The formulas enable robustness estimates and noise-correlation diagnostics for cavity-QED sensing and information-transfer protocols.
