title: RADICAL: Reconfiguration-Aware Direct-Connect AI Cluster using Spatial-and-Wavelength Selective Switching
abstract: We present RADICAL, the silicon-photonic-enabled Reconfiguration-Aware Direct-Connect AI Cluster that integrates a custom spatial-and-wavelength selective switch (SWSS) with the Linux network stack. RADICAL deploys a packaged 4x4x4$λ$ microring-based SWSS into a four-GPU-server cluster using standard SFP28 optical transceivers, and a reconfiguration-aware host-networking interface to demonstrate a direct-connect reconfigurable optical fabric. The SWSS provides dynamic spatial and wavelength routing with 3.2-6.8 dB path loss, average wavelength and spatial crosstalk isolation exceeding 25 dB, and error-free 25 Gbps signal recovery across routing paths. At the system level, RADICAL validates reconfiguration-aware operation through continuous bulk data transfers totaling 6.4 TBytes over 10 minutes. We further demonstrate multitenant AI training across reconfigurable link topologies, including four ResNet-18 instances and six nanoGPT instances, with the latter sustained for more than five hours.
one_liner: A packaged silicon-photonic switch dynamically routes error-free 25-Gbps links in a four-GPU AI cluster.
why_it_matters: It demonstrates an optical fabric operating inside a real network stack and sustaining data transfer and multitenant AI workloads.
detailed_summary: RADICAL integrates a packaged 4×4×4λ microring spatial-and-wavelength selective switch with Linux networking and four GPU servers. Measured paths show 3.2–6.8 dB loss, average spatial and wavelength isolation above 25 dB, and error-free 25-Gbps recovery. The system transfers 6.4 TB in 10 minutes and runs reconfigured multitenant ResNet-18 and nanoGPT training.
main_result: The reconfigurable fabric sustained error-free 25-Gbps routing, bulk transfers, and multi-hour distributed AI training.
application_angle: The architecture could provide topology-adaptive, high-bandwidth optical interconnects for scalable accelerator clusters.

title: Demonstrating RFSoC-based Control of a Fully Connected Exchange-Only Qubit
abstract: Semiconductor triple-quantum dots (TQDs) are a promising platform for scalable quantum information processing, but the community has so far lacked access to affordable and flexible high-speed control electronics. SpinQICK, an open-source spin qubit-control package built on the Xilinx Radio Frequency System-on-Chip (RFSoC), directly addresses this gap by leveraging the high sampling-rate signal generation and advanced digital signal processing (DSP) capabilities of the Quantum Instrumentation Control Kit (QICK) to enable precise time-domain voltage control and readout of semiconductor spin qubits. In this paper, we use spinQICK to demonstrate coherent control, state preparation, and readout of a fully connected triangular exchange-only device. We also introduce and experimentally verify a novel dynamical decoupling (DD) sequence enabled by the triangular TQD and leverage its unique decoupling properties to characterize electrical noise. These results establish spinQICK as a low-cost, flexible platform for semiconductor spin qubit control and provide a pathway for hardware optimization through qubit-level noise diagnostics.
one_liner: Open-source RFSoC electronics control and read out a triangular exchange-only spin qubit while enabling new noise diagnostics.
why_it_matters: The demonstration lowers the electronics barrier for semiconductor-qubit experiments and links flexible control directly to device-noise characterization.
detailed_summary: Using the open-source spinQICK package, the authors demonstrate coherent control, state preparation, and readout of a fully connected triangular triple-quantum-dot device. They introduce and experimentally verify a dynamical-decoupling sequence that exploits the device connectivity. Its decoupling response is then used to characterize electrical noise.
main_result: RFSoC-based spinQICK achieved coherent qubit operation and experimentally validated a connectivity-enabled dynamical-decoupling protocol.
application_angle: Affordable, reprogrammable control hardware and qubit-level noise diagnostics can accelerate semiconductor processor development and optimization.

title: Robustness of Quantum Correlations and Controlled Teleportation Fidelity under Noisy Channels
abstract: In distributed quantum computing, quantum networks provide a potential infrastructure for long-range quantum information processing. Controlled quantum teleportation (CQT) is a key practically relevant protocol that can connect two parties on a network and enables a third party, the controller to allow or abort the secure teleportation of an arbitrary single-qubit state between the two parties. We investigate the robustness of a three-qubit GHZ resource under bit-flip, phase-flip, depolarizing, and amplitude-damping noise. Using the Kraus-operator formalism, we characterize the noisy resource through multipartite quantum discord, genuine multipartite concurrence (GMC), localizable entanglement (LE), and CQT fidelity. We also outline a proof-of-concept photonic implementation for preparing the three-qubit GHZ resource and realizing the CQT protocol, which could enable experimental investigation of the effects of noise. Our results show that bit-flip and amplitude-damping noise generally preserve useful mutipartite quantum correlations over broader noise parameter ranges. Interestingly, multipartite discord exhibits freezing under bit-flip noise over a finite parameter regime. Moreover, discord can persist beyond the sudden death of genuine multipartite entanglement, revealing the distinct robustness of nonclassical correlations. We further demonstrate that CQT fidelity which characterizes the performance of CQT can exceed the classical threshold even after GMC vanishes, while LE more closely reflects the operational usefulness of the noisy resource. These findings highlight the complementary roles of quantum correlations and entanglement in assessing the resilience of GHZ-based protocols.
one_liner: GHZ-based controlled teleportation can remain above the classical fidelity limit after genuine multipartite entanglement vanishes.
why_it_matters: The results show that operational teleportation utility may survive standard entanglement loss and identify localizable entanglement as a useful indicator.
detailed_summary: The study applies Kraus-channel models to a three-qubit GHZ resource under bit-flip, phase-flip, depolarizing, and amplitude-damping noise. It compares multipartite discord, genuine multipartite concurrence, localizable entanglement, and controlled-teleportation fidelity. Discord freezes over a finite bit-flip regime, and teleportation fidelity can exceed the classical threshold even after genuine multipartite concurrence disappears; a photonic proof-of-concept is outlined.
main_result: Controlled-teleportation fidelity retains a quantum advantage in noise regimes where genuine multipartite entanglement has already vanished.
application_angle: The correlation comparison can inform resource qualification and noise-tolerant design for controlled links in quantum networks.

title: Trident: Efficient Load Verification for Yoked Surface Codes using a Three-Level Memory Hierarchy
abstract: Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computers (FTQCs) commonly use the surface code to encode program qubits as error-corrected logical qubits. Unfortunately, the surface code has a poor encoding rate, so recent work has proposed Yoked Surface Codes (YSCs), which concatenate the surface code with a high-rate quantum code. The surface code qubits in YSCs are protected by the checks, or yokes, of the high-rate code. YSCs have 1D and 2D variants, which are $1.8\times$ and $4.5\times$ more efficient than the surface code, respectively. Modern FTQC architectures use a two-level hierarchy: surface codes perform logical operations (compute) while 2D YSCs store idle program qubits (memory). To load a qubit from memory, the FTQC first performs retrieval, which logically moves a program qubit from a 2D YSC into a surface code (8 cycles). However, retrieval is not fault-tolerant, so the FTQC must verify the load by measuring all the yokes of the 2D YSC (178 cycles). As verification dominates memory access latency, eliminating it can provide a speedup of $5.7\times$. Our goal is to reduce the verification overhead of 2D YSCs while retaining their storage efficiency. We exploit the fact that 1D YSCs, though less storage-efficient, incur negligible verification latency. We propose Trident, which expands the two-level hierarchy into a three-level hierarchy by adding a small intermediate level containing a 1D YSC (L1). If most loads hit L1 rather than L2 (2D YSC tier), it can significantly reduce verification overhead. We present two variants: Trident-D (demand-driven) and Trident-P (prefetch-driven), which achieve speedups of $2.8\times$ and $4.2\times$, respectively, while increasing the physical qubit cost of memory by only 4.9%.
one_liner: A three-level quantum-memory hierarchy accelerates verified qubit loading from high-rate yoked surface codes.
why_it_matters: Trident reduces a major fault-tolerant memory bottleneck while adding only 4.9% to the physical-qubit cost of memory.
detailed_summary: Trident inserts a small 1D yoked surface-code tier between compute surface codes and dense 2D yoked-code memory. This tier avoids the 178-cycle verification normally required after retrieval from 2D memory. Demand-driven and prefetch-driven variants achieve simulated speedups of 2.8× and 4.2×, respectively, with a 4.9% memory-qubit overhead.
main_result: The prefetch-driven design reaches a 4.2× speedup while increasing physical memory-qubit cost by only 4.9%.
application_angle: The architecture could reduce memory-access latency in large fault-tolerant quantum computers without sacrificing high-rate storage.

title: Photon-Number Discrimination from Increasing Time-of-Arrival Separation in Wide Superconducting Microstrip Single-Photon Detectors
abstract: Measurements of photon-number-dependent time-of-arrival (TOA) distributions in wide NbN superconducting microstrip single-photon detectors (SMSPDs) are presented. Two \SI{10}{\um}-long devices with widths of \SI{3.2}{\um} and \SI{6.4}{\um} are characterized under pulsed \SI{515}{nm} excitation. The TOA histograms are described by sums of exponentially modified Gaussian (EMG) components, with the wider device exhibiting components assigned to photon numbers up to \(n=8\). Adjacent TOA peaks become more distinguishable relative to their widths at higher photon number, in contrast to the compression of neighboring photon-number timing shifts observed in conventional narrow-wire SNSPDs. For the components assigned to \(n=7\) and \(n=8\), the FWHM-normalized peak separation is \(2.15\), and the fitted EMG distributions yield an equal-prior pairwise TOA-assignment fidelity of \(99.6\%\). The EMG exponential-tail parameter \(τ_n\) decreases strongly with photon number, while the Gaussian-location parameter \(μ_n\) continues to shift between neighboring components. A phenomenological model motivated by absorption-site-dependent vortex processes and collective current redistribution captures these timing trends. These results support wide SMSPDs as a platform for TOA-based photon-number discrimination at high photon number, relevant to multiphoton-state characterization and photonic quantum information processing. The same geometry also provides a setting to examine how the spatial distribution of photon absorption affects vortex-assisted detection.
one_liner: Wide NbN microstrip detectors distinguish high photon numbers through increasingly separated arrival-time distributions.
why_it_matters: The approach offers photon-number information from timing alone and reaches 99.6% pairwise assignment fidelity for seven versus eight photons.
detailed_summary: The authors characterize 3.2-µm- and 6.4-µm-wide NbN superconducting microstrip detectors under pulsed 515-nm excitation. Exponentially modified Gaussian components in the wider device are assigned up to eight photons, with adjacent peaks becoming relatively better separated at higher photon number. The fitted seven- and eight-photon distributions provide 99.6% equal-prior pairwise assignment fidelity.
main_result: The detector resolves timing components through eight photons and distinguishes the seven- and eight-photon components with 99.6% fitted fidelity.
application_angle: Timing-based number resolution could support multiphoton-state characterization and photonic quantum-information processing.

title: Single-step SU(3) Hahn Echo in a Qutrit Atom Interferometer
abstract: The Hahn echo is a well-known dynamical decoupling method that refocuses the dephasing due to energy inhomogeneities of a spin-1/2 ensemble and is widely used to extend phase coherence in quantum computers and sensors. Extensions of such techniques beyond the spin-1/2 have been reported, but have mainly used SU(2) gates, limiting their scalability. Here, we generalize the Hahn echo to qutrits using single-step SU(3) gates and extend the coherence time by more than an order of magnitude. The gates are generated through optimal control theory and implemented in an ultracold atomic ensemble in free fall. A quantum process tomography procedure benchmarks the gates and yields fidelities of ~ 93%, limited mainly by state preparation and measurement errors. Due to the geometry of the laser beams, the generalized Hahn echo also realizes a three-path Mach-Zehnder atomic interferometer with two independent interferometric phase differences. Our results therefore establish SU(3) control for dynamical decoupling of qutrits and multi-path atom interferometers, with the latter opening the possibility for vector force measurements and interferometric tests of the validity of Born's rule.
one_liner: Single-step SU(3) gates extend qutrit coherence and realize a three-path atom interferometer in free fall.
why_it_matters: The experiment advances scalable qutrit control while enabling two-phase interferometry for vector-force sensing and foundational tests.
detailed_summary: Optimal-control pulses implement a generalized Hahn echo with single-step SU(3) gates in a freely falling ultracold atomic ensemble. The sequence extends qutrit coherence by more than an order of magnitude, while process tomography reports gate fidelities near 93%. The beam geometry simultaneously forms a three-path Mach-Zehnder interferometer with two independent phase differences.
main_result: A single-step SU(3) Hahn echo extends qutrit coherence by over 10× and concurrently implements a two-phase, three-path interferometer.
application_angle: The platform supports robust multilevel quantum control, vector-force measurements, and interferometric tests of Born's rule.

title: Traceable Quantum Secret Sharing
abstract: Quantum secret sharing protects distributed quantum information against unauthorized reconstruction, yet existing schemes provide no intrinsic accountability when shares are leaked or forged. This missing capability is particularly relevant in realistic distributed settings, where compromised participants may either expose valid shares or maliciously interfere with reconstruction. Here we establish a framework for traceable quantum secret sharing under these two threat models. We introduce leakage-verifiable and traceable quantum secret sharing (LVT-QSS), which attributes leaked shares through an explicit leakage verification mechanism, and malicious-traceable and accountable quantum secret sharing (MTA-QSS), which identifies participants who submit forged shares during reconstruction. We formulate security definitions for both settings and prove that the proposed protocols satisfy the corresponding guarantees against the relevant adversaries. Numerical simulations under per-share depolarizing noise further quantify the robustness of the proposed schemes and identify verification as the dominant noise sensitive stage. These results incorporate accountability into quantum secret sharing and provide a foundation for traceable distributed quantum cryptography.
one_liner: Two quantum secret-sharing frameworks add attribution for leaked shares and accountability for forged reconstruction inputs.
why_it_matters: Intrinsic tracing could make distributed quantum cryptography more deployable when participants or their devices may be compromised.
detailed_summary: The work defines leakage-verifiable and traceable QSS for attributing exposed shares, plus malicious-traceable and accountable QSS for identifying forged shares during reconstruction. Formal security definitions and proofs establish guarantees under the corresponding adversarial models. Simulations with per-share depolarizing noise indicate that verification is the most noise-sensitive stage.
main_result: The proposed protocols provably trace leaked shares or identify participants supplying forged shares under their respective threat models.
application_angle: These mechanisms add auditability to distributed quantum storage and communication networks involving partially trusted participants.

title: Two-Layer Verification for Fault-Tolerant Magic-State Preparation in High-Rate Quantum Codes
abstract: Encoded magic states are essential for universal fault-tolerant quantum computation, but their resource-efficient preparation in high-rate quantum codes remains challenging. To address this limitation, we propose two-layer verification, which combines local verification of independently prepared subblocks with logical verification after their embedding into a target code. This hierarchy detects harmful error patterns, including even-parity logical-eigenvalue flips that are invisible to a collective product check alone. We demonstrate this scheme for a $[[21,3,5]]$ code by constructing a circuit that embeds three verified seven-qubit Steane-code magic states into the target code. Circuit-level simulations of $T$- and $S$-state preparation show logical-error suppression consistent with the code distance. These results demonstrate the potential of two-layer verification as a design principle for reliable magic-state preparation in quantum codes encoding multiple logical qubits.
one_liner: Hierarchical verification enables fault-tolerant encoded magic-state preparation in a high-rate multi-logical-qubit code.
why_it_matters: The method detects error patterns missed by collective checks and targets a key resource bottleneck for universal fault-tolerant computation.
detailed_summary: The protocol first verifies independently prepared subblocks and then verifies them logically after embedding into a target high-rate code. A constructed circuit embeds three verified seven-qubit Steane-code magic states into a [[21,3,5]] code. Circuit-level simulations for T and S states show logical-error suppression consistent with distance five.
main_result: Two-layer verification prepares encoded T and S magic states with simulated logical-error suppression consistent with the target code distance.
application_angle: The scheme offers a route to reliable magic-state factories for codes that encode multiple logical qubits efficiently.

title: High Resolution Hyperspectral Quantum Infrared Imaging with Undetected Photons
abstract: Quantum sensing in the infrared regime often demands the use of expensive and cryogenically operated detectors. Nonlinear interferometry has paved the way for information transfer from the infrared to the near--infrared or visible regime in various quantum technologies. A particularly interesting application of these interferometers involves spectrally--resolved quantum imaging using undetected photons, enabled by the use of temperature--tunable parametric amplifiers. In this work, we demonstrate spectrally resolved transmission imaging with undetected photons around 1550 nm using a spontaneous parametric down conversion based folded nonlinear interferometric scheme, registering the attenuation of a zebrafish larva as a biological feasibility test. We characterize and calibrate the interferometer, having achieved spectrally resolved interference fringes with a maximum baseline visibility of $\sim 74\%$ in the near--infrared regime. Phase--stepped readout of a grating spectrometer gives a resolving power of $\sim1460$ (from the spectrometer's point spread function) at 1550 nm, and $\sim 730$ from the coherence length, the finest reported for imaging with undetected photons, over an instantaneous spectral window of $\approx 51$ cm$^{-1}$.
one_liner: A nonlinear interferometer delivers high-resolution 1550-nm hyperspectral imaging without detecting the infrared photons.
why_it_matters: It combines infrared sample sensitivity with near-infrared readout, potentially avoiding expensive cryogenic infrared detector arrays.
detailed_summary: A folded SPDC nonlinear interferometer transfers 1550-nm sample information to detected near-infrared light for spectrally resolved transmission imaging. Phase-stepped grating-spectrometer readout achieves resolving power near 1460 from the point-spread function and about 730 from coherence length across an approximately 51 cm⁻¹ window. The system reaches roughly 74% baseline fringe visibility and images attenuation in a zebrafish larva.
main_result: The experiment demonstrates undetected-photon imaging near 1550 nm with a peak resolving power of about 1460 and a biological sample.
application_angle: The technique could enable biomedical and materials hyperspectral infrared imaging using accessible near-infrared detectors.

title: Entangled logical qubits on a superconducting quantum processor
abstract: We demonstrate high-fidelity logical qubit operations using \texttt{ibm\_phoenix}, a square-lattice array of 120 coupled superconducting qubits that are capable of fast reset. Using strategies to exclude underperforming components together with noise informed decoding, we routinely produce surface codes at distance-3 and distance-5 with logical error per round below 1\%. We demonstrate entanglement between two logical qubits, where logical Bell-state fidelities above 93\% are observed for entanglement created via lattice surgery. With three logical qubits and lattice surgery, we perform logical teleportation of a range of states and gates, observing fidelities in the range 78\% - 93\%. Using reset to reduce qubit leakage, we show that repeated rounds of stabilizer measurements continue to exhibit improvements in a stability experiment up to $\sim 2\cdot 10^{-7}$ over 170 measurement rounds.
one_liner: IBM demonstrates entangled surface-code logical qubits, lattice-surgery teleportation, and stable repeated error-correction cycles.
why_it_matters: This integrates logical entanglement, teleportation, leakage reduction, and sub-1% logical error per round on a large superconducting processor.
detailed_summary: On the 120-qubit ibm_phoenix processor, component selection and noise-informed decoding produce distance-3 and distance-5 surface codes with logical error per round below 1%. Lattice surgery generates logical Bell states with fidelities above 93% and enables three-logical-qubit teleportation of states and gates with 78%-93% fidelity. Fast reset suppresses leakage, supporting stability improvements through 170 stabilizer-measurement rounds.
main_result: The processor achieved >93% logical Bell-state fidelity, 78%-93% logical teleportation fidelity, and sub-1% logical error per round.
application_angle: The demonstrated primitives directly support scalable fault-tolerant computation and protected transfer of quantum states and gates between logical qubits.

title: Electron Wavefronts Capture Nanoscale Movies of Hypersound at Surfaces
abstract: Acoustic waves transport mechanical energy and elastic strain through solids, with material composition and shape governing their propagation. In the gigahertz hypersound regime, acoustic wavelengths reach tens to hundreds of nanometres, comparable to nanoscale device dimensions. Harnessing these waves underpins high-frequency signal processing, sensing, electromagnetic coupling and quantum control. Acoustic metrology probes elastic modes and internal interfaces. Yet directly imaging how nanoscale acoustic waves interact with local structure remains challenging, requiring picometre displacement sensitivity combined with high spatiotemporal resolution. Here we demonstrate full-field imaging of laser-induced hypersound at surfaces using reflected electron wavefronts. We introduce ultrafast low-energy electron microscopy (ULEEM), exploiting the intrinsic surface sensitivity of few-electronvolt electrons. Coherent electron pulses down to femtosecond durations reflect from the topmost atomic layers, imprinting the evolving surface profile onto their wavefronts. Defocus converts phase variations into image contrast. In a thin van der Waals material, we image the thermoelastic generation and propagation of picometre-amplitude acoustic waves. Measured dispersion relations, interpreted through elastodynamic modelling, distinguish substrate-supported and locally detached regions, revealing how interfacial contact shapes propagation. Delayed wave emission reveals scattering at buried mechanical defects. Our results establish electron-wavefront imaging of nanoscale surface dynamics, enabling the exploration of ultrafast energy transport, structural transformations and coupled mechanical, electronic and magnetic phenomena.
one_liner: Ultrafast low-energy electron microscopy records full-field nanoscale movies of picometre-amplitude surface hypersound.
why_it_matters: Directly resolving gigahertz acoustic propagation and defect scattering can advance nanoscale metrology, device diagnostics, and phononic quantum control.
detailed_summary: The authors introduce ultrafast low-energy electron microscopy, using femtosecond coherent electron pulses reflected from the topmost atomic layers to encode transient surface profiles. Defocus converts the electron-wavefront phase modulation into image contrast, revealing laser-driven picometre-amplitude acoustic waves in a thin van der Waals material. Dispersion analysis distinguishes supported from locally detached regions, while delayed emission exposes scattering from buried mechanical defects.
main_result: The method directly images nanoscale surface acoustic waves with picometre displacement sensitivity and resolves effects of interfaces and buried defects.
application_angle: It provides a full-field diagnostic for ultrafast energy transport, nanoscale adhesion, mechanical defects, and coupled phononic, electronic, or magnetic devices.

title: From Hollow Waveguides to Mie Voids: Low-Index Light Confinement
abstract: The confinement of light within optically thin media challenges the conventional view that optical localization requires high-index dielectric materials and total internal reflection. Over the past decades, a broad range of photonic phenomena has demonstrated that electromagnetic energy can also be guided and localized inside low-index regions or nanoscale void cavities. What first appears to be a curiosity is, in fact, highly relevant: The interaction between light and matter lies at the heart of much in optics and photonics. It enables sensing, nonlinear optical phenomena, and optical manipulation, yet it also inevitably introduces absorption, dissipation, and loss. Pushing localized, enhanced, or guided energy into a lower-index space thus offers entirely new possibilities for light-matter interaction and dispersion control. In this review, we discuss some of these counterintuitive structures, starting with light guidance within optically thin media, such as hollow-core photonic crystal fibers or antiresonant reflecting optical waveguides. We then discuss the optics of bubbles, that is, low-index inclusions in a higher-index surrounding, and ultimately arrive at the so-called Mie void resonators, optical resonators that support localized electromagnetic modes confined within a region of lower refractive index. All these systems demonstrate that there are (resonant) optics beyond simple total internal reflection. Absence can itself become a functional photonic degree of freedom, opening opportunities across sensing, quantum nanophotonics, metasurfaces, and programmable optical matter.
one_liner: This review unifies hollow guides, low-index inclusions, and Mie voids as platforms for confining light in optically thin regions.
why_it_matters: Moving optical energy away from absorbing matter can reduce loss while enabling new sensing, quantum-nanophotonic, and metasurface designs.
detailed_summary: The review surveys mechanisms that guide or localize light inside low-index regions without relying on conventional total internal reflection. It connects hollow-core photonic-crystal fibers and antiresonant waveguides to bubbles, low-index inclusions, and localized Mie-void resonances. The shared design principle is to control dispersion and field enhancement while reducing overlap with lossy material.
main_result: The article establishes a unified framework for light confinement in hollow guides, low-index inclusions, and nanoscale void resonators.
application_angle: These structures offer low-loss field delivery and enhanced interactions for sensing, quantum nanophotonics, metasurfaces, and programmable optical materials.

title: LYNX - A trapped-ion quantum information processor
abstract: We introduce LYNX, a quantum information processor based on trapped $^{40}$Ca$^+$ ions. It utilizes up to 31 qubits with all-to-all connectivity. We characterize the system performance using rigorous benchmarks, such as randomized benchmarking (RB), GHZ state fidelity estimates, and quantum volume (QV) tests. The LYNX processor shows average 1-qubit gate errors of $8(5)\times 10^{-5}$ tested via standard RB in a 24-qubit register. An average 2-qubit gate error in a 24-qubit register of $2.84(8)\times 10^{-3}$ is demonstrated using interleaved RB. Furthermore, the device passes QV tests using up to 15 qubits which corresponds to a quantum volume of QV$=2^{15}$.
one_liner: LYNX operates up to 31 trapped-ion qubits with all-to-all connectivity and passes quantum-volume tests through 15 qubits.
why_it_matters: Its low gate errors and QV=2^15 benchmark establish a capable, quantitatively characterized trapped-ion processor for larger algorithms.
detailed_summary: LYNX is a trapped-40Ca+ processor supporting as many as 31 qubits with all-to-all connectivity. In a 24-qubit register, standard randomized benchmarking gives an average single-qubit gate error of 8(5)×10^-5, while interleaved benchmarking gives an average two-qubit error of 2.84(8)×10^-3. The processor passes quantum-volume tests through 15 qubits, corresponding to QV=2^15.
main_result: LYNX demonstrates 8(5)×10^-5 single-qubit error, 2.84(8)×10^-3 two-qubit error, and quantum volume 2^15.
application_angle: The combination of all-to-all connectivity and benchmarked multiqubit performance supports near-term algorithms and scalable trapped-ion processor development.

title: Classical Pre-Training of Large Shallow Parametrized Quantum Circuits through Pauli Propagation and deployment on Quantum Hardware
abstract: Scaling parametrized quantum circuits to a larger number of qubits is a central challenge in Quantum Machine Learning: gradient estimation via the parameter-shift rule quickly becomes prohibitively expensive, while gradient-free optimizers offer limited convergence guarantees. We apply the Pauli propagation framework to a broad class of Quantum Machine Learning problems in which the loss is expressed as a function of expectation values of the circuit's observables, while keeping the relevant quantity of interest, such as the quantum state or its samples, classically intractable to compute. By propagating the observables backward through the circuit, we obtain an explicit parametric expression for the loss that can be minimized entirely on classical hardware. We also present complementary strategies to make propagation tractable at large scale, including weight-based and degree-based truncations and pruning heuristics. We demonstrate the approach on two benchmarks run on 64-qubit circuits: Variational Quantum Eigensolver on a two-dimensional Ising model, and training of a discrete-type generative model for binary images. In both cases, the classically pre-trained parameters are deployed on the IBM quantum processor ibm_berlin. For generative learning, we additionally show that the circuits considered here require substantially fewer parametrized gates than IQP-style ansätze, reducing transpilation overhead and making deployment on current quantum hardware feasible.
one_liner: Pauli propagation classically pre-trains shallow 64-qubit variational circuits before their deployment on IBM quantum hardware.
why_it_matters: The approach reduces costly quantum gradient evaluations and makes large variational and generative circuits more practical on current processors.
detailed_summary: The method propagates observables backward through parametrized circuits to form an explicit loss function that can be optimized classically, even when the target state or samples remain classically intractable. Weight- and degree-based truncation plus pruning control the propagation cost at scale. The authors pre-train 64-qubit VQE and binary-image generative circuits and deploy the resulting parameters on ibm_berlin, with the generative ansatz using fewer parametrized gates than IQP-style alternatives.
main_result: Classical Pauli-propagation pre-training enabled hardware deployment of 64-qubit VQE and generative-learning circuits with reduced optimization overhead.
application_angle: It can shift much of variational training off quantum processors, lowering sampling cost, circuit executions, and transpilation overhead for near-term applications.

title: Trace-distance characterization of recurrent pairwise synchronization in cavity-coupled superconducting qubits
abstract: We theoretically investigate recurrent pairwise synchronization in three super?conducting qubits coupled to a common single-mode microwave cavity. The qubits interact indirectly through the cavity field and are driven by a coher?ent microwave field. We obtain the coherent dynamics in the dressed-state basis and quantify pairwise synchronization by the trace distance between reduced single-qubit density matrices. The trace-distance dynamics exhibit oscillatory wave-packet structures, with low-trace-distance regions identifying finite syn?chronization windows. An envelope-threshold procedure is introduced to extract the representative duration of these windows. By varying the middle-qubit coupling strength and the relative coupling ratio of the outer qubits, we con?struct a parameter-dependent map of the synchronization-window duration. The duration decreases rapidly with increasing relative outer-qubit coupling and becomes weakly dependent on the middle-qubit coupling in the stronger-coupling regime. These results provide a reduced-state-based characterization of coherent collective dynamics in multiqubit circuit-QED systems.
one_liner: Trace distance reveals recurrent synchronization windows among three cavity-coupled superconducting qubits and maps their coupling dependence.
why_it_matters: The reduced-state metric offers a compact tool for analyzing and engineering coherent collective dynamics in multiqubit circuit-QED hardware.
detailed_summary: The theoretical study considers three coherently driven superconducting qubits interacting indirectly through a common microwave-cavity mode. Pairwise trace distances between reduced single-qubit states form oscillatory wave packets whose minima define finite synchronization windows. An envelope-threshold analysis shows that window duration falls rapidly with increasing outer-qubit coupling ratio and becomes weakly sensitive to the middle-qubit coupling at stronger coupling.
main_result: The work derives trace-distance synchronization windows and maps how their duration varies with the qubit-cavity coupling configuration.
application_angle: The analysis can guide coupling design and control of synchronized dynamics in cavity-mediated superconducting-qubit networks.

title: From Link Availability to Deadline-Constrained Key Service: A Feasibility Framework for Mobile Free-Space Quantum Key Distribution
abstract: Mobile free-space quantum key distribution (QKD) links can provide secret bits intermittently, whereas applications may need cryptographic key material at specified times. Optical feasibility, positive finite-key output, and deadline-compliant key service are consequently different claims. This technical note formalizes their separation through a time-indexed, security-qualified arrival process and a key-inventory model. Under explicitly stated assumptions, an elementary prefix-feasibility condition characterizes whether all demands can be served without borrowing keys from future contact windows. A stylized finite block model then illustrates why positive long-run optical availability does not ensure positive finite-key output when observations are fragmented into short contacts. Two transparent numerical examples distinguish total key yield from key delivery time and show the conditional benefit of pooling data across acquisition windows. The analysis is intended as a systems-level accounting and benchmarking framework, not a new QKD security proof or a demonstration of hardware performance. It identifies measurements and security assumptions needed to evaluate train, UAV, high-altitude-platform, and satellite-assisted optical QKD against application-level service requirements.
one_liner: A systems framework tests whether intermittent mobile free-space QKD links can deliver finite-key material before application deadlines.
why_it_matters: It prevents optical link availability or aggregate key yield from being mistaken for a usable, deadline-compliant cryptographic service.
detailed_summary: The paper models security-qualified key arrivals and application demand as time-indexed processes connected through a key inventory. It derives a prefix-feasibility condition for serving every demand without borrowing keys from future contact windows. Finite-block examples show how fragmented contacts can yield no secure key despite positive optical availability and examine when pooling observations across windows helps.
main_result: The framework separates optical access, positive finite-key generation, and deadline-compliant delivery through an explicit feasibility condition and inventory model.
application_angle: It supports realistic benchmarking of train, UAV, high-altitude-platform, and satellite-assisted QKD services against timed key demand.

title: High-quality, deep formation and identification of oxygen-vacancy defects in silicon carbide
abstract: Optically addressable paramagnetic defects in silicon carbide (SiC) are attractive for scalable quantum technologies such as quantum sensing. PL5, PL6, and PL7 are promising defects for their high brightness and spin-readout contrast. Although generation by oxygen implantation has been reported very recently, nonuniform spin and optical properties and the limited generation depth of implanted defects hinder both high-sensitivity sensing and conclusive microscopic identification. Here we engineer high-quality defects by decoupling oxygen incorporation and defect formation, realizing highly homogeneous spin-resonance frequencies as well as narrow optical linewidths and long T2* coherence time. Further, we demonstrate defect formation beyond the ion range utilizing oxygen diffusion, exceptional among impurities in SiC. We further provide hyperfine-interaction statistics of 17O and host nuclei across many PL6 defects, making the oxygen-vacancy origin conclusive. Together, the microscopic identification and the demonstrated formation route establish a foundation for developing the oxygen-vacancy spin defect into a versatile quantum platform.
one_liner: Decoupled oxygen incorporation and defect formation produces deep, homogeneous oxygen-vacancy spin defects in silicon carbide.
why_it_matters: Narrow optical lines, uniform spin resonances, and long inhomogeneous coherence directly address reproducibility and depth limits in SiC quantum sensors.
detailed_summary: The authors separate oxygen incorporation from defect formation to create PL5–PL7 centers with homogeneous spin-resonance frequencies, narrow optical linewidths, and long T2* coherence. Oxygen diffusion enables defect formation beyond the implantation ion range. Hyperfine statistics involving 17O and host nuclei across many PL6 centers provide strong microscopic identification of the defects as oxygen-vacancy complexes.
platform_or_system: Optically addressable oxygen-vacancy spins in SiC
main_result: High-quality defects are formed beyond the implantation range, while multi-defect hyperfine measurements conclusively support the oxygen-vacancy assignment of PL6.
application_angle: The fabrication route could enable deeper, more reproducible SiC spin ensembles for scalable quantum sensing and integrated quantum devices.

title: Discrete WKB approach to density profiles in inhomogeneous two-band free-fermion chains
abstract: We extend the discrete WKB method to one-dimensional bipartite tight-binding chains of free fermions with slowly varying hopping amplitudes and on-site potentials. We focus on the inhomogeneous Rice-Mele model, suggesting possible experimental realizations thereof in optical superlattices. We derive explicit semiclassical expressions for the single-particle wave functions and density of states, as well as the sublattice-resolved local particle densities and filling fraction at arbitrary Fermi energy. In particular, we show that the WKB density profiles agree with those obtained from the local-density approximation. We analyze the spatial dependence of the local band edges and its consequences for the global spectral structure, and clarify the role played by the phase-space topology in determining the Bohr-Sommerfeld quantization conditions. Finally, we illustrate our results with two representative examples: a homogeneous Rice-Mele chain subject to a harmonic trap and a fully inhomogeneous chain containing a domain wall.
one_liner: A discrete WKB theory predicts spectra and sublattice-resolved density profiles in slowly varying two-band fermion chains.
why_it_matters: The results offer analytic design and interpretation tools for inhomogeneous Rice–Mele lattices implementable with optical superlattices.
detailed_summary: The work extends discrete WKB analysis to bipartite tight-binding chains with spatially varying hopping and on-site potentials. It derives semiclassical wave functions, density of states, filling fractions, and sublattice-resolved local densities, recovering local-density-approximation profiles. Harmonic confinement and a domain-wall chain illustrate how local band edges and phase-space topology determine the global spectrum and quantization rules.
main_result: Explicit semiclassical formulas reproduce local density profiles and connect spectral quantization to the topology of the chain's classical phase space.
application_angle: The theory can guide preparation and diagnosis of trapped or domain-wall two-band lattices in cold-atom optical superlattices.

title: Supercontinuum-driven broadband Fourier-transform photothermal microspectroscopy
abstract: Chemical characterization of microscopic samples often requires resolving multiple, widely separated vibrational absorption bands, including their positions and spectral shapes. Photothermal microspectroscopy provides a route to localized vibrational measurements by detecting absorption-induced thermal responses with a separate optical probe. However, rapid acquisition of broadband photothermal spectra remains challenging when spectral information is collected through sequential wavelength tuning. Here, we develop a supercontinuum (SC)-driven Fourier-transform photothermal (FT-PT) microspectroscopy platform that combines broadband near-infrared excitation with rapid-scan interferometric acquisition for localized vibrational measurements. In this approach, an interferometrically modulated SC pump induces wavelength-dependent photothermal responses in the sample, which are detected through a co-propagating visible probe beam and reconstructed by Fourier transformation. Using a 1.65-2.35 um spectral window, we demonstrate broadband photothermal spectra of aqueous samples with acquisition rates of approximately one spectrum per second. The system simultaneously resolves multiple molecular absorption features in a water-dimethyl sulfoxide mixture and reproduces the near-infrared absorption characteristics of liquid water with high spectral fidelity. Extending beyond homogeneous liquids, a dark-field detection configuration enables broadband photothermal spectroscopy of an individual 6 um polystyrene particle in an aqueous environment. This SC-based FT-PT microspectroscopy approach provides a rapid and broadband platform for localized vibrational characterization of liquid and microscopic samples, enabling chemical analysis with microscale spatial selectivity.
one_liner: Supercontinuum-pumped Fourier-transform photothermal microscopy acquires broadband near-infrared spectra at about one spectrum per second.
why_it_matters: It combines rapid, non-scanning spectral acquisition with microscale chemical selectivity in liquids and individual particles.
detailed_summary: An interferometrically modulated supercontinuum pump spanning 1.65–2.35 µm generates wavelength-dependent thermal responses that are read with a co-propagating visible probe. Fourier reconstruction produces approximately one broadband spectrum per second and resolves multiple absorption features in water–dimethyl sulfoxide mixtures. Dark-field detection further enables spectroscopy of an individual 6 µm polystyrene particle in water.
main_result: The platform delivers rapid broadband photothermal spectra with high spectral fidelity for bulk liquids and a single micrometer-scale particle in an aqueous environment.
application_angle: It enables localized, label-free chemical analysis of microscopic samples without slow sequential wavelength tuning.

title: Integrated elliptical III-V nanopillar arrays on silicon for dual photodetection and light emission
abstract: Next-generation on-chip photonic devices require compact, energy-efficient components integrating photodetection and light emission on silicon platforms. Achieving broadband photodetection combined with efficient emission in a single nanoscale device remains challenging. Here, we demonstrate elliptical nanopillar arrays monolithically integrated as III-V-on-Si templates, exhibiting broadband photoresponse across visible to near-infrared wavelengths, dynamic neuron-like graded responses under modulated light, and pronounced electroluminescence at around 865 nm under forward bias. The nanostructured elliptical geometry approach enhances optical absorption and carrier dynamics within an active area significantly smaller than commercial detectors, enabling responsivities up to 0.55 A/W at 830 nm in compact nanoarrays. This work advances the development of miniaturized active nanophotonic devices suitable for integrated sensing, emitting and communication circuits, and neuromorphic processing on silicon substrates.
one_liner: Elliptical III–V nanopillar arrays on silicon combine broadband photodetection, graded optical responses, and 865 nm electroluminescence.
why_it_matters: A single compact III–V-on-Si architecture provides both sensing and emission functions while reaching 0.55 A/W responsivity at 830 nm.
detailed_summary: Monolithically integrated elliptical III–V nanopillar arrays exhibit photoresponse from visible to near-infrared wavelengths and electroluminescence near 865 nm under forward bias. Their geometry enhances absorption and carrier dynamics within an active area smaller than conventional detectors. Under modulated illumination, the devices also display graded, neuron-like dynamic responses and reach 0.55 A/W responsivity at 830 nm.
platform_or_system: Elliptical III–V nanopillar arrays on silicon
main_result: The nanoarrays integrate broadband detection and near-infrared emission in one structure, with responsivity up to 0.55 A/W at 830 nm.
application_angle: The devices could support compact sensing, emitting, communication, and neuromorphic functions in silicon photonic circuits.

title: Bounding single-copy information causality violations
abstract: Information causality is a physical principle that constrains bipartite post-quantum nonlocal correlations from information-theoretic assumptions. A direct characterization of the correlations satisfying it, however, remains difficult because the defining entropic condition must hold for all admissible protocols in the corresponding task. Here, we formulate the single-copy information causality problem as an optimization over all protocol parameters and simplify it by proving a deterministic reduction. We then show that generic adaptive multi-copy protocols can be represented as single-copy protocols applied to an effective behavior obtained by local wirings. As a consequence, for families of correlations closed under wirings, excluding single-copy violations suffices to exclude all finite-copy adaptive-protocol violations. We formulate the resulting membership and set-inclusion problems as optimization problems and discuss possible semidefinite programming relaxations. As an application, we study expansions of the information causality functional around zero-capacity channels, generalizing a method recently employed by Gachechiladze and Miklin to derive the Tsirelson--Landau--Masanes boundary from information causality. For expansions centered on channels whose output distribution has full support, imposing the second-order constraints for all single-copy protocols characterizes exactly the set of macroscopic locality in the CHSH scenario. Expanding instead around appropriate constant-output channels with perturbations that change the channel support, we show that every single-copy IC violation can be witnessed already at first order with a channel of arbitrarily small capacity.
one_liner: Single-copy optimization bounds information-causality violations and, for wiring-closed families, controls all finite-copy adaptive protocols.
why_it_matters: The reduction offers a tractable route to classifying nonlocal correlations and constraining resources beyond quantum theory.
detailed_summary: The authors formulate single-copy information causality as an optimization over protocol parameters and prove a deterministic reduction. Adaptive multi-copy protocols are represented as single-copy protocols acting on behaviors generated by local wirings, so wiring-closed families need only pass the single-copy test. Channel expansions recover macroscopic locality at second order in the CHSH scenario and reveal any single-copy violation at first order using arbitrarily low-capacity channels.
main_result: For correlation families closed under local wirings, absence of single-copy information-causality violations excludes every finite-copy adaptive-protocol violation.
application_angle: The framework can sharpen computational certification of admissible nonlocal resources used in device-independent quantum communication and cryptography.

title: A Compact Single-Beam Optically Pumped Magnetometer Based on Absorption Detection
abstract: We demonstrate a compact single-beam optically pumped magnetometer (OPM) employing a pure 87Rb microfabricated vapor cell with 500 Torr buffer gas. The residual magnetic field is actively minimized to below 400 pT through a combination of mu-metal magnetic shielding and internal compensation coils. We systematically characterize the OPM response as a function of laser detuning and optical intensity, and derive the magnetic-field sensitivity from the signal slope and noise amplitude spectral density. A best sensitivity of 11 fT/Hz^1/2 is achieved near the resonance transition at an optimal optical intensity, using a small cell volume of only 0.027 cm^3. Furthermore, a miniaturized OPM prototype was developed using a folded flexible printed circuit board (FPCB) to integrate the vapor cell, a compact heater, and magnetic-field coils into a cubic sensing head. Two coil configurations patterned directly on the FPCB were investigated. Under optimized operating conditions, the OPM prototype achieved a sensitivity of 66 fT/Hz^1/2. These results demonstrate that high-buffer-pressure single-beam OPMs can achieve excellent sensitivity, establishing a pathway toward compact and scalable arrays.
one_liner: A compact single-beam 87Rb magnetometer reaches 11 fT/Hz^1/2 in a 0.027 cm^3 vapor cell and 66 fT/Hz^1/2 as an integrated prototype.
why_it_matters: The combination of femtotesla sensitivity, absorption readout, and an FPCB-integrated sensing head supports scalable compact magnetometer arrays.
detailed_summary: The system uses a pure 87Rb microfabricated vapor cell with 500 Torr buffer gas, mu-metal shielding, and compensation coils that reduce the residual field below 400 pT. Optimizing laser detuning and intensity yields 11 fT/Hz^1/2 sensitivity with a 0.027 cm^3 cell. A cubic prototype integrating the cell, heater, and patterned coils on a folded FPCB achieves 66 fT/Hz^1/2.
main_result: The laboratory sensor reaches 11 fT/Hz^1/2, while the miniaturized FPCB-integrated prototype reaches 66 fT/Hz^1/2.
application_angle: The compact architecture offers a practical route to dense, scalable arrays for biomagnetic and other weak-field measurements.

title: Hardware-Friendly Estimation of LCU-Based Expectation Values via Quantum-to-Classical Workload Shifting
abstract: Estimating the expectation value of an observable $O$ for a quantum state evolved under a general, possibly non-unitary, operator $A$ is a fundamental task in quantum simulation, chemistry, and variational algorithms. Existing linear-combination-of-unitaries (LCU) approaches implement $A$ on hardware, requiring ancilla qubits, controlled unitaries and, in randomized variants, fresh circuit executions for every Monte Carlo sample. These costs are prohibitive on NISQ and early fault-tolerant devices. We propose HERMES (Hardware-Efficient Reusable Measurements for Estimating LCU-based expectation valueS), which moves the processing of $A$ entirely to the classical domain. Expanding $A$ and $O$ in the Pauli basis and sampling pairs of Pauli terms classically, HERMES rewrites $μ= \mathrm{Tr}(OAρA^{\dagger})/\mathrm{Tr}(AρA^{\dagger})$ as a ratio of weighted sums of Pauli expectation values on the unmodified state $ρ$, with no ancillas, controlled unitaries, or quantum implementation of $A$. A two-level measurement reduction scheme (Pauli deduplication and commuting-group partitioning) bounds the number of distinct measurement settings independently of the sample count, unlike randomized LCU methods whose circuit executions grow linearly with it. On ground-state energy estimation of $\mathrm{H}_2$ and $\mathrm{LiH}$ via imaginary-time evolution, HERMES matches or beats Pauli single-ancilla LCU baseline using shallow circuits with no two-qubit gates beyond state preparation under qubit-wise commuting grouping. It is also more robust to noise and completes a noisy $\mathrm{LiH}$ simulation infeasible for the baseline, at the cost of classical overhead growing with the number of Pauli terms in $A$.
one_liner: HERMES estimates LCU-transformed observables using reusable Pauli measurements on the original state, eliminating ancillas and controlled unitaries.
why_it_matters: It shifts non-unitary LCU processing to classical computation, reducing quantum depth and repeated circuit execution on constrained hardware.
detailed_summary: HERMES expands the transformation and observable in Pauli bases, then expresses the target normalized expectation value as weighted sums of measurements on the unmodified quantum state. Pauli deduplication and commuting-group partitioning make the number of distinct settings independent of the Monte Carlo sample count. In H2 and LiH imaginary-time calculations, it matches or improves on a single-ancilla LCU baseline using shallow circuits and tolerates noise well enough to complete a LiH case that the baseline cannot.
platform_or_system: Gate-based quantum processor with classical post-processing
main_result: HERMES reproduces LCU-based expectation estimates without implementing the LCU operator, ancillas, or controlled unitaries on quantum hardware.
application_angle: The method makes non-unitary simulation and quantum-chemistry workflows more accessible to NISQ and early fault-tolerant processors.

title: One-sided-DIQKD using any pure bipartite entangled state secure against all attacks
abstract: Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) allows spatially separated parties to establish a secret key among themselves based on quantum principles. While QKD systems are being deployed worldwide, their reliance on trusted measurements makes them vulnerable. Moreover, existing protocols have largely focussed on the qubit cases, and rely on the maximally entangled state, a costly resource to generate. Here, we consider the one-sided-device-independent (1SDI) QKD protocols, where one of the measurement devices is trusted while the other is untrusted. The resource in this scenario is quantum steering, an asymmetric form of quantum nonlocality. This is inspired by a real-world scenario, where the trusted party can be considered to be a bank, or any large organisation that has sufficient resources to protect its systems and validate them, while the users are vulnerable to attacks. We then demonstrate that a secure key can be obtained using any pure bipartite entangled state in this setup. Considering realistic detectors and sources based on current technology, we demonstrate that even states that are almost separable can be used to extract a secure key. Moreover, for every pure entangled bipartite state, we find the critical detection efficiencies and visibility to obtain a secure key.
one_liner: A one-sided device-independent QKD protocol extracts secure keys from every pure bipartite entangled state, including nearly separable states.
why_it_matters: The result relaxes the need for maximally entangled qubits and quantifies practical detector-efficiency and visibility thresholds against general attacks.
detailed_summary: The protocol assumes one trusted measurement device and one untrusted device, with security supplied by quantum steering. The analysis establishes secure key generation against all attacks for any pure entangled bipartite state, without restricting the resource to maximally entangled qubits. It further evaluates realistic sources and detectors and derives critical detection efficiencies and visibility for each pure entangled state.
main_result: Every pure bipartite entangled state is shown to support secure 1SDI key generation, even arbitrarily close to separability under suitable conditions.
application_angle: The asymmetric trust model suits networks linking well-protected institutions to less-trusted user terminals while easing entangled-source requirements.

title: Scaling the Wavelength to Optimize Ultrafast Laser Processing of Bandgap Materials
abstract: The spectral characteristics of ultrashort laser pulses offer unique possibilities to control interactions in space and time as well as the subsequent material responses. In particular, selecting the wavelength predefines the fundamental mechanisms governing laser-matter interaction, and thus, how energy is deposited. This Chapter provides an overview on how the essential physical effects in ultrafast laser-matter interaction scale with the wavelength, and the consequences for bandgap material processing applications. First, we recall the main spectral properties of bandgap materials and discuss the important question of the expected processing resolutions depending on wavelength. Then, recent studies on the impact of the wavelength in ultrafast laser-dielectric interaction are presented. Finally, we present how the latest developments in infrared ultrafast laser sources can be advantageously utilized to internally process narrow-gap materials despite challenges related to increased nonlinearities.
one_liner: This review maps how wavelength controls energy deposition, resolution, and nonlinear propagation in ultrafast processing of bandgap materials.
why_it_matters: Its wavelength-scaling framework can guide laser-source and process-window selection for internal machining of dielectric and narrow-gap materials.
detailed_summary: The chapter relates wavelength to the excitation and energy-deposition mechanisms governing ultrashort-pulse interactions with bandgap materials. It discusses wavelength-dependent processing resolution and summarizes recent results in ultrafast laser-dielectric interaction. It also assesses how emerging infrared sources enable internal processing of narrow-gap materials while increasing nonlinear-propagation challenges.
platform_or_system: Ultrafast laser processing of bandgap materials
main_result: The work provides a wavelength-scaling framework connecting laser spectrum to processing resolution, deposition physics, and nonlinear limitations.
application_angle: The framework supports rational wavelength selection for precision micromachining and subsurface modification of optical and semiconductor materials.

title: Distributed Quantum-Centric Supercomputing with Multi-Layered Generative Learning for Intermolecular Interactions
abstract: Quantum-centric supercomputing (QCSC) approaches, such as sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD), combine quantum processors with high-performance computers (HPC), offering a promising route toward solving challenging electronic structure problems. However, implementation of QCSC approaches to large active space calculations is constrained by the associated number of qubits, deep quantum circuits, sampling cost, and large-scale Hamiltonian diagonalization. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a distributed QCSC framework that decomposes complex molecular problems into parallel sub-problems requiring fewer qubits, shallower circuits, and reduced shot budgets. A physically motivated, two-step aggregation scheme then reconstructs the global solution: first, a computational bit assignment strategy optimizes a cost function to appropriately map local bit indices to global ones, yielding a mapped tensor product state (MTPS); second, an inter-fragment correlation recovery module restores missing cross-fragment interactions. Herein, we employ a multi-layered generative machine learning architecture, starting with utilizing the recently proposed physics-informed generative SQD (PIGen-SQD) as a distributed QCSC solver, followed by a secondary generative module to model configuration distributions and identify dominant sectors of the global Hilbert space. For water and formamide dimers, our method achieves up to $95\%$ reduction in the diagonalization dimension while enhancing energy accuracy by an order of magnitude over conventional SQD. Furthermore, application to the water hexamer ($\mathrm{(H_2O)_6}$) cage successfully decomposes a 120-qubit problem into six 20-qubit monomeric subsystems, and stitches the monomers under a dimeric approximation, demonstrating excellent agreement with the reference classical methods.
one_liner: A distributed quantum-HPC workflow decomposes a 120-qubit water-hexamer problem into six 20-qubit subsystems and reconstructs global correlations.
why_it_matters: Fragmentation and generative reconstruction reduce qubit, circuit, sampling, and diagonalization demands for quantum-assisted molecular simulation.
detailed_summary: The framework distributes molecular calculations across smaller subsystems and combines their outputs through optimized local-to-global bit mapping and recovery of inter-fragment correlations. A multilayer generative architecture uses physics-informed generative SQD locally and a second model to identify important sectors of the global Hilbert space. Tests on water and formamide dimers reduce diagonalization dimension by up to 95% and improve energy accuracy by an order of magnitude over conventional SQD; a 120-qubit water hexamer is treated as six 20-qubit monomers under a dimer approximation.
platform_or_system: Distributed quantum processors coupled to HPC
main_result: The method reconstructs accurate molecular energies from smaller quantum subproblems while reducing diagonalization dimension by as much as 95%.
application_angle: It offers a scalable route to quantum-assisted electronic-structure calculations that exceed the qubit and sampling capacity of a single processor.

title: All-Dielectric Tight-Binding Photonics via a Band-Gap Vacuum
abstract: Tight-binding photonics bridges condensed-matter physics and optics, providing a powerful framework for engineering band structures and topological phases with light. For photons, however, the vacuum is gapless, so resonators in air carry radiative tails that produce spurious long-range couplings. Here we embed resonators in a photonic band-gap vacuum (BgV), a photonic crystal whose band gap plays for photons the role vacuum plays for bound electrons. The BgV localizes each resonance exponentially, so designed short-range couplings define the lattice Hamiltonian. We thereby experimentally realize a faithful Benalcazar-Bernevig-Hughes Hamiltonian in an all-dielectric photonic crystal, resolving corner resonances and their orbitals in microwave measurements. Unlike the vacuum surrounding electrons, the BgV is itself designable, controlling relative couplings and closed-loop interference through its band dispersion and Bloch modes. Full-wave calculations and extracted models show that uniformly modifying the BgV, with all resonators fixed, switches the quantized polarization of a two-dimensional Su-Schrieffer-Heeger lattice and converts a zero-flux lattice into a $π$-flux one. We also numerically realize three-dimensional pyrochlore and hyperhoneycomb lattices with space groups $R\bar{3}m$ and $C2/c$, the latter a nodal-loop semimetal with topological drumhead surface states. These results establish the BgV as a designable vacuum for all-dielectric tight-binding photonics in two and three dimensions.
one_liner: A photonic-band-gap environment suppresses unwanted long-range coupling and enables faithful all-dielectric tight-binding lattices.
why_it_matters: The designable photonic vacuum enables controlled topological phases and complex 2D and 3D lattice Hamiltonians.

title: Quantum State Search with Classical Interactive Advice
abstract: We study whether a quantum verifier can find a hidden quantum state by exchanging classical messages with an unbounded prover who knows the state. The verifier has access to a reflection oracle about the target. For a Haar-random $n$-qubit target, we prove that achieving constant average fidelity with the target requires $(q+1)^2(B+1)=Ω(2^n)$, where $q$ is the number of verifier queries and $B$ is the total prover-to-verifier communication. The bound allows arbitrary classical interaction and unrestricted computation between queries. Our proof extends the lower bound of Aaronson and Kuperberg (ToC'07) from a single classical proof to an arbitrary classical interaction. As a result, we obtain a quantum-oracle separation of QMA from QCIP. In particular, we give a unitary oracle $\mathcal{U}$ such that there exists a language $L\in\mathrm{QMA}^{\mathcal{U}}$ but $L\notin\mathrm{QCIP}^{\mathcal{U}}$. Our separation holds even for UniqueQMA, the restriction of QMA to verification with a unique quantum witness, which is known to be strictly weaker than QMA in the quantum black-box setting. We further give an oracle construction for a notion known as QMA--QCIP[2] gap problem. This gives average case hardness for a QMA language under classical access to a QCIP[2] decision oracle and is used in establishing negative results on witness encryption and quantum indistinguishability obfuscation.
one_liner: Finding a hidden random quantum state with classical interactive advice requires an exponential tradeoff in queries and communication.
why_it_matters: The lower bound yields quantum-oracle separations between QMA and classical-interaction proof systems.

title: Subsystem quantum Rényi-Bhattacharyya distance in 2D CFTs and its holographic applications
abstract: We develop a systematic method to compute the subsystem fidelity and Rényi fidelity in two-dimensional conformal field theories (CFTs) from the operator product expansion of twist operators, and apply it to the subsystem quantum Bhattacharyya distance (BD) and Rényi-Bhattacharyya distance (RBD). We validate the method against exact results in the free massless fermion and boson theories, and then use it to compute the BD and RBD in holographic CFTs between two heavy primary states, between two thermal states, and between a heavy primary state and a thermal state. When the two states differ in their classical, order-$c$ data, the distances are of order $c$, and the states are distinguishable already at the level of classical gravity; when the leading data coincide, the distances are of order $1/c$ at every order of the short interval expansion, so that the distinguishability becomes a perturbative quantum gravity effect. For a heavy primary state and its thermal counterpart, the leading contribution to the BD appears at order $\ell^8$ and is of order $c^0$, whereas the RBD is generically of order $c$, in line with the earlier finding that a heavy primary state and a thermal state share the same order-$c$ entanglement entropy but have different order-$c$ Rényi entropies in the short interval expansion.
one_liner: A twist-operator method computes subsystem fidelity distances in 2D CFTs and distinguishes classical from quantum-gravity effects.
why_it_matters: It clarifies when locally comparing holographic states probes classical geometry or perturbative quantum gravity.

title: Distributed Phase Tags: A Locality-Preserving Realification Compiler for Misty-State Quantum Programs
abstract: Complex amplitudes can be simulated over real Hilbert spaces by adjoining a two-dimensional real/imaginary degree of freedom. In a multipartite program, however, one globally shared phase tag is not a locality-preserving program transformation: every party would have to act on the same auxiliary system. We recast the distributed real simulation of multipartite quantum mechanics as a syntax-directed compiler into a real misty-state intermediate language. For $n$ parties we give explicit phase-reference codewords $|0\rangle_{P_n}$ and $|1\rangle_{P_n}$ on $n$ local tags and prove that the same real operator $J=XZ$ on any single tag realizes the logical action of multiplication by $i$. If a complex party-local gate is $A=A_R+iA_I$, its real translation is \[ \widehat A_j=A_R\otimes I+A_I\otimes J_j, \] which acts only on party $j$'s data and local phase tag. We prove an intertwining theorem for arbitrary finite party-local pure-state circuits, exact preservation of computational-basis measurement probabilities, preservation of the run-time interaction graph, and one-rebit-per-party overhead. For the canonical three-party GHZ program, the translation lies entirely inside the ordinary black-and-white misty gate fragment: controlled-$J$ replaces the complex phase operation, while the invariant $J_jJ_k|0\rangle_P=-|0\rangle_P$ transfers the required branch sign. This yields a short correctness proof for all four promised GHZ inputs and explains the earlier 64-path cancellation calculation at a single logical phase-code boundary. We distinguish this program realification problem from the weaker task of finding any real strategy with the same correlations, and state precisely which parts are known real-Hilbert-space simulation and which parts belong to the misty-language compilation layer developed here.
one_liner: A compiler simulates multipartite complex quantum programs over real Hilbert spaces using one local phase tag per party.
why_it_matters: It preserves locality, measurement probabilities, and interaction graphs without requiring a globally shared auxiliary system.

title: High-Efficiency Silicon-Lithium Niobate Grating Coupler enabled by Fully-Etched Subwavelength Structures
abstract: A new approach of silicon-lithium niobate (Si-LN) grating couplers (GCs) with a fully-etched structure is proposed. The coupling strength is engineered through subwavelength structures, allowing improved directionality. The adjoint-based inverse design method is simultaneously adopted to achieve efficient coupling between photonic circuits and fibers. Considering the birefringence of LN, the proposed Si-LN GCs are optimized and fabricated for TE mode along the crystallographic Z and Y directions. The experimentally measured coupling efficiencies are -3.3 dB and -3.9 dB along the crystallographic Z and Y directions, respectively. The measured 3-dB bandwidths are broader than 54 nm and the back reflections can be suppressed down to -15 dB over 50 nm for both directions. The proposed Si-LN GCs are realized by only single-step Si etching, offering a practical solution for fast device prototyping in Si-LN photonic integrated circuits.
one_liner: Inverse-designed, fully etched Si–LiNbO3 grating couplers achieve up to −3.3 dB efficiency and bandwidths beyond 54 nm.
why_it_matters: Single-step silicon etching offers a practical route to efficient fiber coupling in hybrid photonic circuits.

title: Non-planar contact structures with Calabi-Yau Fillings and topological quantum computation
abstract: This paper is a non-planar counterpart of the author's earlier work on planar contact structures and topological quantum computation. On a planar page every branch point is paired by a liftable arc, and the pairing matches the Ising representation exactly, in that fixing the channels of the pairs already fixes the state. Here the page has genus g and connected binding, presented as a simple degree-three cover of the disk. Every maximal system of disjoint liftable arcs then has exactly g members and leaves two branch points unused, and the half-twist interchanging the two points is not liftable, although its cube is and lifts to the identity. Ising fusion does not see that leftover pair, determining its channel from the other g and acting there only by scalars, whereas Fibonacci fusion can leave the channel undetermined. The powers of the cube then act by ten distinct relative phases on a single joint eigenspace, while the Calabi-Yau Stein filling stays fixed. An integral residue criterion supplies the Calabi-Yau test, a factorization localized on a contact connected sum is automatically Calabi-Yau, and, unlike in the planar case, a Calabi-Yau factorization need not be the shortest.
one_liner: Non-planar contact structures reveal phase operations invisible to Ising fusion but distinguishable through Fibonacci fusion channels.
why_it_matters: The work links Calabi–Yau Stein fillings and non-planar topology to richer structures for topological quantum computation.

title: Quantum computing for plasma physics in magnetic-confinement fusion
abstract: Plasma simulations for magnetic-confinement fusion (MCF) involve high-dimensional kinetic dynamics, strong nonlinear coupling, complex geometries, and multiscale spatiotemporal behavior, imposing severe computational bottlenecks. While quantum computing offers a potential alternative for accelerating plasma simulation problems, its practical advantage for fusion research has not yet been demonstrated. We review existing quantum computing studies across kinetic dynamics, wave interactions, equilibrium, and macroscopic stability, evaluating their hardware implementations and operational bottlenecks. Current studies remain largely restricted to linearized equations, reduced models, or isolated computational subroutines, leaving a substantial gap from realistic fusion simulations. We summarize key problem characteristics, including high dimensionality, structured dynamics, and measurement requirements, under which plasma applications are most likely to yield a quantum advantage. Guided by these considerations, we highlight potential approaches and present a roadmap toward practical quantum advantage of simulating plasma in MCF.
one_liner: A review assesses quantum algorithms for magnetic-confinement fusion plasmas and maps obstacles to practical quantum advantage.
why_it_matters: It identifies promising plasma problems while emphasizing the gap between reduced demonstrations and realistic fusion simulation.

title: Efficient Block Encodings for Ensembles of Molecular Hamiltonians
abstract: Accurately characterizing molecular properties and reactivity often requires electronic-structure calculations across an ensemble of molecular geometries. Quantum algorithms that process such ensembles coherently could address this challenge, but they require Hamiltonian block encoding circuits that combine advanced factorization techniques with sublinear scaling in ensemble size. Here, we introduce SVD-THC, which extends tensor hypercontraction to sets of Hamiltonians defined at different nuclear geometries through a singular value decomposition of the ensemble. We use SVD-THC to construct a single multiplexed block encoding circuit for all geometries in an ensemble. We then evaluate the approach on ensembles generated by varying internal rotational coordinates in 1-bromo-2-chloroethane as well as in glycine and alanine dipeptides, corresponding to established model systems for peptide conformational landscapes, with up to 5,184 geometries. Across several resolutions of the internal-coordinate grids, the Toffoli complexity of the resulting circuits grows only weakly with the number of geometries, changing by at most 12\% over grids that differ in size by up to 576$\times$. In an energy-thresholding circuit, this yields 35--200$\times$ fewer Toffoli gates than slicing together single-geometry block encodings. This approach could help make coherent processing of molecular geometry ensembles a useful primitive for fault-tolerant quantum computing.
one_liner: SVD-THC enables multiplexed block encodings for thousands of molecular geometries with weak ensemble-size scaling.
why_it_matters: Energy-thresholding circuits use 35–200 times fewer Toffoli gates than combining separate geometry encodings.

title: Conjugate measurement-induced evolution towards maximally mixed states in quadratic quantum systems
abstract: In an earlier work, we showed that, in the interaction-dominant setting, coupling the conjugate variables of a subsystem to distinct environment modes drives the subsystem to a maximally mixed state. Here, we extend the study to the full quadratic dynamics of a single-mode subsystem coupled to a two-mode environment, and identify the phase-space mechanism responsible for the asymptotic behavior. By tracking the exact reduced Weyl characteristic and Wigner functions, we demonstrate that they lose their dependence on local phase-space coordinates on every fixed compact region. In free-particle model, this happens for all values of coupling, whereas in the harmonic oscillator model, it happens above a critical value of the coupling.
