For a squared-distance penalty, the effective tangential dynamics acquires an extrinsic-curvature potential and, in nontrivial normal-rotation sectors, a coupling to the normal-bundle connection. These embedding-dependent terms remain in the strong-penalty limit, generally yielding quantum dynamics different from QCHD. Numerical comparisons for circular, elliptical, and two simultaneous constraints show faster optimization and improved concentration near global minima for the initial states and finite penalty strengths considered.
one_liner: Quantum Constrained Hamiltonian Descent enforces smooth equality constraints intrinsically through quantum motion on the constraint manifold.
why_it_matters: It avoids penalty terms and may improve constrained quantum optimization while revealing curvature effects missed by strong-penalty approaches.

title: Realization of a Superleak in a Quantum Gas
abstract: Ultracold quantum gases offer a controllable and microscopically accessible platform for understanding and engineering superfluidity. Yet, realizing a superleak that selectively transports the superfluid while suppressing normal flow has remained elusive. Here, we harness an optical superlattice to realize such a superleak through dynamical selectivity. The superfluid undergoes coherent Josephson transport, whereas the normal component exhibits slow, thermodynamically limited response, resulting in a flow-rate contrast of 500(49). Exploiting this contrast, we demonstrate repeated filtering of the normal component and dynamical purification of the superfluid, while sustaining coherent driven oscillations for up to 100 cycles. Our results establish a controllable atomic superleak and open possibilities for manipulating transport and thermodynamics in quantum fluids.
one_liner: An optical superlattice realizes an atomic superleak with a 500(49) flow-rate contrast and coherent superfluid oscillations lasting up to 100 cycles.
why_it_matters: The platform enables selective transport and repeated purification of superfluids for controlled studies of quantum-fluid thermodynamics.

title: Entanglement certification of attosecond light fields with photoelectron interferometry
abstract: The emergence of entangled quantum optical states in high-harmonic generation raises a fundamental problem about its characterization, namely, \textit{how can entanglement of extreme-ultraviolet radiation be certified for attosecond light fields?} Here, we provide experimentally accessible separability tests, particularly showing that attosecond photoelectron interferometry provides a direct solution to this problem. This is achieved by a quantum optical treatment of mapping photoelectron interferometry to the measurement of optical correlation functions. This yields a negative-partial-transpose witness for infrared-XUV entanglement and a sufficient witness of genuine multipartite entanglement without auxiliary optical measurements. We evaluate both witnesses on explicit optical states and identify how the protocol can be extended to XUV-XUV entanglement certification. Hence, we establish attosecond photoelectron interferometry as a general framework for entanglement certification across a wide range of optical frequencies.
one_liner: Photoelectron interferometry is mapped to optical correlations that witness infrared-XUV and genuine multipartite entanglement in attosecond fields.
why_it_matters: It offers an experimentally accessible route to certify entanglement at extreme-ultraviolet frequencies without auxiliary optical measurements.

title: Shaping Near Fields of Photonic Modes into Topological Textures
abstract: Topological textures of light, such as optical vortices and skyrmions, are attractive for high-density information encoding and light-matter interactions. In the near field, topologies have primarily been realized using polaritonic platforms that inherently tie the platform to the material dispersion, limiting their footprint due to propagation losses and restricting their operating spectral region. Here, we introduce a route to shape near-field topologies through the geometric engineering of a dielectric metasurface supporting a quasi-bound state in the continuum resonance, without the need for polaritonic surface waves. In-plane deformation of our metasurface bars conserves their resonance-driven near-fields locally, so that the metasurface geometry and the polarization of the illuminating light dictate the generated topology. By shaping silicon unit cells into geometries with rotational symmetry, we create optical topologies with controllable topological charge. Using phase-resolved scattering-type near-field optical microscopy, we experimentally characterize high-purity resonance-locked topologies such as vortices in concentric rings and topological charge doublets in Archimedean spirals. In contrast to conventional topological textures, our purely photonic mode-based field textures are stationary standing waves in the radial direction, without relying on surface-wave propagation or polaritonic dispersion, establishing a spectrally and spatially scalable platform for near-field topological photonics.
one_liner: Geometrically engineered dielectric metasurfaces create stationary near-field vortices and charge doublets without polaritonic surface waves.
why_it_matters: The approach offers spectrally and spatially scalable control of topological near fields for information encoding and light-matter coupling.

title: Fluctuation-free Quantum Battery Charging Enabled by Bell-like Entangled and Separable Charger States
abstract: The implication of entanglement in quantum battery charging remains poorly understood. In addition, intrinsic quantum randomness poses a fundamental challenge to charging uniformity across distinct trials. To address these issues, we study a three-qubit system within a cascaded collision frame, with two qubits acting as the charger and the third serving as the battery. After each collision, an adaptive measurement is performed on the charger, yielding four conditional post-measurement battery states with identical expected stored energy. For arbitrary fixed charger states, we derive analytical expressions for the recurrence relation of stored energy. We find that stored-energy fluctuations depend on whether the dynamics relies on the battery phase \(γ_n\). For two Bell-like families of entangled states, together with their computational basis states termed Bell-like separable states, the dynamics is \(γ_n\)-independent and fluctuations vanish, whereas for other entangled and separable states, fluctuations emerge. These insights establish a paradigm for engineering charger states to design uniform-charging quantum-battery architectures despite inherent quantum randomness.
one_liner: Selected Bell-like entangled and separable charger states eliminate trial-to-trial energy fluctuations in an adaptive three-qubit battery protocol.
why_it_matters: The state-design principle could enable uniform quantum-battery charging despite measurement randomness.

title: Can Entanglement-Induced Feature-Map Designs Improve Projected Quantum Kernels?
abstract: Projected quantum kernels (PQKs) have emerged as a notable approach to circumvent the hardness of machine learning tasks arising from the exponential dimensionality of the quantum Hilbert space. However, recent PQK studies often rely heavily on extensive classical hyperparameter tuning of the radial basis function (RBF) kernel parameter and the support vector machine regularization parameter. The extensive tuning can mask the true representational power of the underlying PQKs induced by quantum feature maps, which has not been explored in detail. Thus, this work aims to expose the structural capabilities of PQKs by isolating and evaluating their native inductive bias through comparisons between untuned and tuned PQKs against the RBF baseline. Furthermore, we propose novel quantum feature maps that leverage two-qubit entanglement to capture multivariate correlations in IoT data. The results show that extensive tuning can lead to competitive performance architectures, while our proposed entanglement topologies exhibit a significantly stronger native inductive bias. This reveals that superior quantum architectural design can yield structurally better PQKs with improvements arising from quantum-mechanical properties rather than from classical hyperparameter tuning.
one_liner: Entangling feature maps give projected quantum kernels a stronger native inductive bias on IoT data beyond gains from classical hyperparameter tuning.
why_it_matters: The study separates quantum architectural value from tuning effects and guides more meaningful quantum-kernel design.

title: Rank-One Loss Maximizes the Spectral Response Strength of Passive Full-Order Exceptional Points
abstract: We consider finite-dimensional non-Hermitian systems in which all modes coalesce at a single exceptional point. For a rank-one anti-Hermitian contribution, the spectral response strength is computed exactly. For passive systems, we then derive a sharp upper bound at fixed exceptional-point decay rate and show that it is reached only when the decay operator has rank one, corresponding to a single independent dissipative direction. This establishes rank-one loss as the optimal configuration for enhancing the response of a full-order exceptional point. The bound holds for arbitrary order and improves on earlier passive estimates beyond second order. Two third-order trimers illustrate the result: a rank-one-loss system saturates the bound, whereas a passive rank-two-loss realization remains below it. The result turns dissipation into a design resource: concentrating the loss into a single effective dissipative direction maximizes the highest-order spectral response of a passive full-order exceptional-point device.
one_liner: A sharp bound proves that rank-one loss uniquely maximizes the spectral response of passive full-order exceptional points at fixed decay rate.
why_it_matters: Concentrating dissipation into one effective channel provides a general design rule for highly responsive non-Hermitian devices.

title: A New Twist on Astigmatic Transformation: Beyond Laguerre-Gaussian Beams
abstract: Astigmatic transformation is widely used to convert the azimuthal phase structure of Laguerre-Gaussian vortex beams into intensity patterns from which the topological charge can be read out. Here, we show that this phase-to-intensity conversion is not just restricted to the Laguerre-Gaussian radial profile. We derive analytical expressions for the astigmatically transformed high-order Bessel--Gauss and perfect optical vortex fields, and find that, despite their substantially different radial structures, the number of intensity minima is directly set by the accumulated azimuthal phase winding. Numerical simulations and experimental measurements on both beam families confirm this result, establishing astigmatic transformation as a direct probe of the topological charge of scalar structured optical fields. We further extend the approach to non-separable vector Bessel-Gauss beams, in which the spatial and polarization degrees of freedom are coupled, and show that polarization-resolved detection allows the topological charge of the constituent spatial modes to be determined independently.
one_liner: Astigmatic transformation reads topological charge from Bessel-Gauss, perfect-vortex, and polarization-resolved vector beams beyond Laguerre-Gaussian modes.
why_it_matters: It broadens a simple phase-to-intensity diagnostic for scalar and vector structured-light fields.

title: Quantum Fokker-Planck solvers as trainable generative models
abstract: We develop and analyze generative models based on quantum solvers of stochastic differential equations. Unlike the common approach based on layered variational quantum circuits with parameterized rotations, we parameterize the potential of a Langevin process. The associated Fokker-Planck (FP) equations are Hermitianized and solved using a linear combination of cosine operators implemented through quantum singular value transformation. By encoding the square root of the stationary density, the model enables sampling through computational-basis measurements and is efficiently controlled by coefficients of the block-encoded diagonal potential. We train the proposed model to match empirical distributions within the family described by FP equations, demonstrating parameter recovery for multivariate probability distributions. Crucially, the model remains trainable at scale. Sample-efficient and convex optimization for in-distribution targets arises from a physics-informed inductive bias and holds regardless of the dimensionality of the problem. We provide circuit constructions and efficient block encodings of the main components of the algorithm and analyze resource requirements. Our approach frames quantum generative learning as quantum model discovery and provides a foundation for extending this framework to high-dimensional, strongly correlated scientific data.
one_liner: A quantum generative model learns distributions by parameterizing Langevin potentials and solving Hermitianized Fokker-Planck equations.
why_it_matters: Physics-informed structure enables convex, sample-efficient training that remains tractable as dimensionality grows.

title: Automating quantum circuit optimization with AI agents
abstract: Compiling quantum algorithms for real devices involves hard optimization problems that can decide whether an algorithm runs at scale. We present a general method for solving such problems with AI agents, with every result certified. It builds on autoresearch loops, in which agents iteratively improve programs against a fixed evaluator and which have recently improved quantum cryptanalysis circuits, and adds two elements: a frozen, exact verifier certifies every result, and this verifier, together with the challenge around it, is built by an agent that formulates the problem with a researcher and validates the verifier against a solved case, deliberately broken solutions and published results before any solution exists. The method applies to any optimization problem whose solutions can be verified exactly and efficiently. We apply it to three compilation problems in quantum simulation, namely fermion-to-qubit encoding, Hamiltonian layout and unitary synthesis. In each, the agents improved substantially on published or standard constructions, reducing the cost being optimized by up to 73% at the largest sizes tested and outperforming a state-of-the-art optimizer for fermion-to-qubit encodings. Every submission is a program accompanied by its agent's notes, so the ideas behind each improvement are recorded in human-readable form; later agents built on them, and we describe them here. These results open the way to automated, certified discovery across quantum circuit design and beyond.
one_liner: AI agents optimize quantum compilation tasks while an independently frozen exact verifier certifies every submitted result.
why_it_matters: The agents cut optimized costs by up to 73%, suggesting a reliable route to automated circuit-design discovery.

title: Finite Systems in the Space of Projective Measurements
abstract: We investigate the dynamics of two-level systems using the quasidistribution $Q$ function projected onto the space of collective measurements. Particular attention is given to evolution under Hamiltonians that are invariant under particle permutations, for pure states that are either invariant or noninvariant under such permutations. This requires constructing an approximate analog of the star product between quasidistribution functions: the projected $Q$ function of a product of two operators is expressed approximately in terms of the individual operators' $Q$ and $P$ functions. We rewrite the Liouville equation to determine approximate state dynamics and compare the result with exact evolution using the Hellinger distance. Overall, the method performs well for permutation-invariant pure states and Hamiltonians, whereas deviations arise for arbitrary pure states and noninvariant Hamiltonians.
one_liner: A projected quasidistribution method approximates two-level-system dynamics in the space of collective measurements.
why_it_matters: It offers an efficient description for permutation-invariant states and Hamiltonians while clarifying where the approximation fails.

title: Orbital-coherence memory in electrical transport and its self-consistent Maxwell response
abstract: An internal electronic coherence changes electrical transport only when it feeds back on the physical current. We develop a reduced description of this feedback and distinguish its exact consequences from the assumptions required for a microscopic realization. An opposite-parity two-orbital Hamiltonian identifies a current-coupled orbital force. Under an explicitly stated moment closure and collision ansatz, it yields a passive three-state response with an exponentially damped oscillatory memory. The resulting conductivity redistributes a fixed optical weight and predicts a nonmonotonic dependence of dc conduction on coherence damping at fixed remaining parameters. The orbital reduction constrains the coupling and internal frequency through a shared bare splitting, providing a test beyond unconstrained spectral fitting. A charge-conserving spatial extension couples to Maxwell equations through a positive energy balance and separates the constitutive response from longitudinal collective and transverse electromagnetic modes. We formulate complex-conductivity and transmission tests, including the limits of parameter identification over a finite bandwidth. The model supplies a conditional connection between orbital dynamics, transport memory, and electromagnetic observables; conductivity alone does not establish a uniquely quantum mechanism, and a material-specific collision calculation and closure-error assessment remain necessary.
one_liner: A reduced three-state model links damped orbital coherence to transport memory and a self-consistent Maxwell response.
why_it_matters: It provides constrained conductivity and transmission tests while warning that transport alone cannot prove a quantum mechanism.

title: Qubits Are Not Enough: Deflation and Measurement Limits in Variational Quantum Modal Analysis
abstract: Amplitude encoding stores an N-degree-of-freedom structural mode using ceiling(log2 N) qubits. This article develops an evaluation framework for variational quantum eigensolvers in finite-element structural dynamics. A Cholesky transformation maps the generalized eigenproblem to a symmetric mass-orthonormal Hamiltonian, ensuring Euclidean quantum-state orthogonality equals structural mass orthogonality. For higher modes, the deflation penalty condition is sharpened to a necessary-and-sufficient threshold, with a Davis-Kahan bound quantifying effects of approximate projectors. Numerical studies separate mapping correctness, ansatz expressibility, preprocessing, Pauli growth, finite-shot uncertainty, and damage localization. For 128-DOF chains, consistent-mass whitening increases transformed-operator density from 0.023 to 0.308 and Pauli terms from 576 to 2950. Exact state-vector experiments show qubit count and circuit expressibility are distinct. At 10^5 shots per Pauli term, first-mode frequency RMS error is 2.45%. In an oracle-state study, 10% stiffness loss is localized in 84.5% of trials. Results sharpen the deflation condition, quantify resource bottlenecks, and claim no speedup.
one_liner: A framework evaluates deflation, preprocessing, measurement, and ansatz limits in variational quantum structural modal analysis.
why_it_matters: It shows that low qubit counts do not remove Pauli-growth and shot-cost bottlenecks, and it claims no quantum speedup.

title: Krylov Complexity and Entropy of Composite Quantum Systems
abstract: We investigate the behaviour of Krylov complexity as the number of degrees of freedom of a quantum system increases. Specifically, we show that for tensor products of commuting subsystems, the leading excess complexity is controlled by a weighted variance of the subsystem Lanczos coefficients. This provides a quantitative measure of dynamical heterogeneity and a precise characterization of synchronous evolution. We also show that Krylov entropy is able to disambiguate the information associated with subsystems composition from that generated by dynamical mismatch, and that the same Lanczos variance controls the leading mismatch contribution to both complexity and the entropy. Our results establish excess complexity and Krylov entropy as complementary probes of the emergence of collective dynamics in large quantum systems.
one_liner: Lanczos-coefficient variance controls leading excess Krylov complexity and entropy mismatch in composite quantum systems.
why_it_matters: The result supplies complementary measures of dynamical heterogeneity and collective behavior as systems grow.

title: Predictive electronic feedback control for narrow-linewidth lasers
abstract: Narrow-linewidth lasers are essential for various key atom-laser interaction processes and optical setups in quantum coherent control, quantum precision measurement, and quantum information science. The Pound-Drever-Hall (PDH) technique is the standard method for the frequency-stabilization of narrow-linewidth lasers, but the inherent time delay in its feedback loop inevitably induces excessive phase noise, commonly known as servo bumps. Previous solutions primarily rely on additional optical components outside the electronic feedback control loop. Here, we propose and implement a generic method based on the Smith predictor to address the time-delay issue entirely within the electronic part of the PDH feedback control loop. We systematically demonstrate its capability to suppress phase noise and reduce servo bumps by adding only a single Field-Programmable Gate Array (FPGA) controller to the loop. This class of methods is demonstrated to be conceptually concise with minimal hardware overhead, effective in practice, and holds potential for a wide variety of future applications.
one_liner: An FPGA-based Smith predictor compensates feedback delay in Pound-Drever-Hall stabilization of narrow-linewidth lasers.
why_it_matters: The electronic-only approach suppresses phase-noise servo bumps with minimal added optical or hardware complexity.

title: Nonlinear quantum noise polarization in macroscopic nonlinear QED
abstract: We construct a quantum theory of light in nonlinearly responding materials with dispersion and absorption and, in particular, show the emergence of non-Gaussian noise associated with nonlinear absorption processes. Our theory is based on a path-integral formulation of the microscopic Huttner-Barnett model including cubic matter self-interaction required for $χ^{(2)}$ nonlinear processes. We show that the noise polarization emerges naturally from a decoupling of the stochastic weights of the bath response which, in case of cubic self-interactions, leads to a decoupling via Airy functions. As the theory is, by construction, consistent with the nonlinear fluctuation-dissipation theorem, it constitutes a viable quantum theory of light in nonlinear media.
one_liner: A path-integral theory derives nonlinear quantum noise polarization in dispersive and absorptive optical materials.
why_it_matters: It captures non-Gaussian noise from nonlinear absorption while remaining consistent with nonlinear fluctuation-dissipation relations.

title: Mutual Information Across Quantum Reference Frame Perspectives
abstract: In quantum information theory, standard notions typically presuppose a fixed partition of the world into subsystems, encoded in a tensor product structure of the Hilbert space. Yet, in some scenarios, the subsystem structure is not uniquely fixed. A case in point is the description of subsystems relative to different quantum reference frames (QRFs), where the tensor product structure, although fixed in a specific QRF, changes across different QRFs. Such a relativity of subsystems underlies many interesting features of QRFs, such as the relativity of entanglement, entropy, and coherence. It also raises a broader question: how do we compare the information across different subsystem perspectives, especially when the corresponding subsystem algebras overlap? Here, we propose a notion of quantum mutual information across different QRF perspectives, which captures the correlations between subsystems relative to different frames of reference. To do so, we focus on an algebraic definition of subsystems. Studying in detail the union and overlap between subsystem algebras relative to different QRFs, we find that the usual definition of mutual information in terms of the chain law overcounts the information associated to the overlap. Based on this insight, we propose a modified chain law and show that the resulting notion of mutual information satisfies subadditivity and connects naturally to other measures found in the literature [1]. Our investigations not only provide a way to quantify the relation between different QRF perspectives from an information-theoretic point of view but also sheds light on some important features of quantum information in absence of a fixed tensor product structure.
one_liner: A modified mutual-information chain law compares overlapping subsystem algebras defined by different quantum reference frames.
why_it_matters: It avoids double-counting shared information and extends correlation measures beyond a fixed tensor-product structure.

title: ConQEC: Concolic Testing for Quantum Error-Correcting Code Implementations
abstract: Quantum error-correcting code (QECC) implementations are hybrid software-control systems: measured syndromes drive decoder dispatch, recovery actions, and logical checks. Existing QECC verification techniques can prove formal obligations, and general quantum testing can expose final failures, but developers still lack a scalable testing workflow that generates concrete faults and explains where a QECC repair path first diverges. This paper presents ConQEC, to our knowledge the first concolic testing framework for QECC implementations. By combining concrete (Pauli) fault replay with symbolic repair-path constraints, ConQEC generates tests that expose not only final logical failures but also fault--syndrome--decoder--recovery (FSDR) diagnostics: the injected fault, observed syndrome, decoder decision, recovery action, oracle result, and earliest divergent stage. Its symbolic encoding of Pauli faults, syndrome predicates, decoder and recovery relations, and oracle checks enables this diagnostic workflow to scale beyond exponentially increasing amplitude-level quantum-state reasoning. We implemented ConQEC and evaluated it on generated source-level QECC families and public QECC artifacts with up to thousands of qubits. ConQEC detects the seeded bug in every experimental case and reports a replay-valid, fault-localizing FSDR witness for each.
one_liner: ConQEC combines concrete Pauli-fault replay with symbolic constraints to test and diagnose quantum error-correction software.
why_it_matters: It found every seeded bug in tests reaching thousands of qubits and produced replayable witnesses locating the first divergence.

title: Nanopillar metasurfaces uniting high optical reflectivity with ultracoherent nanomechanics
abstract: Mechanically compliant mirrors are key components in cavity optomechanics. However, the requirements to achieve the best optical and mechanical performance are usually in direct competition. A high reflectivity for tightly focused beams entails thick reflectors, whereas ultracoherent flexural nanomechanics necessitates thin membranes. We eliminate this trade-off by introducing high-refractive-index nanopillar metasurfaces on top of a thin membrane. We pattern a 50 micrometer-diameter array of nanopillars to form a photonic crystal. The flat band behavior of guided resonances in the photonic crystal enables a reflectivity of 99.82(1)% for a tightly focused beam of 7 micrometer waist. The combination of two guided resonances creates a 100 nanometer-wide high-reflectivity band around 1550 nanometer. Simultaneously, the nanopillar patterning realizes a density-modulated phononic crystal that isolates an ultracoherent localized mechanical mode with a $Q\cdot f$-product of $2\cdot 10^{14}$Hz. The demonstrated nanopillar metasurfaces enable lightweight mirrors for room-temperature quantum optomechanics and for use as levitated mirrors or lightsails.
one_liner: Nanopillar metasurfaces combine 99.82% focused-beam reflectivity with an ultracoherent localized mechanical mode.
why_it_matters: The design removes a key mirror trade-off for room-temperature optomechanics, levitated mirrors, and lightsails.

title: Observation of Polarization Topology in Magneto-Optical BICs
abstract: Polarization topology in momentum space is a fundamental characteristic of photonic bound states in the continuum (BICs), where the winding of far-field polarization defines a quantized topological charge. Although magneto-optical (MO) BICs combine polarization topology with magnetically tunable chirality, experimental characterization remains challenging because time-reversal symmetry (TRS) breaking complicates eigenpolarization extraction. Here, we experimentally resolve the momentum-space polarization topology of an MO BIC by reconstructing its two-dimensional far-field eigenpolarization texture. We extract the resonant output polarization using singular value decomposition of the polarization-resolved angle-resolved reflection matrix without invoking reciprocity. The reconstructed polarization azimuth winds counterclockwise by 2$π$ around the $Γ$-point singularity, yielding a topological charge of q = +1. Moreover, the polarization handedness can be reversed solely by varying the magnetic-bias strength, while the field direction and the measured topological charge remain unchanged. A non-Hermitian coupled-mode model traces this reversal to hybridization between the BIC mode and a leaky mode. This work establishes experimental access to momentum-space polarization topology in nonreciprocal photonics, opening a route to explore topological singularities and their evolution under active TRS breaking.
one_liner: Experiments reconstruct the momentum-space eigenpolarization texture and charge of a magneto-optical bound state in the continuum.
why_it_matters: The method reveals tunable handedness under broken time-reversal symmetry without changing the measured topological charge.

title: Macroscopic Nuclear Resonance Energy Transfer Mediated by Coherent Magnons
abstract: Phonon-mediated nuclear Resonance Energy Transfer (RET) in metal deuterides is severely constrained by inertial rest-mass dilution, lattice fracture limits, and thermal nuclear spin cancellation. Extending the generalized nuclear Dicke model to Ferromagnetic Resonance (FMR) magnons eliminates mass dilution via hyperfine-amplified M1 coupling while unlocking relativistic Dirac M2 coupling via Overhauser spin polarization. We derive a Suhl-clamped FMR scaling law predicting 14.2 MeV (Pd-106) and 11.4 MeV (Ni-58) breakup neutrons, 19.9 MeV alpha particles, and reconciled sub-keV fusion anomalies.
one_liner: A generalized nuclear Dicke model proposes coherent FMR magnons as mediators of macroscopic nuclear resonance energy transfer.
why_it_matters: The model predicts energetic nuclear products while addressing limitations of phonon-mediated transfer in metal deuterides.

title: ArcTN: Efficient Tensor-Network Contraction Planning for Quantum Circuit Simulation
abstract: Tensor-network simulation of quantum circuits depends on contraction orders with low computational cost and small intermediate tensors, found without excessive planning time. We present ArcTN, a contraction-order optimization framework with two search presets. Light keeps planning overhead low, and Heavy spends more effort on refinement. Both combine randomized-greedy construction, subtree reconfiguration, and parallel tempering with stage-specific stopping rules. ArcTN also provides Fixed and Dynamic slicing to meet tensor-size limits and executes the returned orders. On the 30 QC32 quantum-circuit networks completed by all eight compared configurations, Light reduces FLOPs by 61.32% and plans 1.62$\times$ faster than Cotengra Auto/CMA-ES, and Heavy reduces FLOPs by 43.83% and plans 7.21$\times$ faster than Cotengra AutoHQ/Optuna. Heavy also needs 11.85% fewer FLOPs than OMECO TreeSA-8 and plans 1.33$\times$ faster. Dynamic slicing meets the size limits in all 90 runs on 18 scalar-output networks and reduces total sliced FLOPs by 31.99% relative to Fixed slicing, at the cost of longer planning. With a common NumPy executor, Heavy has the lowest combined planning and execution time among five configurations on the runs that all of them completed. On 672 networks built from 320 MQT Bench circuits, Heavy obtains the lowest geometric-mean FLOPs on the 142 large networks while planning 3.1$\times$ and 31$\times$ faster than Cotengra AutoHQ and Hyper128.
one_liner: ArcTN optimizes tensor-network contraction orders using randomized greedy search, subtree refinement, tempering, and adaptive slicing.
why_it_matters: It lowers simulation FLOPs and planning time across quantum-circuit benchmarks while respecting intermediate-tensor limits.

title: Size-independent Logarithmic Sobolev Inequalities for Quantum Gibbs Samplers
abstract: We propose a new method for proving $L^2$ and modified logarithmic Sobolev inequalities with constants independent of system size for quantum Gibbs samplers whose Lindblad generators satisfy Kubo-Martin-Schwinger (KMS) detailed balance. We first establish the $L^2$ logarithmic Sobolev inequality by transporting it along a temperature-dependent path from the infinite-temperature product state to the target Gibbs state while maintaining a size-independent decay rate for the sandwiched Rényi-2 divergence. A tensor-power argument, combined with the quantum asymptotic equipartition property, then transfers this decay bound to relative entropy, yielding the modified logarithmic Sobolev inequality. This approach provides a general framework for proving size-independent logarithmic Sobolev inequalities for quantum Gibbs samplers. We apply it to two regimes: one-dimensional quantum spin chains at every finite temperature, and finite-range quantum spin systems at sufficiently high temperature in any fixed dimension.
one_liner: A temperature-path method proves size-independent logarithmic Sobolev inequalities for broad classes of quantum Gibbs samplers.
why_it_matters: The bounds support system-size-independent mixing guarantees for 1D finite-temperature and high-temperature finite-range systems.

title: Mixed State Deep Thermalization under Generic Quantum Errors
abstract: Pure-state deep thermalization predicts that, after sufficient scrambling, projected ensembles approach universal distributions that contain information beyond the reduced density matrix. In realistic quantum systems, however, noise is unavoidable and the projected states are generally mixed. Whether mixed-state deep thermalization admits an analogous universal limiting distribution has remained unclear. Here we answer this question for quantum dynamics containing local quantum channels, i.e., errors. We show that the late-time mixed-state projected ensemble is completely determined by the normalized Choi state of the error channel and is universal, independent of the microscopic details of the underlying unitary dynamics. We establish this result analytically for dual-unitary circuits, global Haar-random dynamics, and local Haar-random circuits at large local dimension, and verify it numerically in qubit circuits and kicked Ising dynamics. In a solvable setting, we further find exponentially fast convergence to the limiting ensemble. Our results extend deep thermalization to noisy quantum dynamics and establish a direct correspondence between quantum errors and universal random mixed-state ensembles.
one_liner: Late-time mixed-state projected ensembles under local errors are universally fixed by the error channel's normalized Choi state.
why_it_matters: This extends deep thermalization to noisy dynamics and links quantum errors directly to universal random mixed-state ensembles.

title: GEM-PIC-RZ: a Galilean electromagnetic particle-in-cell code in quasi-cylindrical geometry with nonuniform grids
abstract: Laser-plasma accelerators span scales from the micrometre wavelength of the driving laser to acceleration lengths of millimetres or metres. Full particle-in-cell (PIC) simulations resolve the laser carrier but are constrained by the Courant condition, whereas quasi-static models are computationally efficient but do not resolve it. We present GEM-PIC-RZ, a quasi-cylindrical implementation of the Galilean electromagnetic PIC scheme. The method retains the slow evolution of the forward field and therefore resolves the laser carrier while allowing a propagation step governed by the evolution of the laser and plasma rather than by the cell size. User-defined nonuniform grids and a charge-conserving regularization of the bubble closure support efficient simulations across these scales. Comparisons with the full PIC code FBPIC show agreement for the laser wake, the depletion and redshift of a few-cycle pulse, and ionization injection; the measured CPU time is about 2\,\% of that for FBPIC in the reported runs; the injected charge carries a model uncertainty of about 15\,\% from the regularization. An envelope model, in contrast, underestimates the depletion of the few-cycle pulse fivefold. Self-injection in a sharp density down-ramp is not yet reproduced and remains an open problem.
one_liner: GEM-PIC-RZ resolves laser carriers on nonuniform quasi-cylindrical grids using a Galilean electromagnetic PIC formulation.
why_it_matters: Reported runs reproduce several full-PIC effects at about 2% of FBPIC's CPU time, though down-ramp self-injection remains unresolved.

title: Multiport photonic routing with a single cavity-based electro-optic phase shifter per port
abstract: Programmable photonic meshes can perform general linear transformations, but universal transformations on $N$ modes require $O(N^2)$ programmable phase shifters, which cannot simultaneously achieve low drive voltage, gigahertz speed, zero static power, lossless modulation, and a compact footprint. Signal routing does not require universal transformations, which allows considerable circuit simplifications. We present a compact reflective circuit architecture that connects all input-output pairs across $N$ modes in $N$ steps using only $O(N)$ programmable phase shifters. The circuit comprises a single passive $N\times N$ interferometer and a single column of programmable reflective phase shifters. We demonstrate the architecture by implementing a $3\times 3$ router in x-cut thin-film lithium niobate with a passive multimode interferometer and phase shifters based on single-sided photonic-crystal nanobeam cavities. Our programmable devices exhibit a $1.92$ GHz/V resonance tuning efficiency via the Pockels effect, a footprint of $100\,μ\mathrm{m}^2$, sub-5-V drive voltage, and a 6.2 GHz electro-optic bandwidth. Through voltage-space characterization and physical modeling, we identify routing states with extinction ratios exceeding 11 dB at each output and demonstrate sequential routing at an equipment-limited speed of 10 MHz. Our results establish cavity-enhanced Pockels switching as a routing layer for classical and quantum computing interconnects across visible and near-infrared wavelengths.
one_liner: A 3×3 lithium-niobate photonic router uses one cavity-based electro-optic phase shifter per port and a passive interferometer.
why_it_matters: The O(N) architecture combines compact, low-voltage, gigahertz-bandwidth switching with routing extinction above 11 dB.

title: Quantum Complexity and Stabilizer-State Expansions: From Pairing to Deformation in Fermionic Systems
abstract: Understanding how collective phenomena such as pairing and deformation emerge in interacting fermionic systems, and how the correlations underlying them shape the resources required for their simulation, is a central challenge in many-body physics. We investigate various aspects of quantum complexity in a fermionic system exhibiting two main forms of collectivity, specifically deformation and pairing, through entanglement, non-stabilizerness, and fermionic non-Gaussianity. In the deformed phase, high entanglement coexists with low non-stabilizerness, while the superfluid pairing phase, by contrast, exhibits substantial multipartite entanglement and non-stabilizerness, together with maximal fermionic anti-flatness. In a second step we examine how to describe the phase diagram of the system in a classically scalable and symmetry-preserving way, by combining stabilizer-state expansion and variational basis optimization. A physics-guided decomposition of the Hamiltonian identifies the relevant stabilizer states, which can be constructed from graph states. A single stabilizer state captures the deformed phase to a large extent, and, although the number of stabilizer states required to describe the pairing phase grows exponentially with system size, a symmetry-preserving basis rotation yields a high-fidelity approximation using far fewer states. This rotated state can then serve as a practical starting point for quantum refinement.
one_liner: Entanglement and non-stabilizerness distinguish deformed and paired fermionic phases and guide compact stabilizer expansions.
why_it_matters: Symmetry-preserving basis rotation sharply reduces the stabilizer resources needed to approximate the challenging pairing phase.

title: Photoelectrons resolve the phase-dependent variance of bright squeezed vacuum
abstract: The variance of bright squeezed vacuum (BSV) is not only strong but also phase dependent, yet recent strong-field experiments with BSV have recorded only its magnitude. A coherent field of the same color provides the phase reference that resolves this phase-dependent noise. Strong-field ionization of xenon by this light shows that the photoelectron yield follows the BSV quadrature along the coherent field, and that the nonlinearity of ionization amplifies the quadrature noise many times over in the electron yield. The noise is moreover distributed unevenly over the photoelectron momentum distribution, differing by an order of magnitude between ionization channels. Strong-field ionization thus offers a phase-sensitive, channel-resolved detector of quantum light, while the quadrature noise of quantum light offers a probe of the intensity dependence of individual ionization pathways.
one_liner: Xenon photoelectrons reveal the phase-dependent quadrature variance of bright squeezed vacuum through nonlinear ionization.
why_it_matters: The method enables phase-sensitive, channel-resolved detection of quantum light and probing of strong-field ionization pathways.

title: SILMARILS-MV: Information-Theoretically Secure Multi-Verifier Signatures with Dealer-Free Key Issuance and Linear Aggregation for Permissioned Blockchains
abstract: Permissioned blockchains authenticate transactions, votes and quorum certificates with computationally secure signatures, and post-quantum replacements inflate consensus traffic by orders of magnitude. Information-theoretic alternatives have required a trusted authority, quantum channels, per-signature interaction, or single-use keys with bounded transfer. We present SILMARILS-MV, a multi-verifier unconditionally secure signature in which a signature is the vector $α= A\,e(m)$ and each verifier holds a secret functional $c_i = Γ^T λ(x_i)$ derived from virtual anchors $Γ$ that nobody learns. Against unbounded adversaries corrupting up to $ω$ verifiers and any signers, and observing every decision, an honest verifier accepts a forged or invalid signature with probability at most $Q/q + 1/(q-1)$, a bound that is tight in its leading term. The scheme is strongly unforgeable, non-repudiable, transferable across unboundedly many hops, and linearly aggregatable. Keys are issued by the validators through perfectly secure MPC for $t < n/3$, without broadcast. To scale, we let the committee itself sign: in threshold notarization, finality certificates have constant size $32(ω+1)$ bytes and per-validator issuance cost no longer depends on $n$. Arbiter-verified keys give clients 32-byte signatures, robust redistribution supports membership changes and share refresh, and verifiers can be enrolled retroactively. A certificate verifies in 2.4 microseconds. In an analytic normal-case model at 1000 validators, threshold notarization needs 71 KiB of authentication traffic per validator per block, 22x less than ML-DSA-44 for admitted verifiers. In a Rust HotStuff prototype with 100 validators, SILMARILS-MV commits 2.8x more transactions per second than ML-DSA-44 with 67x less cryptographic CPU, and Monte-Carlo attacks match the bounds.
one_liner: SILMARILS-MV provides dealer-free, information-theoretically secure multi-verifier signatures with linear aggregation.
why_it_matters: It targets efficient permissioned-blockchain authentication with compact certificates and substantially lower traffic and CPU costs.

title: Temporal Degeneracy Limits Message Passing Decoding of QLDPC Codes Under Repeated Noisy Syndrome Measurements
abstract: Practical quantum computations can require logical error rates of $10^{-12}$ or lower. Quantum low-density parity-check (QLDPC) codes are promising candidates for reaching such rates with low qubit overhead, provided that their syndromes can be decoded efficiently. Repeated noisy syndrome measurements introduce temporal degeneracy into the space-time decoding graph. We characterize the temporal kernel, whose vectors have zero total data parity, and show that it is generated by elementary temporal codewords of weight $d_v+2$, where $d_v$ is the variable-node degree. For $(d_v,d_c)$-regular parity-check matrices with fixed degrees $d_v,d_c>2$ and girth greater than four, we derive counting bounds and construct degenerate error patterns of weight $(d_v+2)/2$ for even $d_v$ and $d_v+1$ for odd $d_v$, with multiplicity $Θ(nr)$ in the blocklength $n$ and number of measurement rounds $r$. Under the isolation assumption, these patterns cause local failures of deterministic isotropic message-passing decoders under a flooding schedule. These failures depend on the node degrees rather than the minimum distance; for the bivariate bicycle (BB) codes considered, their weight is equal to four. Monte carlo simulations and fixed-weight importance sampling quantify harmful low-weight degenerate error patterns for the min-sum (MS) decoder beyond the isolation assumption. Motivated by the identified symmetries, we propose space-time anisotropic min-sum decoding with syndrome-guided realizations. Its complexity is linear in the number of Tanner graph edges for fixed maximum number of iterations and number of decoders. Numerical results on BB codes show threshold-like behavior acrossthe tested code sizes and improved failure probabilities relative to MS decoding with ordered statistics decoding post-processing.
one_liner: Temporal degeneracy creates low-weight failure patterns for message-passing decoders of QLDPC codes with noisy syndromes.
why_it_matters: An anisotropic min-sum decoder exploits space-time structure to improve failure rates while retaining linear complexity.

title: Sub-monolayer tracking of molecular states at buried interfaces
abstract: Phenomena responsible for emerging technologies originate from novel molecular states at buried interfaces. Yet quantitatively resolving these features is out of reach in most cases. Resonant scattering has demonstrated sensitivity to these local states but is limited due to a lack of accurate interpretive models. We leverage a machine learning (ML)-optimized optical model to analyze polarized resonant soft X-ray scattering (RSoXS) from molecular thin films. This new analysis establishes the direct and quantitative interpretation of molecular orientation, chemical identity and packing states as a function of depth with sub-monolayer resolution - reaching beyond the diffraction limit via locking energy and polarization through the optical model. From our analysis, we discover a gradient evolution of molecular orientation and packing emerging from the interface, indicative of competing surface versus bulk growth dynamics and contradicting hypotheses of substrate patterning. This nondestructive insight into buried interfacial formation and final state opens possibilities in controlling interfacial states and phenomena in next-generation technologies.
one_liner: An ML-optimized optical model extracts depth-dependent molecular orientation, identity, and packing from polarized RSoXS data.
why_it_matters: It enables nondestructive sub-monolayer characterization of buried interfaces and reveals competing surface and bulk growth dynamics.

title: Noise-Assisted Quantum Entanglement: Memory-Enhanced Coherence in Stochastic Jaynes-Cummings Dynamics
abstract: We investigate qubit entanglement dynamics in a two-qubit cavity system with stochastically fluctuating coupling strength, comparing white noise (Markovian) and Ornstein-Uhlenbeck noise (non-Markovian) processes. We analytically solve the system dynamics for both Fock and coherent cavity states and systematically characterize how initial qubit configurations affect entanglement generation and preservation. Our results reveal distinct dynamical regimes: in the Fock-state cavity, initial states in the single-excitation subspace generate robust qubit entanglement in decoherence-free subspaces, while initially entangled states in the double-excitation subspace exhibit inevitable decay without protective symmetries. For coherent cavities, we identify a critical photon-number threshold in the intermediate coherent-state amplitude regime where dynamics transition from low-frequency to high-frequency entanglement oscillations, while universal entanglement loss occurs at large amplitudes. Remarkable resilience against entanglement sudden death emerges under strong non-Markovian noise with long correlation times, where repeated revivals occur. These findings establish cavity photon statistics and environmental memory time as key control parameters for engineering qubit entanglement dynamics in qubit-cavity systems, revealing how system-environment correlations govern quantum information preservation.
one_liner: Stochastic Jaynes-Cummings analysis shows how cavity photon statistics and noise memory govern two-qubit entanglement dynamics.
why_it_matters: Long-correlated non-Markovian noise can sustain repeated entanglement revivals and mitigate sudden death in suitable regimes.

title: QuantumMatterExplorer: An Autonomous Agent for the Discovery of Quantum Many-Body Phases of Matter
abstract: Mapping the phase diagram of a new quantum Hamiltonian demands expert judgement at every step: which observables to measure, where in parameter space to compute, or how to separate genuine order from finite-size artefacts. We introduce QuantumMatterExplorer, an autonomous agent that takes only a Hamiltonian and its parameter ranges as input and returns a phase diagram obtained from its own numerical simulations. The agent is built on a large language model and is designed to reason over a long horizon, maintain a persistent written plan, and drive a set of computational tools, with density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) calculations cross-checked against independent exact diagonalization. The agent combines a large language model with persistent planning, a library of expert computational-physics skills, and density-matrix renormalization group calculations validated against independent exact diagonalization. It adaptively selects quantities to evaluate, refines parameter scans, and performs finite-size analyses as evidence accumulates. After validating the approach on Hamiltonians with known transitions, we challenge it with a frustrated bilinear-biquadratic spin-1 chain with single-ion anisotropy, whose two-dimensional phase diagram was published only recently and is unlikely to appear in any training corpus. Given no hint about the expected physics, the agent proposes which observables to probe, and identifies candidate Néel, Haldane and dimerized phases, in broad agreement with the reference phase diagram. It also detects incommensurate correlations and infers the frustration-dependent geometry of the phase boundaries, all within an eight-hour compute budget. These results open a practical route to the autonomous computational discovery of new phases of quantum matter.
one_liner: An autonomous LLM agent maps quantum phase diagrams using adaptive DMRG simulations cross-checked by exact diagonalization.
why_it_matters: It demonstrates a practical route toward autonomous numerical discovery of many-body phases with limited expert input.

title: Additive uncertainty relations via pseudospectral methods
abstract: Given Hermitian observable $A$, the variance of $A$ is given by the difference of expectations $\langle A^2\rangle - \langle A\rangle^2$, where the expectation of an observable implicitly assumes a choice of state for the underlying system. As a sub-case of a general lower bound for the sum of variances for finitely many arbitrary elements in a $C^*$-algebra, we prove that the sum of the variances for $d$ observables $A_1, \dots , A_d$ is greater than some expression in the expectations $\langle i[A_j,A_k]\rangle$ for $j\neq k$ plus the square of the smallest singular value of the associated localizer. In special cases, this expression is just a root mean square average. Our technique also derives a general containment between the Clifford pseudospectra and quadratic pseudospectra for $d$ observables.
one_liner: Pseudospectral methods yield lower bounds on sums of observable variances using commutators and localizer singular values.
why_it_matters: The framework generalizes additive uncertainty relations to arbitrary finite families of elements in a C*-algebra.

title: Can Spontaneous Time-Translation Symmetry Breaking Be Quantized Without Explicit Branches?
abstract: Can classically branched dynamics associated with spontaneous time-translation-symmetry breaking be quantized without explicitly retaining the branches of the Hamiltonian? We investigate this question using a reduced phase space. formulation in which the Hamiltonian is single-valued, while the critical structure of the classical Legendre map is encoded in a singular, momentum-dependent symplectic geometry. Quantization of the reduced Poisson algebra yields a deformed position-momentum commutator whose singularities determine distinct regular momentum sectors. Using the positive measure induced by the reduced symplectic structure, we identify a bounded central sector and two unbounded outer sectors. In the central sector, states with vanishing mean momentum obey a nonzero lower bound on position uncertainty, subject to the operator-domain assumptions of the representation. We further identify a possible field-theoretic connection with k-essence, where nonlinear scalar-field kinetics can produce finite-velocity degeneracies of the Legendre map. The relationship between the resulting reduced quantum description and branch-matching quantization remains unresolved and requires a comparison of the corresponding Hilbert spaces and operator domains.
one_liner: A reduced quantization replaces branched Hamiltonians with singular symplectic geometry and a deformed position-momentum algebra.
why_it_matters: It offers a branch-free view of time-translation symmetry breaking while exposing unresolved domain and Hilbert-space issues.

title: Zero photoemission from icosahedral superatoms
abstract: Photoemission is expected to occur when the photon energy exceeds the binding energy of an electron, with the photoemission yield generally remaining non-zero above this threshold. Yet, it can be suppressed at specific photon energies, a phenomenon known as the Cooper minimum. Although complete suppression represents an extreme limit of this phenomenon, such zero photoemission has previously been reported only for atoms with an outermost s-type orbital and has never been observed in non-atomic systems. Here, we demonstrate the deliberate realization of zero photoemission from Ag12W-, an artificial icosahedral superatom, by observing a vanishing photoemission cross section 0.85 eV above the detachment threshold and reproducing this behavior in theoretical simulations. These simulations predict that zero photoemission can be common in nearly spherical nanoclusters, a prediction we experimentally confirm using Ag12Mo-, an isoelectronic counterpart of Ag12W-. Because superatoms offer systematic control over both size and elemental composition using the periodic table, our findings establish a route toward active control of photoemission in finite-size quantum systems and stimulate further investigations of underexplored physical phenomena such as nondipole effects.
one_liner: Experiments and simulations demonstrate complete photoemission suppression above threshold in icosahedral silver-based superatoms.
why_it_matters: Controllable zero photoemission extends Cooper-minimum physics beyond atoms and may enable engineered emission in nanoclusters.

title: Cross-coupled photon avalanche drives room-temperature intrinsic optical bistability
abstract: Optically bistable materials promise technological advances in optical information processing, memristive devices, and multiparametric sensing. However, optical bistability is predominantly observed under cryogenic conditions or is governed by subtle thermo-optical nonlinearities. Here, we report on Ho3+-activated nanocrystals that exhibit cavity-free intrinsic optical bistability (IOB) at ambient conditions. Non-thermal IOB stems from a cross-coupled photon avalanche (XPA) mechanism enabled by a low-phonon-energy double-perovskite host, which reduces nonradiative losses and facilitates excited-state population via XPA, even when the pump intensity is below threshold. Time-resolved luminescence measurements support the proposed XPA, as evidenced by a double-rise profile consistent with two reservoir states interlocked in energy looping. IOB with high-contrast photoswitching (up to 46 dB) is observed at room temperature across multiple visible emission lines, enabling wavelength-division multiplexing and compatibility with common detectors. IOB is preserved across nano- to microscale crystals and different double-perovskite compositions, broadly enabling information photonics and advanced sensing.
one_liner: Ho3+-doped double-perovskite nanocrystals exhibit cavity-free, nonthermal optical bistability at room temperature.
why_it_matters: High-contrast multicolor switching at ambient conditions could support compact photonic memory, multiplexing, and sensing.

title: Asymptotic scars arising from the remnants of quantum phase transitions
abstract: Many-body localisation, Hilbert space fragmentation and quantum many-body scars (QMBS) are well-established mechanisms of ergodicity breaking in quantum systems. Recently, asymptotic quantum many-body scars (AQMBS), non-thermal states whose stability grows with system size, have been proposed theoretically and probed experimentally. Here, we show that AQMBS arise naturally as remnants of certain quantum phase transitions. For a broad class of frustration-free Hamiltonians, we prove that their gapless excitations survive deformation into a scarred Hamiltonian as states whose energy variance is bounded by the excitation gap. Consequently, the gapless excitations at a quantum critical point become AQMBS of the scarred Hamiltonian. Their fidelity relaxation time is then set by the critical scaling of the gap, determined by the dynamic critical exponent. Modelling the critical Fredkin and Motzkin chains and the two-dimensional PVBS model, we obtain AQMBS whose variances directly reflect the dynamic exponents of the underlying transitions. Where the gap of the Motzkin chain closes super-exponentially, we find exponentially stable AQMBS, for which we also observe numerical evidence of volume-law entanglement.
one_liner: Gapless excitations of certain quantum critical systems persist after deformation as increasingly stable asymptotic many-body scars.
why_it_matters: The work links scar lifetimes and energy variances directly to critical-gap scaling and dynamic critical exponents.

title: Real-space construction and selection rules of center-of-mass momentum eigenstates in two-dimensional many-body lattices
abstract: We present a comprehensive framework for the real-space construction of center-of-mass (c.m.) momentum eigenstates in two-dimensional (2D) quantum many-body systems. Unlike standard momentum-space approaches, our real-space formalism explicitly captures the non-uniformity of cyclic subspace dimensions, which are fundamentally governed by the spatial symmetries of the many-body configurations and particle statistics. We demonstrate that performing 2D real-space translations on multi-particle states naturally induces non-trivial translation phase factors associated with the characters of these stabilizer subgroups, leading to a renormalization of permissible momentum values. Notably, we identify an anomalous cross-dimensional momentum coupling in highly symmetric particle distributions, where the permissible momentum values in one direction are strictly constrained by those in the perpendicular direction. We emphasize the algorithmic necessity of this coupling, as neglecting it leads to missing or duplicated basis states in numerical implementations. Concrete examples are provided to demonstrate the practical implementation and physical consequences of this framework.
one_liner: A real-space framework constructs 2D center-of-mass momentum eigenstates while accounting for stabilizers and particle statistics.
why_it_matters: Its cross-dimensional selection rules prevent missing or duplicated basis states in many-body numerical calculations.

title: Material criteria for angular-momentum transfer from twisted photons to photoelectrons
abstract: We study the material requirements for transferring the total-angular-momentum (TAM) projection of a twisted photon to the orbital angular momentum (OAM) of a photoelectron emitted from an $n$-type semiconductor surface. Within a single-valley effective-mass model of surface photoemission, we calculate OAM-resolved spectra for GaAs, InSb, $\mathrm{InAs}_{0.34}\mathrm{Sb}_{0.66}$, and $\mathrm{Hg}_{0.76}\mathrm{Cd}_{0.24}\mathrm{Te}$ irradiated by twisted photons with Laguerre--Gaussian--like momentum profile. The OAM transfer is characterized by the mean electron OAM, its root-mean-squared width, and the fraction of electrons with OAM-projection equal to the photon TAM-projection. Efficient transfer requires the transverse momentum of the conduction electron to be much smaller than the transverse momentum width of the photon, which favors low temperatures, small conduction-band effective masses, and shallow donor levels. GaAs is less favorable within the present model because of its larger effective mass and deeper donor levels. We also discuss the demanding photon-wave packet parameters, possible extensions to Dirac and Weyl semimetals, and post-emission OAM selection. Although the generation of vortex electrons with a vanishing OAM uncertainty via photoemission seems challenging, we argue that it is still possible to generate single-electron vortex states with a finite OAM dispersion.
one_liner: A semiconductor photoemission model identifies conditions for transferring twisted-photon angular momentum to electron orbital motion.
why_it_matters: The results guide material and source choices for producing vortex electrons with controlled orbital-angular-momentum dispersion.

title: Kinetic competition controls loss-induced exceptional points of Hubbard pairs
abstract: Two-body loss can bind two fermions in a Hubbard lattice, yet the binding threshold in the infinite lattice need not be an exceptional point (EP). At fixed total momentum $\mathbf{K}$, the hops of the two particles interfere into a relative-motion hopping along each lattice direction, which sets the kinetic energy of the relative motion. On a hypercubic lattice, the threshold $g_c=1/[πρ_2(0)]$ is an EP precisely when the maximum kinetic energy along one direction exceeds the sum of the transverse maxima. This dominance keeps every transverse-momentum scattering channel propagating near the band center, making the local pair Green function purely imaginary there. Two real-energy scattering zeros associated with coherent perfect absorption then coalesce at the threshold into a second-order EP of the analytically continued pair problem, where loss restores the parity-time symmetry of the pair's scattering solutions. Without a dominant direction, binding occurs without coalescence and without breaking of that symmetry. Total momentum can therefore select EP sectors even on isotropic lattices. More broadly, the kinetic structure of the two-particle continuum determines whether loss-induced binding and exceptional degeneracy coincide.
one_liner: The kinetic structure of a Hubbard pair determines whether loss-induced binding coincides with an exceptional point.
why_it_matters: It shows that total momentum and directional hopping competition can select exceptional-point sectors in isotropic lattices.

title: Quantum Cryptomania with Classical Communication without One-Way Functions
abstract: In classical cryptography, one-way functions are necessary for most of cryptography. In the quantum world, however, Kretschmer at {TQC'21} and subsequent works have demonstrated that quantum versions of various primitives in minicrypt, such as signatures and private-key encryption, do not require quantum-computable one-way functions (\textsf{qOWF}s). However, the question of the necessity of \textsf{qOWF}s for primitives in Cryptomania like public-key encryption with classical public keys and ciphertexts (\textsf{qPKE}) has remained open. We provide a comprehensive picture of the relationship between \textsf{qPKE} and \textsf{qOWF}. First, our main result is a black-box separation between \textsf{qOWF}s and \textsf{qPKE}. In particular, we show that relative to a unitary, real, and self-inverse oracle, there exists a \textsf{qPKE} scheme (with classical keys and ciphertexts), but \textsf{qOWF}s do not exist. Further, our oracles admit a point-function obfuscation construction, thus ruling out black-box construction of \textsf{qOWF} from point function obfuscations. On the positive side, we construct \textsf{qPKE} from quantum indistinguishability obfuscation for quantum circuits with classical obfuscated descriptions and efficiently verifiable one-way puzzles, which is known to be a potentially weaker assumption than \textsf{qOWF}s, due to an existing black-box separation. Our construction is the quantum analog of the classical construction of \textsf{PKE} from one-way functions and indistinguishability obfuscation in the quantum computation with classical communication (QCCC) setting.
one_liner: An oracle separation shows quantum public-key encryption with classical communication can exist without quantum one-way functions.
why_it_matters: The result reshapes the known assumption hierarchy for quantum cryptography and limits possible black-box constructions.

title: Quantum Evolution Networks Learn Long-Time Coherent Dynamics in Driven Spin Registers
abstract: Predicting and controlling driven quantum systems requires access to dynamics across physical parameters, initial states, and evolution times. A reusable neural model must capture this dependence while preserving unitary structure and maintaining accuracy over long-time coherent evolution. Here we introduce Quantum Evolution Networks (QENs), which map physical parameters and time to complete propagators for periodically driven three-spin registers. Shared networks learn unitary one-period propagators and compatible within-period paths, enabling predictions through known periodic composition without query-specific numerical integration. For transverse driving, the fifth-percentile fidelity, minimized over input states and sampled times, is 0.9947 over 24 periods on 256 held-out configurations. A leading-order analysis of spectrally resolved endpoint residuals predicts multicycle process error more accurately than quadratic or spectrum-averaged estimates. Interventions at matched single-period infidelity produce orders-of-magnitude differences in multicycle infidelity, demonstrating the importance of residual orientation. Compatible component replacements identify how endpoint and within-period approximations limit reconstruction accuracy. These results establish a reusable neural representation of the studied propagator families and connect its learned residual structure to its observed long-time reliability.
one_liner: Quantum Evolution Networks learn complete propagators for driven three-spin registers while retaining high long-time fidelity.
why_it_matters: Reusable propagator models could accelerate prediction and control across parameters without repeated numerical integration.

title: Bogoliubov Dynamics and Zitterbewegung in Optical Dirac Systems
abstract: We develop a bosonic Bogoliubov description of Zitterbewegung in time-dependent optical-Dirac systems. Within the optical-Dirac framework, the anomalous pair-creation and pair-annihilation terms of a bosonic Bogoliubov Hamiltonian correspond to couplings between the positive- and negative-frequency sectors, whose coherence underlies the Zitterbewegung response. When the constitutive parameters vary in time, the resulting moving-frame connection generates dynamical interbranch coupling and positive--negative-frequency coherence. Under periodic modulation, this coupling becomes resonant near $Ω\simeq2ω_0$, leading to parametric amplification of the coherence and consequently to an enhanced Zitterbewegung motion.
one_liner: A bosonic Bogoliubov model relates optical Zitterbewegung to coherence between positive- and negative-frequency sectors.
why_it_matters: Periodic modulation can resonantly amplify this coherence, offering a mechanism to enhance trembling motion in optical Dirac systems.

title: Performing a Quantum Subroutine Using Cluster States
abstract: Quantum subroutines, like their classical counterparts, serve as essential components of larger algorithms. They can be realized using gate based architectures or measurement based quantum computation (MBQC), where computation proceeds through adaptive measurements on highly entangled cluster states. In this work, we implement a phase oracle as a reusable subroutine within the MBQC framework using experimentally feasible cluster states. Unlike prior demonstrations of Grover's algorithm in MBQC that omit explicit oracle construction, our approach provides a transparent formulation of the oracle subroutine, including its measurement patterns, byproduct correlations, density-matrix simulations, and corresponding MBQC measurement circuits.
one_liner: An experimentally feasible cluster-state construction implements a reusable phase oracle as an explicit MBQC quantum subroutine.
why_it_matters: It makes oracle construction transparent for measurement-based algorithms and supports practical experimental realization.

title: Bose-Einstein condensate in a shell: nonlinear modes and symmetry breaking
abstract: The state of a quantum particle confined to a spherical surface is commonly described using spherical harmonics, which play a crucial role in solving many scientific problems featuring spherical symmetry. A mean-field description of a system of many interacting quantum particles confined to a spherical shell naturally leads to nonlinear generalizations of spherical harmonics. In this study, we analyze the emergence of such nonlinear modes in a shell-shaped Bose-Einstein condensate with both repulsive and attractive two-particle interactions. We find several classes of nonlinear modes. The first kind is an analytical continuation of a single spherical harmonic or their superposition for nonvanishing atom-atom interaction. Some of these solutions have planar counterparts in the form of Townes solitons and Townes vortices, which either appear stable even in the case of attractive interactions or can be stabilized by three-particle interactions. The second kind originate from symmetry-breaking bifurcations in the case of a repulsive interaction, and therefore have no linear counterparts. Moreover, we demonstrate the existence of a breathing dynamics that oscillates primarily between an unstable soliton and a stable vortex necklace state. Our findings show that the physics of nonlinear matter waves on curved geometries differs substantially from that in planar systems, suggesting the feasibility of observing these unconventional wave patterns experimentally.
one_liner: Shell-shaped Bose-Einstein condensates host nonlinear spherical modes, symmetry-broken states, and soliton-vortex breathing dynamics.
why_it_matters: It reveals curved-geometry matter-wave phenomena absent in planar condensates and suggests experimentally observable patterns.

title: Near-field maps of topological edge states of molecular aggregates
abstract: Self-assembled two-dimensional molecular aggregates provide a versatile platform for engineering excitonic states, including topologically nontrivial edge states. However, these edge-states are difficult to probe optically: they have weak far-field transition strengths, and far-field spectra do not reveal whether an excitation is localized at the edge. For an aggregate consisting of two sublattices of molecules with genuinely complex transition dipoles, we show that spatially resolved near-field spectroscopy encodes the full spatial structure of these states. The resulting near-field maps do not mirror the site populations, but instead exhibit strongly nonuniform, interference-like features. We demonstrate that a convolutional neural network can reconstruct the complex expansion coefficients of the eigenstates from these maps, and that this reconstruction is robust against substantial random noise.
one_liner: Near-field spectroscopy and a neural network recover complex topological edge-state amplitudes in molecular aggregates.
why_it_matters: The method enables spatially resolved detection of optically weak excitonic edge states despite substantial noise.

title: Fundamental bound on Wigner negativity generation from environmental collisions
abstract: Beyond quadratic potentials, classical evolution laws are typically thought to arise from quantum theory as an approximate description. Here we show that classical evolution laws can emerge exactly, provided the environment interacts with the system via collisions. We use this to derive an inequality that lower bounds the distribution of environmental momentum kicks by the absolute value of the Fourier transform of the potential. We show that violating this inequality is necessary and sufficient for a non-quadratic potential to generate negativity from the set of positive Wigner functions. A simple consequence of this is a lower bound on the heating rate for a quantum system to evolve effectively classically. We illustrate our results using the theory of a levitated nanoparticle subject to photon recoil and background gas collisions. We derive the strength of external potential needed to generate Wigner negative states in an optical tweezer and propose an experimental test of whether a nanoparticle in an optical lattice is operating in a non-classical regime.
one_liner: A necessary-and-sufficient bound links environmental momentum kicks to Wigner-negativity generation by nonquadratic potentials.
why_it_matters: It quantifies when collisional environments enforce classical dynamics and guides nonclassical levitated-particle experiments.

title: Finite Nonsignalling Resources Suffice to Simulate Entangled Qubits
abstract: A longstanding question in Bell nonlocality is whether finite-alphabet nonsignalling resources can reproduce the continuum of measurement correlations of partially entangled qubits. Here we resolve this problem by showing that every fixed pure two-qubit state admits an exact simulation of all local projective-measurement statistics using shared randomness and finitely many Popescu-Rohrlich (PR) boxes, without communication or postselection. The boxes operate in parallel, with a worst-case bound independent of the measurement settings: at most $128\cot^4θ$ calls for the Schmidt state $\cosθ|00\rangle+\sinθ|11\rangle$, $0<θ<π/4$. The key is an exact finite-selection method that reduces input-dependent continuous sampling to a choice from a fixed-length shared random list, implemented through a finite PR-box network. The construction extends to arbitrary mixed two-qubit states and local binary-outcome POVMs. This reveals a fundamental separation between the continuity of quantum measurement correlations and the alphabet size of the resources needed to simulate them, shedding light on the resource-theoretic structure of Bell nonlocality.
one_liner: Any fixed entangled two-qubit state can be simulated exactly for all projective measurements using finitely many parallel PR boxes.
why_it_matters: It separates continuous quantum correlations from the finite-alphabet nonsignalling resources sufficient to reproduce them.

title: Quantum theory of laser noise in coherent-scattering levitated optomechanics
abstract: State purity is a key resource for experimental tests of quantum mechanics with massive objects. Cavity cooling of a levitated nanoparticle via coherent scattering stands out as a strategy to prepare highly pure states of its roto-translational motion. In several cases, though, the performance of cooling by coherent scattering is limited by the classical fluctuations of the laser field. Here we present a quantum theory of coherent-scattering experiments which includes the effect of the laser amplitude and phase noise. We derive a master equation for the noise-averaged particle's dynamics, valid for both center-of-mass and rotational degrees of freedom, and quantify the cooling performance for different levels of noise in state-of-the-art experiments. We compute approximate analytical expressions for the laser-noise-induced heating rates and excess phonon number in both regimes of weak and strong optomechanical coupling. Moreover, our model can be applied to laser noise processes with generic power spectral densities and finite correlation times. This work offers a toolbox to quantify and optimize the state purity in coherent-scattering experiments, and opens new avenues towards the preparation of quantum states with levitated systems.
one_liner: A quantum model quantifies amplitude- and phase-noise heating in coherent-scattering cooling of levitated nanoparticles.
why_it_matters: It provides practical tools for optimizing motional state purity under realistic laser-noise spectra.

title: Revealing and Mitigating Transmittance and Reflectance Errors in Integrating-Sphere Characterization of High-Albedo Scattering Media
abstract: Accurate optical characterization of high-albedo scattering media is fundamentally limited by integrating-sphere measurement errors.
